messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Sign function?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Sign function?
messages.body_plain:
How does branching make this problem easier? It's more code than just throwing a fabs() and a sign function into the thing. And if gamma < 0, I'd still need to put its sign back into place, so the point is moot, no?

I haven't tried the cbrt function, but I'm not sure it'd make a difference.

Also, this is the exact parameterization used by Azzalini, it's well tested, and it performs well.
Attached are my derivations of the CP -> DP parameterization; heck, if the stan team wanted to encourage the use of the SN distribution, the CP parameterization is generally better and easier to understand. It's also got some benefits over the DP (stan's current method) when estimating models with some heterogeneity in skewness or variance; if you do regression on the location parameter (DP) with heterogeneity in variance or skewness, you /will/ get the 'wrong' answer, it'll be nonsensical. On CP this isn't so much an issue, because you're estimating means, not location parameters, and the model will be correct.  That is, conceptually, if you have a two-group scenario where the means are exactly equal, but they differ in variance, then the model will suggest the location parameters are very different (which is true, but probably irrelevant to your question, since location != expected value).

> > Nevertheless, it's a useful function. Sure, it can break some gradients, but it doesn't break the gradient of the one I'm working on.
> > It's purely a computational oddity.  The problem is parameterizing a skew-normal in terms of mean, sigma, and gamma, rather than the direct parameterization of xi, omega, and alpha. I've worked out how to do it, and it performs very well, but one part of it needs a sign function.

> >
> >     r = gamma/fabs(gamma)*(2*fabs(gamma)/(4-pi()))^(1.0/3.0); <- Here. The non-sign version has (2*gamma/(4-pi))^(1/3), but this produces only positive gammas, because negative ones result in NaN. This is conceptually nonsense, so you just use the abs value, then put the sign back on. This is how the author of the SN papers reparameterized the model, to avoid a likelihood oddity at alpha=0, and to reduce correlation of parameters. In stan, this method works excellently, but there is no sign function. This is a useful case of the sign function, and it doesn't break the gradient; if anything, it actually fixes the gradient (without this method, you get NaN and 1000s of divergences. With the method, 0 errors, 0 divergences).

messages.subject: clarification/question about LOO and pareto's K
messages.subject_clean: clarification/question about LOO and pareto's K
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I'd like to make sure that my understanding of LOOic and pareto's K is correct so that I can really use this method to compare my multiple models.

According to the manual, looic estimate from the loo package is 2*elpd_loo, elpd_loo is the expected log pointwise predictive density. In plain English, (elpd_loo) expected log pointwise predictive density is the probability to predict the ith data point with current data set without the ith data point. So it is expressed as eqn (4) and (5) <http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/unpublished/loo_stan.pdf> of Vehtari A., Gelman A., and Gabry J. 2016. This is Bayesian because we are using the posterior probability of parameters and the probability of the ith data given the estimated parameters to calculate elpd_loo. In other words, looic is a measure of how good this model is to fit the data.

The loo package uses a Pareto-smoothed importance sampling (PSIS) method to estimate the expected log pointwise predictive density. In this method, there is a critical parameter K (Pareto's K) for each data point to judge whether this data point being accurately predicted. If this point is not being predicted accurately (low probability I guess??), the Pareto's K would be large. According to the manual, large Pareto's K (>0.7) means the model posterior would be too different if one data point is being removed. This suggest that the model is not capturing the data well (i.e. some data points with high K are highly influential and not being considered by the model).
Following this logic, I can not trust the looic estimate if most (say>80%) of the Pareto's K is higher than 0.7.

To deal with the issue with high Pareto's K, one can either change the model structure or transform the data. Are there any other solutions?

Am I understanding the loo and interpreting it correctly?
Thank you for your help!
OSCAR

Nothing. I was more taken back by the notion that the sign function is intentionally not implemented, even though there are instances where the sign function would be needed. It just seems odd to me; there are all sorts of ways people could break the continuity of the gradient using the functions already implemented, why disallow a legitimate mathematical function purely because it /could/ break continuity?

I actually like your solution better because I x/|x| isn't defined at 0, but your method is, I think.

> > On Apr 1, 2017, at 1:08 PM, Stephen Martin <hwki...@gmail.com> wrote:

> > Attached are my derivations of the CP -> DP parameterization; heck, if the stan team wanted to encourage the use of the SN distribution, the CP parameterization is generally better and easier to understand. It's also got some benefits over the DP (stan's current method) when estimating models with some heterogeneity in skewness or variance; if you do regression on the location parameter (DP) with heterogeneity in variance or skewness, you /will/ get the 'wrong' answer, it'll be nonsensical. On CP this isn't so much an issue, because you're estimating means, not location parameters, and the model will be correct.  That is, conceptually, if you have a two-group scenario where the means are exactly equal, but they differ in variance, then the model will suggest the location parameters are very different (which is true, but probably irrelevant to your question, since location != expected value).

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Sign function?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Sign function?
messages.body_plain:
First, rather than taking signum(x) and then using it as
a multiplicand, it's much more effcient to branch in Stan
because branching doesn't add anything to the expression graph.
That's the real reason we don't have it.  Branching on
parameters also breaks differentiability and we should be
raising warnings when users try it.

The issue we have with the built-ins is that we can put
warnings in the manual, but users won't see those.  We could
have every use of such a function raise a warning and we
might in the future (like warnings on branching on parameters).

We have a bunch of step-like functions which break
differentiability and just have warnings next to them in
the manual.  The functions we do supply are the ones that are
in the C++ standard library, and they have C++ signatures like:

  double floor(double);

C++ allows double values to be assigned to integers (up to
user to deal with overflow), but Stan doesn't.  That's the
built-in limitation in Stan and I did that intentionally so
as to preserve distinct typing.

The function we're seriously missing is the round to integer
function.  Most examples we've seen of users who want to use
it would be breaking our samplers, so we're reluctant.  We might
just build in some interpolation functions.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: clarification/question about LOO and pareto's K
messages.subject_clean: clarification/question about LOO and pareto's K
messages.body_plain:
Hi Oscar,

On Sunday, April 2, 2017 at 12:21:48 AM UTC+3, Chang Feng Hsun wrote:
> According to the manual, looic estimate from the loo package is 2*elpd_loo, elpd_loo is the expected log pointwise predictive density.

looic is -2*elpd and thus they are eqaul up to this historically used multiplier -2. I prefer elpd scale.

> In plain English, (elpd_loo) expected log pointwise predictive density is the probability to predict the ith data point with current data set without the ith data point.

Be more careful with the difference between probability density and probability. If the predicted observations are discrete, then we have probabilities. I f the predicted observations are continuous we have densities. Otherwise correct.

> So it is expressed as eqn (4) and (5) <http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/unpublished/loo_stan.pdf> of Vehtari A., Gelman A., and Gabry J. 2016. This is Bayesian because we are using the posterior probability of parameters and the probability of the ith data given the estimated parameters to calculate elpd_loo.

It's Bayesian because we integrate over the the posterior distribution to get the predictive distribution (which can be continuous or discrete), and we are estimating the predictive performance of the predictive distribution.

> In other words, looic is a measure of how good this model is to fit the data.

It's a measure of how good the model is predicting future data assuming that the future data comes from the same distribution as the observed data.

>
> The loo package uses a Pareto-smoothed importance sampling (PSIS) method to estimate the expected log pointwise predictive density. In this method, there is a critical parameter K (Pareto's K) for each data point to judge whether this data point being accurately predicted. If this point is not being predicted accurately (low probability I guess??),

Not necessarily low probability...

> the Pareto's K would be large. According to the manual, large Pareto's K (>0.7) means the model posterior would be too different if one data point is being removed.

but more accurately this what you wrote, that is, the full data posterior is too different compared to leave-one-out posterior for the importance sampling to work well.

> This suggest that the model is not capturing the data well (i.e. some data points with high K are highly influential and not being considered by the model).

This suggests that there can be a significant model misspecification (and some data points are considered too much). But there also cases where the model can be true one (just with unknown parameters), but still the full posterior and loo-posterior can be too different for the importance sampling to work well. This is common, for example, in case of flexible latent variable models such as Gaussian processes.

> Following this logic, I can not trust the looic estimate if most (say>80%) of the Pareto's K is higher than 0.7.

In this case, you can not trust elpd (or looic) estimate computed with the importance sampling.

>
> To deal with the issue with high Pareto's K, one can either change the model structure or transform the data. Are there any other solutions?

You can use k-fold-CV to compute corresponding elpd (or looic), which you can trust more, because it's not using the importance sampling.

Aki

>
> Am I understanding the loo and interpreting it correctly?
> Thank you for your help!
> OSCAR

Hi all,

I've been working on putting together a case study for estimating
ultimate losses from a book of insurance business - an alternative to
the more traditional 'Chain Ladder' methods.

I have a public github repo with the data and the Rmarkdown in this repo:

https://github.com/kaybenleroll/stancasestudy_losscurves

I imagine I may need to make a few edits etc, but at this point I am a
bit too close to it, so happy to let others make some comments. I'm
also happy to move this into the example-models repo if that is a
better location for it.

Anyway, let me know if this is of interest, as I have ideas for
iterating further on these case studies if wanted, as I'll be working
on this stuff anyway.

--
Mick Cooney
mickc...@gmail.com

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Using external software inside Stan
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Using external software inside Stan
messages.body_plain:
It's party hat time!

Got a really simple exampled coded up (using the cmdStan stuff BGoodrich recommended). Here's the direct comparison from what I had to Stan (model here: https://github.com/bbbales2/modal_cpp/blob/master/test.stan):

Parameter     HMC (100 samples)  Stan (100 samples), posteriors shown as mean +- 1 standard deviation
c11           1.7 +- 0.019       1.7 +- 0.017
a             1.0 +- 0.0024      1.0 +- 0.0024
c44           0.45 +- 0.00078    0.45 +- 0.0007
sigma         0.43 +- 0.062      0.44 +- 0.069

I told Gmail to use a fixed space font so hopefully that worked.

Not exactly a whole lot of samples (my forward model is pretty slow [200ms/eval] and I wanted to see results), and I made the problem really easy by giving Stan good guesses (the HMC had pretty good guesses too), but woohoo anyway! I'll need to add a few things to put the full mechanics model in and test some harder problems (and see if I can get away without the guesses) but it looks like we have liftoff!

To get everything working, I needed to define a template specialization of my mechanics function that took in vars for parameters as well as one that took doubles. The linker wanted a version of each (code here: https://github.com/bbbales2/modal_cpp/blob/master/stan_mech.hpp).

Does NUTS use the 2nd version (the non-var specialization)? I added some debug print statements and it looks like the variational inference code uses it.

I'll follow up again after I've done more tests and attach a write up.

Thanks folks! This is gonna be super useful.

Ben

Running the tests in ‘tests/testthat.R’ failed.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Gamma reparametrization into mode / sd - Question on jacobian transformation
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Gamma reparametrization into mode / sd - Question on jacobian transformation
messages.body_plain:
You need the Jacobian of the f:R^2 -> R^2 function

  f(alpha, beta) = sqrt(alpha / beta^2),  (alpha - 1) / beta

if you're going to declare alpha and beta as parameters and
put a prior on sqrt(alpha / beta^2) and (alpha - 1) / beta.
I'd also recommend sqrt(alpha) / beta as it does less arithmetic
and should also be more stable for small beta.

Alternatively, you can declare a parameter

  vector[N] sqrt_alpha_over_beta;

and define

  sqrt_alpha_over_beta ~ ...

and then derive the inverse of f to get alpha and beta back.
Then you won't need a Jacobian as you're putting the distribution
right on the parameter.

- Bob

> bet[Species[n]]' + B

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Explicitly Correlated Parameters
messages.body_plain:
I appreciate the reply Bob.

On Fri, Mar 31, 2017 at 2:55 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

> What I'm saying is that if you have multiple intercepts (say one
> global one and then group-level intercepts), then you only get
> identification through the prior because you can add to the global
> intercept and subtract from the group intercepts and get the same
> value.  Usually this is mitigated with using n-1 intercepts if
> there are n groups and pinning one to zero.

In my case, I didn't have a global intercept. Just group-level intercepts. I've made the above mistake before.

> You're making a normal-normal model of B_n in the first case and a normal
> model in the second case.  I don't think you want to do the former unless
> you have some kind of explicit measurement-error model, and even then, it's
> usually on the data side.

I was a little confused by this. The B_n's are the varying coefficients, not the actual data. So in the former, I have correlated coefficients B_n, and then I gave the mean of the B_n a prior. You seem to be saying in other places that this is the correct approach.

> Yup, challenging, but usually worth the effort in model understanding and
> peace of mind that your code works.

One thing I had realized from this was that when I used actual OLS intercepts/slopes/standard errors and simulated the errors as normal, it almost always resulted in very low N_eff. But when I replaced the empirical intercept distribution with some simpler distribution, the N_eff were almost always more reasonable. I tried a lot of options, but the least disruptive thing I did was get the percent ranks of the intercepts and convert it into a normal distribution. So it was very similar, except didn't have the fat tails. This got like 250/1000 N_eff, which was substantially better than the actual intercepts.

However, when I tried to adjust the Stan code (a version not including the correlated parameters, but similar) to include a t distribution for the intercepts, the posterior distribution of the degrees of freedom parameter didn't really change much from the prior and the final results weren't really any different. I was a little disappointed after that.

This approach was also interesting because it made clear how non-normal the joint distribution of the intercepts and slopes was. The intercepts were t distributed and the slopes (and standard errors) were log normally distributed. There probably also was some sort of non-normal dependence between the two. Even when I tried regressing the intercepts against the slopes and errors and including t errors in them, the simulated plots of the intercepts and slopes looked different from the empirical ones.

Suffice it to say, I think the non-normality of the parameters is what is driving my problem. At this point, I don't see how to resolve it other than removing the varying intercepts (I was actually able to use intercepts that vary by larger groups, just not the lowest level ones).

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Explicitly Correlated Parameters
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Explicitly Correlated Parameters
messages.body_plain:
Right now I'm playing around with the distribution on the standard deviation on the intercept as that seems like a key issue. It seems biased too low. So instead of half normal, I'm trying a normal parameter (chosen carefully!) that's transformed to log normal. I'm also curious to see if switching the normal for cauchy helps.

One idea I just had that I hadn't considered before is that I didn't make the problem simple enough when I was trying to identify the problem. I could remove the independent variable and slopes completely and re-estimate.

On Mon, Apr 3, 2017 at 1:53 PM, John Hall <john.mic...@gmail.com> wrote:
> I appreciate the reply Bob.
>
> On Fri, Mar 31, 2017 at 2:55 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> > What I'm saying is that if you have multiple intercepts (say one
> > global one and then group-level intercepts), then you only get
> > identification through the prior because you can add to the global
> > intercept and subtract from the group intercepts and get the same
> > value.  Usually this is mitigated with using n-1 intercepts if
> > there are n groups and pinning one to zero.
>
> In my case, I didn't have a global intercept. Just group-level intercepts. I've made the above mistake before.
>
> > You're making a normal-normal model of B_n in the first case and a normal
> > model in the second case.  I don't think you want to do the former unless
> > you have some kind of explicit measurement-error model, and even then, it's
> > usually on the data side.
>
> I was a little confused by this. The B_n's are the varying coefficients, not the actual data. So in the former, I have correlated coefficients B_n, and then I gave the mean of the B_n a prior. You seem to be saying in other places that this is the correct approach.
>
> > Yup, challenging, but usually worth the effort in model understanding and
> > peace of mind that your code works.
>
> One thing I had realized from this was that when I used actual OLS intercepts/slopes/standard errors and simulated the errors as normal, it almost always resulted in very low N_eff. But when I replaced the empirical intercept distribution with some simpler distribution, the N_eff were almost always more reasonable. I tried a lot of options, but the least disruptive thing I did was get the percent ranks of the intercepts and convert it into a normal distribution. So it was very similar, except didn't have the fat tails. This got like 250/1000 N_eff, which was substantially better than the actual intercepts.
>
> However, when I tried to adjust the Stan code (a version not including the correlated parameters, but similar) to include a t distribution for the intercepts, the posterior distribution of the degrees of freedom parameter didn't really change much from the prior and the final results weren't really any different. I was a little disappointed after that.
>
> This approach was also interesting because it made clear how non-normal the joint distribution of the intercepts and slopes was. The intercepts were t distributed and the slopes (and standard errors) were log normally distributed. There probably also was some sort of non-normal dependence between the two. Even when I tried regressing the intercepts against the slopes and errors and including t errors in them, the simulated plots of the intercepts and slopes looked different from the empirical ones.
>
> Suffice it to say, I think the non-normality of the parameters is what is driving my problem. At this point, I don't see how to resolve it other than removing the varying intercepts (I was actually able to use intercepts that vary by larger groups, just not the lowest level ones).
>

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Case Study on Loss Reserving in Insurance
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Case Study on Loss Reserving in Insurance
messages.body_plain:
On 3 April 2017 at 07:30, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> That looks great.  Does anyone who knows anything about
> R or insurance want to take a look?  I can look it over and
> give you feedback on the Stan, but that's about it.

Happy to get any feedback people are willing to give.

>
> One thing I noticed off the bat is that your functions
>
>   real growth_factor_loglogistic(real t, real omega, real theta) {
>     real factor;
>
>     factor = ((t^omega) / (t^omega + theta^omega));
>
>     return(factor);
>   }
>
> are more easily written as one-liners
>
>
>   real growth_factor_loglogistic(real t, real omega, real theta) {
>     return (t^omega) / (t^omega + theta^omega);
>   }
>
> but it's better not to repeat computations for efficiency, so
> that should be:
>
>
>   real growth_factor_loglogistic(real t, real omega, real theta) {
>     real pow_t_omega = t^omega;
>     return pow_t_omega / (pow_t_omega + theta^omega);
>   }
>
>
> You don't need the parens around the return or extra parens
> for assignment.

Yep, no problem. I wasn't really thinking about speed as the data is
very sparse and small, but it is good to get into good habits as
quickly as possible.

>
> This:
>
> for(i in 1:n_data) {
>     loss[i] ~ normal(loss_mean[cohort_id[i], t_idx[i]],
>                      premium[cohort_id[i]] * loss_sd);
> }
>
> would be more efficient vectorized:
>
>   vector[n_data] lm;
>   for (i in 1:n_data)
>     lm[i] = loss_mean[cohort_id[i], t_idx[i]];
>   loss ~ normal(loss_mean, loss_sd * premium[cohort_id]);
>
> where premium needs to be a vector.  It's actually even more efficient
> if size(premium) << n_data to just use
>
>   (loss_sd * premium)[cohort_id]
>
> so the multiplication applies to the smaller vector.
>

Okay, need to refactor a little to get that done, but should be a problem.

> This
>
> for(i in 1:n_cohort) {
>     for(j in 1:n_time) {
>       loss_sample[i, j] = LR[i] * premium[i] * gf[t_idx[j]];
>       step_ratio [i, j] = 1.0;
>     }
>   }
>
> can also be vectorized in the inner loop:
>
> for (i in 1:n_cohort)
>   loss_sample[i] = LR[i] * premium[i] * gf[t_idx];
>
> and that variable step_ratio gets defined as 1 and then most
> of the values redefined.  You can use rep_vector(1.0, N) and
> rep_row_vector(1.0, N) to create vectors of row vectors filled with
> the value 1.
>
> loss_mean is also getting assigned and reassigned.  the initial
> assignments can be filled, but better even to not redundantly
> assign.
>

Initially, I didn't initialise step_ratio at all, but that didn't work
out too well. To initialise a matrix, is there a way to do it
directly, as I kept getting mismatches when trying to use rep_vector
and rep_row_vector. Am I better tweaking the types so that step_ratio
is instead a matrix of row or column vectors or something like that?

> This can also be vectorized:
>
>  for(i in 1:n_cohort) {
>       tempmin[i] = LR[i];
>       tempmax[i] = LR[i];
>     }
>
> tempmin = LR;
> tempmax = LR;
>
> but you don't need to do that assignment before taking min and
> max---none of the operations in Stan modify their arguments.
>

Ah, okay, looking at it again, not sure what I was thinking there, I
think I had it originally for a more compex model that needed that,
and forgot I could simplify further.

Will change that too.

> I don't know if you were getting divergent translations, but it
> can be useful to use the non-centered parameterization for coefficients
> with hierarchical priors.
>
>
>   real<lower=0> LR[n_cohort];
>
>   real mu_LR;
>   real<lower=0> sd_LR;
>
>
>   LR ~ lognormal(mu_LR, sd_LR);
>
> It's a little trickier with lognormals than normals, but the idea's
> the same.
>

No divergent transitions so far, so I haven't had to look at using
NCP, but I imagine this type of thing will be needed once I start
looking at multiple insurers and multiple LOB.

> Finally, you can compress this:
>
>  if(growthmodel_id == 1) {
>       gf[i] = growth_factor_weibull    (t_value[i], omega, theta);
>     } else {
>       gf[i] = growth_factor_loglogistic(t_value[i], omega, theta);
>     }
>
> to just
>
> gf[i] = growthmodel_id == 1
>       ? growth_factor_weibull(t_value[i], omega, theta)
>       : growth_factor_loglogistic(t_value[i], omega, theta);
>
> The conditional operator only evaluates its arguments if the
> branch evaluates to true.
>

WIll do, makes it much easier to read. I often forget about the '?:' operator.

Thanks for all that Bob, how does the text and the graphs read? I had
more diagnostics for the later sections but thought it may have been
too much and a selection of the diagnostics was enough at that point
as it is more readable this way.

I'm also conscious that there may be too many visualisations and not
enough explanatory text in this though, so if anyone feels I need to
flesh this out further, please let me know.

I have a few other iiterations of this model planned, so was going to
work on that once people are happy with this simple version.

--
Mick Cooney
mickc...@gmail.com

> On Apr 3, 2017, at 5:36 PM, John Hall <john.mic...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Right now I'm playing around with the distribution on the standard deviation on the intercept as that seems like a key issue. It seems biased too low. So instead of half normal, I'm trying a normal parameter (chosen carefully!) that's transformed to log normal. I'm also curious to see if switching the normal for cauchy helps.

How are you assessing bias?  Are you talking about the posterior
mean as an estimate of the parameter?  I'd recommend looking at posterior
interval coverage for simulated data --- that'll let you assess whether
your model's coded properly.  Then it's a different matter to asses whether
it matches some real data set.

> One idea I just had that I hadn't considered before is that I didn't make the problem simple enough when I was trying to identify the problem. I could remove the independent variable and slopes completely and re-estimate.

This is a key step in debugging.  Isolate the problem in
a reproducible example that is as simple as possible.  Often
by the time you've done that, the debugging job is done.

This is one of the main reasons we suggest building models
up from simpler models wherever possible.  It's tedious to
build up one feature at a time, but at least you know exactly
where the problem comes from when it arises.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Models with an analytic solution
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Models with an analytic solution
messages.body_plain:
Two things we could do to speed things up:

1.  Recognize conjugacy and marginalize out intermediate
parameters.  Sufficient statistics can also be calculated
in a lot of cases.  I don't see how to make this automatic,
but there's a lot we could provide in the way of built-in
special functions that could be used to speedup particular
models without much work.

2.  Provide built-in functions for common models with
analytic gradients---I got a 3.5 x speedup for logistic
regression doing this, so we're going to want to roll out
all the basic GLMs this way.

- Bob

> On Mar 27, 2017, at 9:34 AM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> On Monday, March 27, 2017 at 9:25:26 AM UTC-4, Jing Dong wrote:
> For models with an analytic solution, does STAN compute the posterior estimates analytically or still use MCMC?
>
> MCMC. The Stan language has almost no logic capabilities and cannot infer when there is an analytical solution.
>
> May I be less worried about the convergence of these models?
>
> No, but convergence is rarely a problem for Stan. Mixing can be a problem but if the model is simple enough to have an analytical solution, then NUTS will probably mix really quickly.
>
> Ben
>

> On Apr 4, 2017, at 7:59 AM, Mick Cooney <mickc...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> On 3 April 2017 at 07:30, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>> That looks great.  Does anyone who knows anything about
>> R or insurance want to take a look?  I can look it over and

>
> Happy to get any feedback people are willing to give.
>
>>
>> One thing I noticed off the bat is that your functions
>>
>>  real growth_factor_loglogistic(real t, real omega, real theta) {
>>    real factor;
>>
>>    factor = ((t^omega) / (t^omega + theta^omega));
>>
>>    return(factor);
>>  }
>>
>> are more easily written as one-liners
>>
>>
>>  real growth_factor_loglogistic(real t, real omega, real theta) {
>>    return (t^omega) / (t^omega + theta^omega);
>>  }
>>
>> but it's better not to repeat computations for efficiency, so
>> that should be:
>>
>>
>>  real growth_factor_loglogistic(real t, real omega, real theta) {
>>    real pow_t_omega = t^omega;
>>    return pow_t_omega / (pow_t_omega + theta^omega);
>>  }
>>
>>
>> You don't need the parens around the return or extra parens
>> for assignment.
>
> Yep, no problem. I wasn't really thinking about speed as the data is
> very sparse and small, but it is good to get into good habits as
> quickly as possible.
>
>>
>> This:
>>
>> for(i in 1:n_data) {
>>    loss[i] ~ normal(loss_mean[cohort_id[i], t_idx[i]],
>>                     premium[cohort_id[i]] * loss_sd);
>> }
>>
>> would be more efficient vectorized:
>>
>>  vector[n_data] lm;
>>  for (i in 1:n_data)
>>    lm[i] = loss_mean[cohort_id[i], t_idx[i]];
>>  loss ~ normal(loss_mean, loss_sd * premium[cohort_id]);
>>
>> where premium needs to be a vector.  It's actually even more efficient
>> if size(premium) << n_data to just use
>>
>>  (loss_sd * premium)[cohort_id]
>>
>> so the multiplication applies to the smaller vector.
>>
>
> Okay, need to refactor a little to get that done, but should be a problem.
>
>
>> This
>>
>> for(i in 1:n_cohort) {
>>    for(j in 1:n_time) {
>>      loss_sample[i, j] = LR[i] * premium[i] * gf[t_idx[j]];
>>      step_ratio [i, j] = 1.0;
>>    }
>>  }
>>
>> can also be vectorized in the inner loop:
>>
>> for (i in 1:n_cohort)
>>  loss_sample[i] = LR[i] * premium[i] * gf[t_idx];
>>
>> and that variable step_ratio gets defined as 1 and then most
>> of the values redefined.  You can use rep_vector(1.0, N) and
>> rep_row_vector(1.0, N) to create vectors of row vectors filled with
>> the value 1.
>>
>> loss_mean is also getting assigned and reassigned.  the initial
>> assignments can be filled, but better even to not redundantly
>> assign.
>>
>
> Initially, I didn't initialise step_ratio at all, but that didn't work
> out too well. To initialise a matrix, is there a way to do it
> directly, as I kept getting mismatches when trying to use rep_vector
> and rep_row_vector. Am I better tweaking the types so that step_ratio
> is instead a matrix of row or column vectors or something like that?
>
>> This can also be vectorized:
>>
>> for(i in 1:n_cohort) {
>>      tempmin[i] = LR[i];
>>      tempmax[i] = LR[i];
>>    }
>>
>> tempmin = LR;
>> tempmax = LR;
>>
>> but you don't need to do that assignment before taking min and
>> max---none of the operations in Stan modify their arguments.
>>
>
> Ah, okay, looking at it again, not sure what I was thinking there, I
> think I had it originally for a more compex model that needed that,
> and forgot I could simplify further.
>
> Will change that too.
>
>
>> I don't know if you were getting divergent translations, but it
>> can be useful to use the non-centered parameterization for coefficients
>> with hierarchical priors.
>>
>>
>>  real<lower=0> LR[n_cohort];
>>
>>  real mu_LR;
>>  real<lower=0> sd_LR;
>>
>>
>>  LR ~ lognormal(mu_LR, sd_LR);
>>
>> It's a little trickier with lognormals than normals, but the idea's
>> the same.
>>
>
> No divergent transitions so far, so I haven't had to look at using
> NCP, but I imagine this type of thing will be needed once I start
> looking at multiple insurers and multiple LOB.
>
>
>> Finally, you can compress this:
>>
>> if(growthmodel_id == 1) {
>>      gf[i] = growth_factor_weibull    (t_value[i], omega, theta);
>>    } else {
>>      gf[i] = growth_factor_loglogistic(t_value[i], omega, theta);
>>    }
>>
>> to just

>>      ? growth_factor_weibull(t_value[i], omega, theta)

messages.body_plain:
As to the text it would have helped me to lay the data
out more exactly up front.  It's the usual bottleneck I have
in getting started understanding these notebooks.

Also, why are we working with two different growth curves?
Are we going to evaluate models involving one versus the other?

As to comparisons, I'd prefer to see more posterior predictive
checks or fake-data fit checks and fewer (if any) traceplots or
R-hat plots.  You can just mention they're all within expected
tolerances (R-hat << 1.05 for multiple diffuse initializations
and high enough n_eff for whatever your application is) and
that will cut down on a lot of the clutter.

Captions on figures help a lot if I just want to browse.

You never mention the references in the text.  If these
models are all well known, a pointer up front to the textbook
and a hint that you'll use the same terminology is a great
help.

I find overlaid histograms hard to decode, but Michael really
likes them---I see you're using a clever contrastive scheme, which
is an improvement, but I still find it hard to read.

- Bob

> On Apr 4, 2017, at 7:59 AM, Mick Cooney <mickc...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> On 3 April 2017 at 07:30, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>> That looks great.  Does anyone who knows anything about
>> R or insurance want to take a look?  I can look it over and
>> give you feedback on the Stan, but that's about it.
>
> Happy to get any feedback people are willing to give.
>
>>
>> One thing I noticed off the bat is that your functions
>>
>>  real growth_factor_loglogistic(real t, real omega, real theta) {
>>    real factor;
>>
>>    factor = ((t^omega) / (t^omega + theta^omega));
>>
>>    return(factor);
>>  }
>>
>> are more easily written as one-liners
>>
>>
>>  real growth_factor_loglogistic(real t, real omega, real theta) {
>>    return (t^omega) / (t^omega + theta^omega);
>>  }
>>
>> but it's better not to repeat computations for efficiency, so
>> that should be:
>>
>>
>>  real growth_factor_loglogistic(real t, real omega, real theta) {
>>    real pow_t_omega = t^omega;
>>    return pow_t_omega / (pow_t_omega + theta^omega);
>>  }
>>
>>
>> You don't need the parens around the return or extra parens
>> for assignment.
>
> Yep, no problem. I wasn't really thinking about speed as the data is
> very sparse and small, but it is good to get into good habits as
> quickly as possible.
>
>>
>> This:
>>
>> for(i in 1:n_data) {
>>    loss[i] ~ normal(loss_mean[cohort_id[i], t_idx[i]],
>>                     premium[cohort_id[i]] * loss_sd);
>> }
>>
>> would be more efficient vectorized:
>>
>>  vector[n_data] lm;
>>  for (i in 1:n_data)
>>    lm[i] = loss_mean[cohort_id[i], t_idx[i]];
>>  loss ~ normal(loss_mean, loss_sd * premium[cohort_id]);
>>
>> where premium needs to be a vector.  It's actually even more efficient
>> if size(premium) << n_data to just use
>>
>>  (loss_sd * premium)[cohort_id]
>>
>> so the multiplication applies to the smaller vector.
>>
>
> Okay, need to refactor a little to get that done, but should be a problem.
>
>
>> This
>>
>> for(i in 1:n_cohort) {
>>    for(j in 1:n_time) {
>>      loss_sample[i, j] = LR[i] * premium[i] * gf[t_idx[j]];
>>      step_ratio [i, j] = 1.0;
>>    }
>>  }
>>
>> can also be vectorized in the inner loop:
>>
>> for (i in 1:n_cohort)
>>  loss_sample[i] = LR[i] * premium[i] * gf[t_idx];
>>
>> and that variable step_ratio gets defined as 1 and then most
>> of the values redefined.  You can use rep_vector(1.0, N) and
>> rep_row_vector(1.0, N) to create vectors of row vectors filled with
>> the value 1.
>>
>> loss_mean is also getting assigned and reassigned.  the initial
>> assignments can be filled, but better even to not redundantly
>> assign.
>>
>
> Initially, I didn't initialise step_ratio at all, but that didn't work
> out too well. To initialise a matrix, is there a way to do it
> directly, as I kept getting mismatches when trying to use rep_vector
> and rep_row_vector. Am I better tweaking the types so that step_ratio
> is instead a matrix of row or column vectors or something like that?
>
>> This can also be vectorized:
>>
>> for(i in 1:n_cohort) {
>>      tempmin[i] = LR[i];
>>      tempmax[i] = LR[i];
>>    }
>>
>> tempmin = LR;
>> tempmax = LR;
>>
>> but you don't need to do that assignment before taking min and
>> max---none of the operations in Stan modify their arguments.
>>
>
> Ah, okay, looking at it again, not sure what I was thinking there, I
> think I had it originally for a more compex model that needed that,
> and forgot I could simplify further.
>
> Will change that too.
>
>
>> I don't know if you were getting divergent translations, but it
>> can be useful to use the non-centered parameterization for coefficients
>> with hierarchical priors.
>>
>>
>>  real<lower=0> LR[n_cohort];
>>
>>  real mu_LR;
>>  real<lower=0> sd_LR;
>>
>>
>>  LR ~ lognormal(mu_LR, sd_LR);
>>
>> It's a little trickier with lognormals than normals, but the idea's
>> the same.
>>
>
> No divergent transitions so far, so I haven't had to look at using
> NCP, but I imagine this type of thing will be needed once I start
> looking at multiple insurers and multiple LOB.
>
>
>> Finally, you can compress this:
>>
>> if(growthmodel_id == 1) {
>>      gf[i] = growth_factor_weibull    (t_value[i], omega, theta);
>>    } else {
>>      gf[i] = growth_factor_loglogistic(t_value[i], omega, theta);
>>    }
>>
>> to just
>>
>> gf[i] = growthmodel_id == 1
>>      ? growth_factor_weibull(t_value[i], omega, theta)
>>      : growth_factor_loglogistic(t_value[i], omega, theta);
>>
>> The conditional operator only evaluates its arguments if the
>> branch evaluates to true.
>>
>
> WIll do, makes it much easier to read. I often forget about the '?:' operator.
>
>
> Thanks for all that Bob, how does the text and the graphs read? I had
> more diagnostics for the later sections but thought it may have been
> too much and a selection of the diagnostics was enough at that point
> as it is more readable this way.
>
> I'm also conscious that there may be too many visualisations and not
> enough explanatory text in this though, so if anyone feels I need to
> flesh this out further, please let me know.
>
> I have a few other iiterations of this model planned, so was going to
> work on that once people are happy with this simple version.
>
> --
> Mick Cooney
> mickc...@gmail.com

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Cutpoint Priors
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Cutpoint Priors
messages.body_plain:
I am running an IRT/ordered categorical logistic model and using a weakly informative normal prior on the differences between cutpoints. I'm also getting a lot (i.e., about 10) warnings about improper values (negative values and infinity) for the cutpoints coming from the ordered_logistic function.

So here's a question -- should the ordered vector type naturally handle the fact that the normal prior is being put over the differences between cutpoints, i.e. by transforming to the unconstrained scale such that the normal prior is really a half-normal prior? Or should the normal prior be explicitly truncated at zero? Or, would it be better to use an exponential prior given that all values below zero are meaningless for ordered cutpoint differences?

I can post some data if y'all want to see it.

Thanks much for any advice,

Bob

On Wednesday, March 15, 2017 at 7:48:00 PM UTC-4, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> My intuition is that with N data points with 0 inside a particular bin, that the estimated bin width would be of order 1/N.  But I guess I should do an experiment.
>
> Yes, a gamma prior with shape parameter 2 will get the point estimate away from 0 (as in this paper:  http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/chung_etal_Pmetrika2013.pdf ).  I luuuvv this idea but it's all about point estimation.  I don't like it for full Bayes.
>
> Again, I guess it's time for some experiments.  Also it's interesting the point that you're making about constraints, as this also came up in my rounded-data example.  It's making me wonder if we need to think again about our automatic transformations to the unconstrained scale.
>
> A
>
> > On Mar 15, 2017, at 7:41 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> >
> > Yup, understood.  The MLE will actually collapse the boundaries
> > into each other if there's no data, whereas the Bayesian one
> > will never get there.
> >
> > Now we're just guessing how close the cut points will go
> > to each other in some of the posterior draws, which will
> > depend on the prior and how much data there is in the other
> > bins.  I haven't fit one of these in a while, so I may be
> > misremembering how bad the numerical issues will be.
> > Either way, the distance on the unconstrained scale needs
> > to go to -infinity to get it exponentiation to zero, so it
> > can cause issues if you get lots of data in the other bins.
> >
> > Of course, instead of a uniform on the inter-cut-point distances,
> > you can use something that avoids zero like a gamma with the
> > appropriate params.
> >
> > - Bob
> >
> >> On Mar 15, 2017, at 6:10 PM, Andrew Gelman <Gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
> >>
> >> No, that's not what I meant.  If you have uniform priors on the distances between the cutpoints, and you have a bit of data, then your posterior won't be collapsed near 1e-10 or even near 0.001.  That sort of collapsing behavior can occur with point estimates, and it can occur with hierarchical models (the "funnel") but it should not hold with flat priors.  If you happen to have zero data in some cells, maybe you'll get the difference between cutpoints to be estimated at 0.01 or something like that.
> >> A
> >>
> >>> On Mar 15, 2017, at 2:43 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> >>>
> >>> In theory, you won't ever get exactly collapsed cut points
> >>> in the posterior, but that doesn't mean that in practice you
> >>> won't get close enough to cause underflow and other problems.
> >>>
> >>> Same as if you start drawing theta ~ beta(1e-10, 1e-10).  Sure,
> >>> you shouldn't draw theta = 0 or theta = 1 in theory, but that's
> >>> what's going to happen with floating point arithmetic on computers.
> >>> You can get around that problem with just a little stronger prior.
> >>>
> >>> - Bob
> >>>
> >>>> On Mar 13, 2017, at 5:59 PM, Andrew Gelman <Gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
> >>>>
> >>>> Collapse if cutpoints can occur with point estimation but should not occur with full Bayes.
> >>>>
> >>>>> On Mar 13, 2017, at 3:47 PM, Tobias Konitzer <tobias....@gmail.com> wrote:
> >>>>>
> >>>>> I am wondering how to derive cut-points with only using prior counts in the different categories, but no information from the data other than that. It sounds like Bob's approach above does this, but how do I go from K (assuming K= number of categories) prior probabilities to K-1 cut-points? Does the above not estimate the first cut-point? In that case, we would calculate the predicted probability of k=1 as 1-sum(prob k=k), akin to estimating the probability of falling into the maximum category in standard ordinal logistic regression?
> >>>>>
> >>>>> And, would that approach, without some scale taken from predictors, be good enough to avoid collapse?
> >>>>>
> >>>>> Thanks,
> >>>>> Tobi
> >>>>>
> >>>>> On Thursday, April 14, 2016 at 1:53:28 PM UTC-7, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> >>>>> The transform for the simplex uses stick-breaking.  but
> >>>>> there's no ordering --- what do you mean by ordering of
> >>>>> the cutpoints?  The usual thing to do here is take the
> >>>>> cumulative sums, so you get an increasing sequence to scale:
> >>>>>
> >>>>> parameters {
> >>>>> simplex[K] theta;     // gaps between cutpoints
> >>>>> real<lower=0> kappa;  // scale for cutpoints
> >>>>>
> >>>>> transformed parameters {
> >>>>> ordered[K] cutpoints;
> >>>>> cutpoints <- cumulative_sum(theta) * kappa;
> >>>>>
> >>>>> model {
> >>>>> theta ~ dirichlet(rep_vector(alpha, K));
> >>>>>
> >>>>> Then if you put a Dirichlet prior on theta, with alpha >> 1, it'll keep
> >>>>> the cutpoints apart.  And it's best to define that vector as
> >>>>> transformed data.
> >>>>>
> >>>>> - Bob
> >>>>>
> >>>>>> On Apr 14, 2016, at 12:11 AM, Dustin Tran <dustinv...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >>>>>>
> >>>>>> What about a truncated stick breaking prior? The size-biasedness of TSB priors will
> >>>>>> (1) force an ordering for the cutpoints;
> >>>>>> (2) make draws of cutpoints live on [0,1] which you can scale willy-nilly;
> >>>>>> (3) reinforce what Ben said on adding prior information via pseudocounts in the parameters of a Dirichlet prior (here, use Beta stick-breaking priors, which is what Ben essentially does based on the running sum in the make_cutpoints function).
> >>>>>>
> >>>>>> Dustin
> >>>>>>> On Apr 13, 2016, at 11:43 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
> >>>>>>>
> >>>>>>> HI, are you saying that a simple flat prior on the cutpoints won’t work?  Or a super-weak prior such as normal(0,10)?
> >>>>>>>
> >>>>>>> I’m surprised that you get “cutpoint collapse” if you’re doing full Bayes (as opposed to maximum likelihood).
> >>>>>>>
> >>>>>>> If you want to put some prior info as below, I recommend putting the normal priors on the _differences_ between the cutpoints, not the cutpoints themselves.  Otherwise you have this weird thing going on where the cutpoints are all being pulled toward each other.
> >>>>>>>
> >>>>>>> A
> >>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>> On Apr 13, 2016, at 9:38 AM, Lei Zhang <bnuzhan...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>> Sorry to bring this up again. I am (still) facing the cutpoint-collapse problem when fitting an ordered-logistic model. After reading this thread and several others, I am still not sure (1) how to properly specify the prior of the cutpoint parameters, and (2) is there a way to model the cutpoint hierarchically like below? I tried something before but it seems that it doesn't guarantee that c[n,k+1] > c[n,k], hence it won't compile. I would highly appreciate any suggestions!
> >>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>> ordered[K] c_mu;
> >>>>>>>> vector<lower=0>[K] c_sd;
> >>>>>>>> ordered[K] c[N];
> >>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>> for (n in 1:N)
> >>>>>>>> for (k in 1:K)
> >>>>>>>>     c[n,k] ~ normal(c_mu[k], c_sd[k]);
> >>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>> On Wednesday, May 20, 2015 at 8:27:28 PM UTC+2, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> >>>>>>>> Cool.  I like that idea.
> >>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>> Just ordering obviously isn't enough for the uniform distribution
> >>>>>>>> on an ordered vector to be proper.
> >>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>> What does happen for reasons I still don't fully understand is
> >>>>>>>> that
> >>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>> ordered[K] cutpoints;
> >>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>> cutpoints ~ normal(0, 5);
> >>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>> provides the same distribution for cutpoints as
> >>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>> vector[K] cutpoints_raw;
> >>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>> cutpoints_raw ~ normal(0, 5);
> >>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>> cutpoints <- sort(cutpoints_raw);
> >>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>> You can put a prior directly on the gaps with
> >>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>> vector[1] cutpoint0;
> >>>>>>>> vector<lower=0>[K - 1] cutpoint_gaps;
> >>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>> cutpoint_gaps ~ normal(0, 2);
> >>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>> ordered[K] cutpoints;
> >>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>> cutpoints <- append_col(cutpoint, cutpoint + cutpoint_gaps);
> >>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>> I'm not sure how to constraint the lowest cut point, cutpoint0.
> >>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>> - Bob
> >>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>>> On May 19, 2015, at 10:53 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >>>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>>> One of the reasons the paper is unwritten is because I think it is better to bring the prior information through the parameters of a Dirichlet prior on the conditional probabilities of being in each category given that the predictors are at the sample means. In code, it would look like
> >>>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>>> functions {
> >>>>>>>>> vector make_cutpoints(vector probabilities, real scale) {
> >>>>>>>>>  vector[rows(probabilities)-1] cutpoints;
> >>>>>>>>>  real running_sum;
> >>>>>>>>>  running_sum <- 0;
> >>>>>>>>>  for(c in 1:(rows(cutpoints))) {
> >>>>>>>>>    running_sum <- running_sum + probabilities[c];
> >>>>>>>>>    cutpoints[c] <- logit(running_sum);

messages.body_plain:
ODE models are notorious for be non-identified — especially
when the data are sparse there end up being many parameters
consistent with the measurements.  This is especially likely
when you have unobserved states in the system of ODEs.

Because the model is fundamentally multimodal, there’s not
much you can do besides change the model or add data,
especially to unobserved components.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Definition of 'divergent transition'
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Definition of 'divergent transition'
messages.body_plain:
Trying to precisely define "high curvature" out of context makes
no more sense than trying to define "stiff ordinary differential
equation" out of the context of a solver.  High curvature is just
the amount of curvature that will cause divergences in our
Hamiltonian simulations.

By definition, the Hamiltonian is the sum of the potential energy plus
the kinetic energy.  In physical systems with no outside forces imparted,
the Hamiltonian remains constant over time (as the particle moves).

In Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, potential energy is negative
log density at the position of a particle representing the parameters,
whereas kinetic energy is derived from momentum, which is
imparted as standard normal at the start of each iteration.

We simulate the particle's trajectory using the leapfrog
integrator, which tends to preserve the Hamiltonian to within a very
small tolerance (1e-8 or so).  We raise divergence errors when the
Hamiltonian drifts very far away (something like a factor of 1e100 or
something ridiculous like that) from its initial value.

The full details and practical ramifications are described here:

  http://mc-stan.org/documentation/case-studies/divergences_and_bias.html

I'll also update the manual to include a crisp definition:

  https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/2122#issuecomment-291982907

- Bob

at a single value.  If you rerun, do you get the same modes?

Alternatively, if you can somehow deduce one of the modes has almost
all of the probability mass (not density), then you can initialize
around that mode with a small step size and you'll stay near it.
You can sometimes achieve this naturally with an appropriate prior.

messages.body_plain:
It's a bit like if you're walking down a slope; you want to stay smoothly on the slope.  One divergence would be if you go 'too fast' and become airborne (like a car going over a hill), right? Another would be if your feet started entering the ground?

On Wednesday, April 5, 2017 at 3:20:30 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Trying to precisely define "high curvature" out of context makes
> no more sense than trying to define "stiff ordinary differential
> equation" out of the context of a solver.  High curvature is just
> the amount of curvature that will cause divergences in our
> Hamiltonian simulations.
>
> By definition, the Hamiltonian is the sum of the potential energy plus
> the kinetic energy.  In physical systems with no outside forces imparted,
> the Hamiltonian remains constant over time (as the particle moves).
>
> In Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, potential energy is negative
> log density at the position of a particle representing the parameters,
> whereas kinetic energy is derived from momentum, which is
> imparted as standard normal at the start of each iteration.
>
> We simulate the particle's trajectory using the leapfrog
> integrator, which tends to preserve the Hamiltonian to within a very
> small tolerance (1e-8 or so).  We raise divergence errors when the
> Hamiltonian drifts very far away (something like a factor of 1e100 or
> something ridiculous like that) from its initial value.
>
> The full details and practical ramifications are described here:
>
>   http://mc-stan.org/documentation/case-studies/divergences_and_bias.html
>
> I'll also update the manual to include a crisp definition:
>
>   https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/2122#issuecomment-291982907
>
> - Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi Stephen,

We currently don't have a targeted version for a release version of Riemannian HMC. An implementation of the algorithm has been available in the source code for quite some time (thanks to Michael!).

There are at least two technical challenges before we would be comfortable releasing it (and we'd love help):
1. implementing higher order automatic differentiation for functions in the Stan language
  - currently, we're able to differentiate (get gradients) through all of the functions in the Stan language (there are ways to intentionally break this, but we try to not make it easy)
  - we don't have the same for higher order automatic differentiation, which is required for RHMC
2. compiling
  - it won't work on Windows under the gcc 4.6.3 compiler. I'm not sure if it's a problem with the new RTools compiler

For tradeoffs, see Andrew's email. There's the additional time of compilation time. We haven't experimented too much, but higher order autodiff takes much longer to compile.

Daniel

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Finite Mixture model in binary data
messages.body_plain:
Just based on my experience with mixture modeling in Stan (and other packages), bernoulli mixtures are very unstable because one of the components will tend to disappear while the other component(s) capture all the variance, even when you have strong reason to believe multiple components exist. You can use the advice on mixture component identification and strong priors to avoid this outcome, but it is harder with binary outcomes to get a reasonable solution, probably because mixtures were designed for modeling continuous outcomes. I would consider even setting hard constraints on the mixing parameters (i.e., 60-40 or 70-30 as the range of possible component mixtures). The great thing about Stan is that you can use a variety of constraint possibilities to get what you're looking for.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Definition of 'divergent transition'
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Definition of 'divergent transition'
messages.body_plain:
You're talking about Metropolis with standard HMC.

We're not doing that with NUTS.  Instead we take all
the points on the trajectory (which moves forward and
backward in time randomly) and choose one randomly
with probability proportional to the density with
an adjustment to favor draws from the second half of
the trajectory (the bias toward the second half is
in the original NUTS paper as is the NUTS criterion;
it's explained more thoroughly in Michael's exhaustive
sampling paper).

It has roughly the same effect---we want to take the
next draw from the true Hamiltonian trajectory.

It's the step size relative to the curvature.  You're
using small steps along a gradient (only first order
approximation) to try to follow something whose geometry
is typically better approximated with the curvature
information in second derivatives (the Hessian matrix).
In that way it's like gradient descent vs. Newton steps in
optimization.

- Bob

> On Apr 6, 2017, at 5:05 AM, Tran <trungd...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thank you Bob for a clear explanation!
>
> So in case we are at a position with high curvature, after L leapfrog steps the proposal will have low chance of being accepted because the Hamiltonian at the proposed position is far from the current one. In case of rejecting we still stay at the current position and another new proposal is proposed and again with low probability of being accepted. In other words the chain only moves when the H(new)-H(current) is negative or sightly positive since the probability of MH step is
>
> min(1, exp(-H(new)+H(current)).
>
> In that case only moves with short distances will be accepted and it explains why we often have 'stuck' in the region of high curvature. Is it correct?
>
>
> Does it hold in the other direction? I mean when we have high curvature we have a warning of divergence but does the divergence implies high curvature?
>
> Best,
> Tran.

messages.body_plain:
The problem is just that a Bernoulli mixture reduces to
a single Bernoulli unless there's external structure,
say with mixing ratio lambda in (0, 1) and chances of
success theta[1], theta[2] in (0, 1), for y in { 0, 1 }
we have:

  p(y | lambda, theta)

    = lambda * bernoulli(y | theta[1])
      + (1 - lambda) * bernoulli(y | theta[2])

    = bernoull(y | lambda * theta[1]
                   + (1 - lambda) * theta[2])

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Mixing in ODE model
messages.body_plain:
Have you made a generated quantities block and looked at the posterior predictives? That's what I'd do in a situation like this.

The reason I'm asking is it seems strange that the 'sigma_fit' parameter would be multimodal (and 3.0 vs 5.0 seems like a big difference). If I'm reading your model correctly, it's saying:

C ~ normal(ode, sigma_fit)
V ~ normal(ode, sigma_fit)

So I think this is the sort of modeling you'd do if you have measurement noise, and, if it is measurement noise, hopefully it corresponds to the precision of some instrument, which hopefully only has one precision (and maybe someone might have a vague idea what it should be too). It also seems weird that two processes (C and V) have the same noise level as well.

Anyway, it's probably worth doing a generated quantities and just checking which modes explain your data better and going from there.

I wouldn't try to read too much into the log probabilities thing.

Ben

This math exchange answer https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/1054048/negative-binomial-distribution-sum-of-two-random-variables tells us that for the special case where \phi (remember that \phi \equiv r) does change but p doesn't, then we have another neg_binomial for the sum of such iid random variables.

Unfortunately, this is not the case in general when you change \phi, but keeps \mu. There might be other special cases, but if we follow the one in such answer, then p=\mu / (\mu+\phi) must be keep constant for the sum to be another negative binomial.

I just added more precise definitions to the manual
and provided links to Michael's cotangent disentegration paper
on divergences (on arXiv).

If you really want to understand this, I'd suggest reading
Michael's case study (on the Stan web site) or watching
his video from StanCon (also linked from the documentation page
of the web site).  Cole's overview is a great place to start.

- Bob

> On Apr 6, 2017, at 12:55 PM, Trung Dung Tran <trungd...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thank you so much for your help, Bob and Cole!
>
> Tran.
>
> On 6 April 2017 at 17:42, Cole Monnahan <mon...@uw.edu> wrote:
> Tran: I try to give an intuitive explanation of these concepts in the following paper (i.e., few equations, illustrative figures, no prior knowledge expected). It may be helpful or useful as a primer to the more technical papers.
>
> onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/2041-210X.12681/full <http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/2041-210X.12681/full>
>
> Cheers,
> Cole
>
>
>
> On Thursday, April 6, 2017 at 2:05:24 AM UTC-7, Tran wrote:
> Thank you Bob for a clear explanation!
>
> So in case we are at a position with high curvature, after L leapfrog steps the proposal will have low chance of being accepted because the Hamiltonian at the proposed position is far from the current one. In case of rejecting we still stay at the current position and another new proposal is proposed and again with low probability of being accepted. In other words the chain only moves when the H(new)-H(current) is negative or sightly positive since the probability of MH step is
>
> min(1, exp(-H(new)+H(current)).
>
> In that case only moves with short distances will be accepted and it explains why we often have 'stuck' in the region of high curvature. Is it correct?
>
>
> Does it hold in the other direction? I mean when we have high curvature we have a warning of divergence but does the divergence implies high curvature?
>
> Best,
> Tran.
>
> --

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Cutpoint Priors
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Cutpoint Priors
messages.body_plain:
The ordered vector deals with keeping the parameters ordered
and also applies the Jacobian for the transform.

So you can put priors on the differences you want (zero-avoiding
priors like gamma or lognormal being a popular choice).

parmaeters {
  ordered[K] c;
  ...
model {
  for (k in 2:K)
    (c[k] - c[k - 1]) ~ ...;
  ...

This is OK because the Jacobian of the difference is constant,
so doesn't need to be accounted for.  You may also want positive
ordered vectors depending on the application; same thing works
for those.

The above is still an improper prior because nothing's locating the
overall position.  That can be fixed by putting a prior on c[1].

  c[1] ~ ...

or really on any of the c[n] values or even on their sum.

You can even vectorize if every diff gets the same
prior:

  (c[2:K] - c[1:(K - 1)]) ~ ...

- Bob

> On Apr 5, 2017, at 9:40 AM, Bob K <bobku...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> I am running an IRT/ordered categorical logistic model and using a weakly informative normal prior on the differences between cutpoints. I'm also getting a lot (i.e., about 10) warnings about improper values (negative values and infinity) for the cutpoints coming from the ordered_logistic function.
>
> So here's a question -- should the ordered vector type naturally handle the fact that the normal prior is being put over the differences between cutpoints, i.e. by transforming to the unconstrained scale such that the normal prior is really a half-normal prior? Or should the normal prior be explicitly truncated at zero? Or, would it be better to use an exponential prior given that all values below zero are meaningless for ordered cutpoint differences?
>
> I can post some data if y'all want to see it.
>
> Thanks much for any advice,
>
> Bob
>
> On Wednesday, March 15, 2017 at 7:48:00 PM UTC-4, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> My intuition is that with N data points with 0 inside a particular bin, that the estimated bin width would be of order 1/N.  But I guess I should do an experiment.
>
> Yes, a gamma prior with shape parameter 2 will get the point estimate away from 0 (as in this paper:  http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/chung_etal_Pmetrika2013.pdf ).  I luuuvv this idea but it's all about point estimation.  I don't like it for full Bayes.
>
> Again, I guess it's time for some experiments.  Also it's interesting the point that you're making about constraints, as this also came up in my rounded-data example.  It's making me wonder if we need to think again about our automatic transformations to the unconstrained scale.
>
> A
>
> > On Mar 15, 2017, at 7:41 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> >
> > Yup, understood.  The MLE will actually collapse the boundaries
> > into each other if there's no data, whereas the Bayesian one
> > will never get there.
> >
> > Now we're just guessing how close the cut points will go
> > to each other in some of the posterior draws, which will
> > depend on the prior and how much data there is in the other
> > bins.  I haven't fit one of these in a while, so I may be
> > misremembering how bad the numerical issues will be.
> > Either way, the distance on the unconstrained scale needs
> > to go to -infinity to get it exponentiation to zero, so it
> > can cause issues if you get lots of data in the other bins.
> >
> > Of course, instead of a uniform on the inter-cut-point distances,
> > you can use something that avoids zero like a gamma with the
> > appropriate params.
> >
> > - Bob
> >
> >> On Mar 15, 2017, at 6:10 PM, Andrew Gelman <Gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
> >>
> >> No, that's not what I meant.  If you have uniform priors on the distances between the cutpoints, and you have a bit of data, then your posterior won't be collapsed near 1e-10 or even near 0.001.  That sort of collapsing behavior can occur with point estimates, and it can occur with hierarchical models (the "funnel") but it should not hold with flat priors.  If you happen to have zero data in some cells, maybe you'll get the difference between cutpoints to be estimated at 0.01 or something like that.
> >> A
> >>
> >>> On Mar 15, 2017, at 2:43 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> >>>
> >>> In theory, you won't ever get exactly collapsed cut points
> >>> in the posterior, but that doesn't mean that in practice you
> >>> won't get close enough to cause underflow and other problems.
> >>>
> >>> Same as if you start drawing theta ~ beta(1e-10, 1e-10).  Sure,
> >>> you shouldn't draw theta = 0 or theta = 1 in theory, but that's
> >>> what's going to happen with floating point arithmetic on computers.
> >>> You can get around that problem with just a little stronger prior.
> >>>
> >>> - Bob
> >>>
> >>>> On Mar 13, 2017, at 5:59 PM, Andrew Gelman <Gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
> >>>>
> >>>> Collapse if cutpoints can occur with point estimation but should not occur with full Bayes.
> >>>>
> >>>>> On Mar 13, 2017, at 3:47 PM, Tobias Konitzer <tobias....@gmail.com> wrote:
> >>>>>
> >>>>> I am wondering how to derive cut-points with only using prior counts in the different categories, but no information from the data other than that. It sounds like Bob's approach above does this, but how do I go from K (assuming K= number of categories) prior probabilities to K-1 cut-points? Does the above not estimate the first cut-point? In that case, we would calculate the predicted probability of k=1 as 1-sum(prob k=k), akin to estimating the probability of falling into the maximum category in standard ordinal logistic regression?
> >>>>>
> >>>>> And, would that approach, without some scale taken from predictors, be good enough to avoid collapse?
> >>>>>
> >>>>> Thanks,
> >>>>> Tobi
> >>>>>
> >>>>> On Thursday, April 14, 2016 at 1:53:28 PM UTC-7, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> >>>>> The transform for the simplex uses stick-breaking.  but
> >>>>> there's no ordering --- what do you mean by ordering of
> >>>>> the cutpoints?  The usual thing to do here is take the
> >>>>> cumulative sums, so you get an increasing sequence to scale:
> >>>>>
> >>>>> parameters {
> >>>>> simplex[K] theta;     // gaps between cutpoints
> >>>>> real<lower=0> kappa;  // scale for cutpoints
> >>>>>
> >>>>> transformed parameters {
> >>>>> ordered[K] cutpoints;
> >>>>> cutpoints <- cumulative_sum(theta) * kappa;
> >>>>>
> >>>>> model {
> >>>>> theta ~ dirichlet(rep_vector(alpha, K));
> >>>>>
> >>>>> Then if you put a Dirichlet prior on theta, with alpha >> 1, it'll keep
> >>>>> the cutpoints apart.  And it's best to define that vector as
> >>>>> transformed data.
> >>>>>
> >>>>> - Bob
> >>>>>
> >>>>>> On Apr 14, 2016, at 12:11 AM, Dustin Tran <dustinv...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >>>>>>
> >>>>>> What about a truncated stick breaking prior? The size-biasedness of TSB priors will
> >>>>>> (1) force an ordering for the cutpoints;
> >>>>>> (2) make draws of cutpoints live on [0,1] which you can scale willy-nilly;
> >>>>>> (3) reinforce what Ben said on adding prior information via pseudocounts in the parameters of a Dirichlet prior (here, use Beta stick-breaking priors, which is what Ben essentially does based on the running sum in the make_cutpoints function).
> >>>>>>
> >>>>>> Dustin
> >>>>>>> On Apr 13, 2016, at 11:43 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
> >>>>>>>
> >>>>>>> HI, are you saying that a simple flat prior on the cutpoints won’t work?  Or a super-weak prior such as normal(0,10)?
> >>>>>>>
> >>>>>>> I’m surprised that you get “cutpoint collapse” if you’re doing full Bayes (as opposed to maximum likelihood).
> >>>>>>>
> >>>>>>> If you want to put some prior info as below, I recommend putting the normal priors on the _differences_ between the cutpoints, not the cutpoints themselves.  Otherwise you have this weird thing going on where the cutpoints are all being pulled toward each other.
> >>>>>>>
> >>>>>>> A
> >>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>> On Apr 13, 2016, at 9:38 AM, Lei Zhang <bnuzhan...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>> Sorry to bring this up again. I am (still) facing the cutpoint-collapse problem when fitting an ordered-logistic model. After reading this thread and several others, I am still not sure (1) how to properly specify the prior of the cutpoint parameters, and (2) is there a way to model the cutpoint hierarchically like below? I tried something before but it seems that it doesn't guarantee that c[n,k+1] > c[n,k], hence it won't compile. I would highly appreciate any suggestions!
> >>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>> ordered[K] c_mu;
> >>>>>>>> vector<lower=0>[K] c_sd;
> >>>>>>>> ordered[K] c[N];
> >>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>> for (n in 1:N)
> >>>>>>>> for (k in 1:K)
> >>>>>>>>     c[n,k] ~ normal(c_mu[k], c_sd[k]);
> >>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>> On Wednesday, May 20, 2015 at 8:27:28 PM UTC+2, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> >>>>>>>> Cool.  I like that idea.
> >>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>> Just ordering obviously isn't enough for the uniform distribution
> >>>>>>>> on an ordered vector to be proper.
> >>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>> What does happen for reasons I still don't fully understand is
> >>>>>>>> that
> >>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>> ordered[K] cutpoints;
> >>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>> cutpoints ~ normal(0, 5);
> >>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>> provides the same distribution for cutpoints as
> >>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>> vector[K] cutpoints_raw;
> >>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>> cutpoints_raw ~ normal(0, 5);
> >>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>> cutpoints <- sort(cutpoints_raw);
> >>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>> You can put a prior directly on the gaps with
> >>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>> vector[1] cutpoint0;
> >>>>>>>> vector<lower=0>[K - 1] cutpoint_gaps;
> >>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>> cutpoint_gaps ~ normal(0, 2);
> >>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>> ordered[K] cutpoints;
> >>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>> cutpoints <- append_col(cutpoint, cutpoint + cutpoint_gaps);
> >>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>> I'm not sure how to constraint the lowest cut point, cutpoint0.
> >>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>> - Bob
> >>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>>> On May 19, 2015, at 10:53 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >>>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>>> One of the reasons the paper is unwritten is because I think it is better to bring the prior information through the parameters of a Dirichlet prior on the conditional probabilities of being in each category given that the predictors are at the sample means. In code, it would look like
> >>>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>>> functions {
> >>>>>>>>> vector make_cutpoints(vector probabilities, real scale) {
> >>>>>>>>>  vector[rows(probabilities)-1] cutpoints;
> >>>>>>>>>  real running_sum;
> >>>>>>>>>  running_sum <- 0;
> >>>>>>>>>  for(c in 1:(rows(cutpoints))) {
> >>>>>>>>>    running_sum <- running_sum + probabilities[c];
> >>>>>>>>>    cutpoints[c] <- logit(running_sum);
> >>>>>>>>>  }
> >>>>>>>>>  return scale * cutpoints;
> >>>>>>>>> }
> >>>>>>>>> }
> >>>>>>>>> data {
> >>>>>>>>> int<lower=1> N;            # observations
> >>>>>>>>> int<lower=1> K;            # predictors
> >>>>>>>>> int<lower=3> C;            # outcome categories
> >>>>>>>>> matrix[N,K]  X;            # "standardized" predictor matrix
> >>>>>>>>> vector[K] xbar;            # vector of predictor means
> >>>>>>>>> int<lower=1,upper=C> y[N]; # ordinal outcome
> >>>>>>>>> vector[C] pseudocounts;    # prior value for concentrations in Dirichlet prior
> >>>>>>>>> real<lower=0> nu;          # scale for Cauchy priors
> >>>>>>>>> }
> >>>>>>>>> transformed data {
> >>>>>>>>> matrix[K,K] middle;
> >>>>>>>>> middle <- xbar * transpose(xbar);
> >>>>>>>>> }
> >>>>>>>>> parameters {
> >>>>>>>>> vector[K] beta_raw;        # coefficients
> >>>>>>>>> simplex[C] probabilities;  # of falling in each category given xbar
> >>>>>>>>> }
> >>>>>>>>> transformed parameters {
> >>>>>>>>> vector[K] beta;
> >>>>>>>>> vector[C-1] cutpoints;
> >>>>>>>>> for (k in 1:K) beta[k] <- nu * tan(pi() * (Phi(beta_raw[k]) - 0.5));
> >>>>>>>>> cutpoints <- make_cutpoints(probabilities, sqrt(quad_form(middle, beta) + 1));
> >>>>>>>>> }
> >>>>>>>>> model {
> >>>>>>>>> vector[N] eta;
> >>>>>>>>> eta <- X * beta;                                          # linear predictor
> >>>>>>>>> for(n in 1:N) y[n] ~ ordered_logistic(eta[n], cutpoints); # likelihood
> >>>>>>>>> probabilities ~ dirichlet(pseudocounts);                  # our intuitive prior
> >>>>>>>>> beta_raw ~ normal(0,1); # prior implies beta ~ cauchy(0,nu)
> >>>>>>>>> }
> >>>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>>> Ben
> >>>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>>> On Tuesday, May 19, 2015 at 8:25:50 PM UTC-4, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> >>>>>>>>> Hi, Ben and I actually have an (unwritten) paper on this.  The short answer is that we do think there’s a place for a weakly informative prior here.  One challenge is that the scale of the cutpoints themselves is hard to know ahead of time, so we were talking about setting up a prior by putting in a small bit (possibly a fractional bit) of pseudo-data in each bin.
> >>>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>>>> On May 19, 2015, at 5:46 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >>>>>>>>>>
> >>>>>>>>>> Is there a natural prior for cut points (specifically in
> >>>>>>>>>> an ordered logistic regression) or is the ordered constraint
> >>>>>>>>>> sufficiently strong that the uniform prior is well-posed?

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] About the Riemannian geometry in Stan
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] About the Riemannian geometry in Stan
messages.body_plain:
As to (1), I think they're implemented pretty much everywhere
other than for the ODE solver, but they're not tested thoroughly,
which amounts to the same thing for us.

And yes, Riemannian involves an O(N^3) matrix decomposition for
dimension N problems at each step, whereas Euclidean NUTS with
diagonal mass matrix is only O(N) per step.  In cases of high
curvature, the Euclidean algorithm will fail or grind to a halt
with a very high constant factor due to small step size.

- Bob

> On Apr 5, 2017, at 9:30 PM, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:
>
> Hi Stephen,
>
> We currently don't have a targeted version for a release version of Riemannian HMC. An implementation of the algorithm has been available in the source code for quite some time (thanks to Michael!).
>
> There are at least two technical challenges before we would be comfortable releasing it (and we'd love help):
> 1. implementing higher order automatic differentiation for functions in the Stan language
>   - currently, we're able to differentiate (get gradients) through all of the functions in the Stan language (there are ways to intentionally break this, but we try to not make it easy)
>   - we don't have the same for higher order automatic differentiation, which is required for RHMC
> 2. compiling
>   - it won't work on Windows under the gcc 4.6.3 compiler. I'm not sure if it's a problem with the new RTools compiler
>
> For tradeoffs, see Andrew's email. There's the additional time of compilation time. We haven't experimented too much, but higher order autodiff takes much longer to compile.
>
>
> Daniel
>
>
>
> On Wed, Apr 5, 2017 at 9:09 PM, Stephen Martin <hwki...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Will Riemannian be the default after a certain version, or are there tradeoffs to be made between euclidean and riemannian?
>
> On Wednesday, April 5, 2017 at 11:10:32 AM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Only from the C++ core, not from any of the interfaces.
>
> - Bob
>
> On Apr 4, 2017, at 8:26 PM, Hamed Nikbakht <hamednik...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> >
> > Hi,
> >
> > Does this version of Stan consider Riemannian geometry to visit the corner better?
> >
> > Thank you,
> > Hamed
> >
> > --

messages.body_plain:
> On Apr 6, 2017, at 2:54 PM, Trung Dung Tran <trungd...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi Bob,
>
> Yes, I really want to understand at least to the basic level of the algorithm behind Stan from that I might know the reason why my particular model does not give true values.

You want to check interval coverage, not "values".  See the
Cook, Gelman, and Rubin paper, for example.

> If not then it takes time to guess why a model for a real data set does not work.
>
> Before I thought that Stan also has problem at the boundary (with constraints) even (if I understand correctly) Stan do transform from constrained to unconstrained. In that case of boundary problem, Stan will give warning of divergence.
>
> For example with a scale parameter sigma we set sigma > 0 and in log-scale it will be -infinity to +infinity.
>
> When sigma ->0, log(sigma) -> -infinity and even sigma change a little bit (0.1 -> 0.05), log(sigma) changes a 0.7 unit and it can lead to a large difference for Hamiltonian. In this case I thought Stan also give warnings.
>
> Do you think this is a correct understanding of mine?

No.  The Hamiltonian is always conserved.

What happens is that we wander off in the unconstrained space, then
when we transform back (using, e.g., exp()), we get underflow or
overflow, which then leads to warnings when we plug the values into
distributions that require finite parameters.

- Bob
