messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] About the Riemannian geometry in Stan
messages.body_plain:
So it really depends on the problem at hand. With high curvature, euclidean will often fail or will explore slowly due to smaller step sizes needed. Otoh, with high curvature, riemannian will not fail or explore slowly, but per-step it will take longer. So if you have regions of the posterior with large curvature, Riemannian could mix and explore faster (or more sample more efficiently) than euclidean, whereas with less difficult curvature euclidean may be more efficient?

On Thursday, April 6, 2017 at 1:20:31 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> As to (1), I think they're implemented pretty much everywhere
> other than for the ODE solver, but they're not tested thoroughly,
> which amounts to the same thing for us.
>
> And yes, Riemannian involves an O(N^3) matrix decomposition for
> dimension N problems at each step, whereas Euclidean NUTS with
> diagonal mass matrix is only O(N) per step.  In cases of high
> curvature, the Euclidean algorithm will fail or grind to a halt
> with a very high constant factor due to small step size.
>
> - Bob
>
>
>
>
> > On Apr 5, 2017, at 9:30 PM, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:

> > Hi Stephen,
> >
> > We currently don't have a targeted version for a release version of Riemannian HMC. An implementation of the algorithm has been available in the source code for quite some time (thanks to Michael!).
> >
> > There are at least two technical challenges before we would be comfortable releasing it (and we'd love help):
> > 1. implementing higher order automatic differentiation for functions in the Stan language
> >   - currently, we're able to differentiate (get gradients) through all of the functions in the Stan language (there are ways to intentionally break this, but we try to not make it easy)
> >   - we don't have the same for higher order automatic differentiation, which is required for RHMC
> > 2. compiling
> >   - it won't work on Windows under the gcc 4.6.3 compiler. I'm not sure if it's a problem with the new RTools compiler
> >
> > For tradeoffs, see Andrew's email. There's the additional time of compilation time. We haven't experimented too much, but higher order autodiff takes much longer to compile.
> >
> >
> > Daniel
> >
> >
> >

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Definition of 'divergent transition'
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Definition of 'divergent transition'
messages.body_plain:
It may be worth pointing out that divergences can be caused by large approximation errors in the Hamiltonian, or a NaN. Obviously the latter case would be divergent if the Hamiltonian could be calculated, and are related. As far as I know there is no way to tell the difference between these cases in Stan.

In some models in fisheries we have holes in the posterior where the log density is undefined (essentially 0 probability). This results from poorly parameterized models. The behavior of the divergences is different than those where the step size is simply too big.

On Thu, Apr 6, 2017 at 12:22 PM, Trung Dung Tran <trungd...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Thank you so much for an useful explanation and correction!
>
> I was attracted from Stan when I see it is better for ordinal variables when running a ordered logit model. I would continue use it not only because of its performance but also of the help from the team like you.
>
> Tran.
>
> On 6 April 2017 at 21:11, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> >
> > > On Apr 6, 2017, at 2:54 PM, Trung Dung Tran <trungd...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > Hi Bob,
> > >
> > > Yes, I really want to understand at least to the basic level of the algorithm behind Stan from that I might know the reason why my particular model does not give true values.
> >
> > You want to check interval coverage, not "values".  See the
> > Cook, Gelman, and Rubin paper, for example.
> >
> > > If not then it takes time to guess why a model for a real data set does not work.
> > >
> > > Before I thought that Stan also has problem at the boundary (with constraints) even (if I understand correctly) Stan do transform from constrained to unconstrained. In that case of boundary problem, Stan will give warning of divergence.
> > >
> > > For example with a scale parameter sigma we set sigma > 0 and in log-scale it will be -infinity to +infinity.
> > >
> > > When sigma ->0, log(sigma) -> -infinity and even sigma change a little bit (0.1 -> 0.05), log(sigma) changes a 0.7 unit and it can lead to a large difference for Hamiltonian. In this case I thought Stan also give warnings.
> > >
> > > Do you think this is a correct understanding of mine?
> >
> > No.  The Hamiltonian is always conserved.
> >
> > What happens is that we wander off in the unconstrained space, then
> > when we transform back (using, e.g., exp()), we get underflow or
> > overflow, which then leads to warnings when we plug the values into
> > distributions that require finite parameters.
> >
> > - Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Explicitly Correlated Parameters
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Explicitly Correlated Parameters
messages.body_plain:
I'm hoping to hang my hat on the non-linear relationship between intercepts and standard deviations.

I had tried normalizing the variables in the past and it didn't make nearly as much a difference as when I did simulations where the relationship was more linear or uncorrelated. I also multiplied the number of iterations by 10 (to 10,000 total post-warm up across 4 chains) and that didn't make a noticeable impact.

When normalizing, I had subtracted each series by the overall mean and divided by the overall standard deviation. So in this case, the cross-sectional variation in the intercepts and standard deviations increased by about a factor of 10, but not up to 1. The standard deviation of the intercepts becomes something like 0.1 empirically, but most of the time when I run Stan it still gets shoved down to 0.01 in some of the simpler variations and divergences (in a simple simulation, but preserving the non-linearity).

It doesn't make sense to me to subtract the series mean and divide by the series standard deviation. If I fit a hierarchical model, all the means should be 0 and the standard deviations 1, which kind of defeats the purpose of doing a hierarchical regression. This actually makes the standard deviation of the cross sectional means even smaller (and more more divergences).

On Wed, Apr 5, 2017 at 6:11 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

> Thanks for the report.
>
> You'll find Stan has a lot easier time adapting if the parameters
> are on the scale of 1 rather than 1e-3.  If you give Stan long
> enough to warmup, it should adapt to the right scales, but it might
> take a while.
>
> - Bob
>

> >
> >
> >

> > How are you assessing bias?  Are you talking about the posterior

> > interval coverage for simulated data --- that'll let you assess whether

> > it matches some real data set.
> >
> > The actual value (of the standard deviation on the hierarchically varying intercept) was closer to 0.01 and I was getting like 0.001. The intervals were way different. This was also what was driving the divergences. Basically, this standard deviation was getting too low. I played around a little with the specification and was getting better results.
> >
> > Also, I started using some of the diagnostics from Michael Betancourt's case study on the subject. They are definitely valuable.
> >
> >
> > This is a key step in debugging.  Isolate the problem in
> > a reproducible example that is as simple as possible.  Often
> > by the time you've done that, the debugging job is done.
> >
> > This is one of the main reasons we suggest building models
> > up from simpler models wherever possible.  It's tedious to

messages.body_plain:
Not really, according to that example, it's p that must be constant, where p is the probability of sucess of the usual negative binomial parameterization of undergraduate courses, here I'll call it neg_binomial_undergrad (it doesn't exist on Stan, of course).

Then if you have something like:

y[1] ~ neg_binomial_undergrad(p, phi1)

y[2] ~ neg_binomial_undergrad(p, phi2)
Then:

(y[1] + y[2]) ~ neg_binomial_undergrad(p, phi1 + phi2)

On Stan neg_binomial_2, you'll have to use the fact that:

mu = p * phi/ (1 - p)

Then, you have:

y[1] ~ neg_binomial_2(p * phi1/ (1 - p), phi1)

y[2] ~ neg_binomial_2(p * phi2/ (1 - p), phi2)

(y[1] + y[2]) ~ neg_binomial_2(p * (phi1 + phi2)/ (1 - p), phi1 + phi2)

Not that useful, but as I said there might be other special cases of sum of independent negative binomial random variables that gives another negative binomial that I'm not aware of.

A quick test to check the results on R:

p = .4
phi1 = 11.5
phi2 = 4.6
first_ = rnbinom(1e6, phi1, mu=p * phi1/ (1 - p)) + rnbinom(1e4, phi2, mu=p * phi2/ (1 - p))
second_ = rnbinom(1e6, phi1 + phi2, mu=p * (phi1 + phi2)/ (1 - p))
mean(first_)
mean(second_)
var(first_)
var(second_)
mean(first_**3)
mean(second_**3)
quantile(first_)
quantile(second_)

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Definition of 'divergent transition'
messages.body_plain:
On Apr 6, 2017, at 6:03 PM, Cole Monnahan <mon...@uw.edu> wrote:

> It may be worth pointing out that divergences can be caused by large approximation errors in the Hamiltonian, or a NaN. Obviously the latter case would be divergent if the Hamiltonian could be calculated, and are related. As far as I know there is no way to tell the difference between these cases in Stan.
>
> In some models in fisheries we have holes in the posterior where the log density is undefined (essentially 0 probability). This results from poorly parameterized models. The behavior of the divergences is different than those where the step size is simply too big.

+1!!!!

>
> On Thu, Apr 6, 2017 at 12:22 PM, Trung Dung Tran <trungd...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Thank you so much for an useful explanation and correction!
> >
> > I was attracted from Stan when I see it is better for ordinal variables when running a ordered logit model. I would continue use it not only because of its performance but also of the help from the team like you.
> >
> > Tran.
> >
> > On 6 April 2017 at 21:11, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > > On Apr 6, 2017, at 2:54 PM, Trung Dung Tran <trungd...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > >
> > > > Hi Bob,
> > > >
> > > > Yes, I really want to understand at least to the basic level of the algorithm behind Stan from that I might know the reason why my particular model does not give true values.
> > >
> > > You want to check interval coverage, not "values".  See the
> > > Cook, Gelman, and Rubin paper, for example.
> > >
> > > > If not then it takes time to guess why a model for a real data set does not work.
> > > >
> > > > Before I thought that Stan also has problem at the boundary (with constraints) even (if I understand correctly) Stan do transform from constrained to unconstrained. In that case of boundary problem, Stan will give warning of divergence.
> > > >
> > > > For example with a scale parameter sigma we set sigma > 0 and in log-scale it will be -infinity to +infinity.
> > > >
> > > > When sigma ->0, log(sigma) -> -infinity and even sigma change a little bit (0.1 -> 0.05), log(sigma) changes a 0.7 unit and it can lead to a large difference for Hamiltonian. In this case I thought Stan also give warnings.
> > > >
> > > > Do you think this is a correct understanding of mine?
> > >
> > > No.  The Hamiltonian is always conserved.
> > >
> > > What happens is that we wander off in the unconstrained space, then
> > > when we transform back (using, e.g., exp()), we get underflow or
> > > overflow, which then leads to warnings when we plug the values into
> > > distributions that require finite parameters.
> > >
> > > - Bob

Well, it's good to mention, if don't already know, that there's an import special case that might be useful, it's when they independent and identically distributed:

y[1] ~ neg_binomial_undergrad(p, phi)
y[2] ~ neg_binomial_undergrad(p, phi)

(y[1] + y[2]) ~ neg_binomial_undergrad(p, 2*phi)

On Stan we would have:

y[1] ~ neg_binomial_2(mu, phi)

y[2] ~ neg_binomial_2(mu, phi)

(y[1] + y[2]) ~ neg_binomial_2(2*mu, 2*phi)

mu = 4.4
phi = 11.5
first_ = rnbinom(1e6, phi, mu=mu) + rnbinom(1e6, phi, mu=mu)
second_ = rnbinom(1e6, 2*phi, mu=2*mu)

mean(first_)
mean(second_)
var(first_)
var(second_)
mean(first_**3)
mean(second_**3)
quantile(first_)
quantile(second_)

messages.body_plain:
No, this will be true only in the limit of phi going to infinity, where both random variable will be Poisson distributed and therefore their sum will also be Poisson.

See for instance when phi=0.1

set.seed(12)
phi = 0.1
mu1 = 1
mu2 = 10
first_ = rnbinom(1e6, phi, mu=mu1) + rnbinom(1e6, phi, mu=mu2)
second_ = rnbinom(1e6, 2*phi, mu=mu1+mu2)

mean(first_)
mean(second_)
var(first_)
var(second_)
mean(first_**3)
mean(second_**3)
quantile(first_)
quantile(second_)

> mean(first_)

[1] 11.03025
> mean(second_)
[1] 10.98656

messages.body_plain:
On 07/04/2017 00:54, stefano wrote:
> Thanks Marco,
>
> 1) but then what is the best approach to model sums of neg_binomials

It will depend on your assumptions and on what you have.

Do you observe the variables individually? If so, just model them individually on Stan.

Or do you only observe their sum and know that they are individually negative binomial distributed? If that's the case, maybe you could model the individual components as parameters in Stan, constrained so that their sum is your observed sum and attempt to place all the information you have on the relation among them as prior distributions.

>
> 2) I am still trying to understand how good is this approximation

Yeah, obviously, the lower the value of phi, the worse should be the approximation is since we are getting further apart from the Poisson case and also the further apart mu1 and mu2 are from each other, the worse it should since you are getting further apart from the special case of i.i.d random variables. But how worse it gets it possibly pretty hard question.

>
> Let's say that in median I have 800 as count value, and empirically phy = 2, for those parameters

> set.seed(12)
> phi = 2
> mu1 = 50

> mean(first_)

> [1] 180821

> P.S. Why do you analyse mean(first_**3) and mean(second_**3)?

The third moment and the quantiles are just an extra to make "sure" the random variable have the same or different distribution.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Definition of 'divergent transition'
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Definition of 'divergent transition'
messages.body_plain:
> On Apr 6, 2017, at 6:03 PM, Cole Monnahan <mon...@uw.edu> wrote:
>

> It may be worth pointing out that divergences can be caused by large approximation errors in the Hamiltonian, or a NaN. Obviously the latter case would be divergent if the Hamiltonian could be calculated, and are related. As far as I know there is no way to tell the difference between these cases in Stan.
>
> In some models in fisheries we have holes in the posterior where the log density is undefined (essentially 0 probability). This results from poorly parameterized models. The behavior of the divergences is different than those where the step size is simply too big.

There are really four ways I can think of to diverge:

1. Hamiltonian diverges but remains finite (finite divergence)

2. update target with NaN or -infinity (non-finite divergence)

3. a. execute a reject() statement (exception)

   b. pass an illegal argument to a function (exception)

Cases (2) or (3) may arise from

* an infinite step in the Hamiltonian because floating-point arithmetic
  fails for a well-defined Hamiltonian

* there are holes in your density

The arithmetic causes make (2) and (3) just like (1), as Cole points
out in his first paragraph.

Non-arithmetic causes, like holes in the density, can be equally
disastrous for estimation, as they cause HMC to fall back into a kind of
rejection sampler, which will usually mix poorly if there's not a smooth
boundary.  Whatever you do, you want to be careful to test the calibration
of the model on simulated data.

Stan reports these slightly differently.  If the NaN or infinite value
gets all the way through (unlikely), we'll report a divergence as usual.
Otherwise, we try to report the root cause from the function that
got an illegal argument or the reject statement.

- Bob

>
> On Thu, Apr 6, 2017 at 12:22 PM, Trung Dung Tran <trungd...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Thank you so much for an useful explanation and correction!
>
> I was attracted from Stan when I see it is better for ordinal variables when running a ordered logit model. I would continue use it not only because of its performance but also of the help from the team like you.
>
> Tran.
>
> On 6 April 2017 at 21:11, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> > On Apr 6, 2017, at 2:54 PM, Trung Dung Tran <trungd...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hi Bob,
> >
> > Yes, I really want to understand at least to the basic level of the algorithm behind Stan from that I might know the reason why my particular model does not give true values.
>
> You want to check interval coverage, not "values".  See the
> Cook, Gelman, and Rubin paper, for example.
>
> > If not then it takes time to guess why a model for a real data set does not work.
> >
> > Before I thought that Stan also has problem at the boundary (with constraints) even (if I understand correctly) Stan do transform from constrained to unconstrained. In that case of boundary problem, Stan will give warning of divergence.
> >
> > For example with a scale parameter sigma we set sigma > 0 and in log-scale it will be -infinity to +infinity.
> >
> > When sigma ->0, log(sigma) -> -infinity and even sigma change a little bit (0.1 -> 0.05), log(sigma) changes a 0.7 unit and it can lead to a large difference for Hamiltonian. In this case I thought Stan also give warnings.
> >
> > Do you think this is a correct understanding of mine?
>
> No.  The Hamiltonian is always conserved.
>
> What happens is that we wander off in the unconstrained space, then
> when we transform back (using, e.g., exp()), we get underflow or
> overflow, which then leads to warnings when we plug the values into
> distributions that require finite parameters.
>
> - Bob

messages.body_plain:
If you want to use the model_code argument to pass the Stan program as a string (instead of using a separate file) then you can't put the name of the Stan program string in quotes. So

fit <- stan(model_code = "scode", data = schools_dat, iter = 1000, chains = 4)

won't work. It needs to be

fit <- stan(model_code = scode, data = schools_dat, iter = 1000, chains = 4)

We definitely recommend using a file instead of a string, but that should at least work.

Jonah

messages.body_plain:
I just mean rather than having

  alpha ~ normal(0, 1e-3);

define

  alpha_raw ~ normal(0, 1);

  alpha = 1e-3 * alpha_raw;

Then the parameters over which Stan is actually sampling, alpha_raw,
will be unit scale, but you'll still have your original value alpha.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Two-step estimation of hierarchical models
messages.body_plain:
Like I said, my model is more complex than the example above. It was just meant as a minimal example to illustrate the question.

In the real model, z is a matrix of roughly size 30,000*4. z_measurement are ordinal measurements, with around three outcomes per element of z. Y is also a matrix with ordinal outcomes. So it is like a bunch of IRT-models, where I identify latent traits along five different dimensions, and hence close to 500,000 evaluations of the categorical logit to calculate the likelihood. I use 2000 iterations total, 1000 adaptation, with several chains in parallel. I am using standard priors. Model converges nicely, with average tree-size around 6, and generally no divergent transitions. I'm not saying Stan is slow - it is doing lots of work.

You are right - I'm ignoring feedback from Y and X to z (akin to the "cut" function in Bugs), but it could speed things up a lot. I also doubt it would have a strong influence on the posterior densities of z, at least it hasn't with my data when I make changes to X. So I was wondering if anyone had tried this in a setting where I could pass general, posterior densitites as "data".

Best,
op

messages.body_plain:
The formulas didn't come through.

You want to compute the Jacobian for

 f : (alpha, beta) -> (alpha, sqrt(alpha) / beta)

Then you can put priors on alpha and on sqrt(alpha) / beta.
You probably wouldn't also want a prior on beta, but if
you include one, it just gets multiplied into the density (added
to the log density).

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Based on stan expert opinion scaling parameters is quite important to improve numerical stability. However so far I didn't find any guidelines - is it better to divide parameter by some constant or take log or some other tricks. I wish there was some discussion in the manual or github. For example, the approximated posterior in unscaled parameter space looks like:
theta4 ~ lognormal(-7.87,0.99)
theta7 ~ lognormal(12.55,0.91)
Does it make sense to work in the parameter space of scaled_theta4=exp(theta4) and scaled_theta7=log(theta7) or is it better to define scaled_theta4=theta4*0.0006 where 0.0006=mean(rlnorm(10000,-7.87,0.99) and scaled_theta7=theta7/400000 where 40000=mean(rlnorm(10000,12.55,0.91))?

Experts tell us that divergent transitions may lead to bias (there is a lot in this list) but it is hard to mine this info and glue together to get a good guidance. I wonder if scaling parameters has anything to do with divergent transitions. It would be great to summarize this info similar to https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Prior-Choice-Recommendations.

The model I am working with is a PBPK model defined as a system of ODEs. Solving ODEs has some tolerances associated with it. In a PBPK model material balances have to be conserved (in=out) however because of ODE solver the material balances range in -10-3 to 10-3. May this be a cause for divergent transitions?

Thanks for any insight,
Linas

messages.body_plain:
It's all about the unconstrained scale.  The closer
you can get to zero mean and unit covariance multinormal,
the better.

If there's too much correlation or varying curvature,
reparameterization can help.  See the chapter in the manual
and the Betancourt/Girolami paper on hierarchical models.

Yes, performance will be sensitive to the tolerance of the ODEs.
We're not even sure if this is model dependent.  There are
absolute and relative tolerances.

- Bob

Did you ever end up solving your problem?  I am working on a something slightly similar and your comment "But then I have a horrible feeling that the indexes will get flipped." with some results I ran have me worried as well.

I am trying to modify some of Rob Trangucci's code for running a 2 dimensional gaussian process (see post Options for speeding up gaussian process regression). The only change I am trying to make is to change the outcome from a normal to a Poisson making it a log gaussian cox process LGCP.   I was able to change the matrix to an array but I think the indexes got flipped because when I simulated data the length scales look like they flipped their estimates.

Attached is the R code that simulates the rate data and the stan code that runs it.  Here is the r code that simulated the data, ran the stan model and the output.
## exponentiated quadratic covariance matrix function
cov_exp_quad <- function(x, alpha, len_scale, jitter) {
  dim_x = length(x)
  cov_ret <- matrix(NA_real_, dim_x, dim_x)
  for (i in 1:(dim_x - 1)) {
    cov_ret[i, i] = alpha ^ 2 + jitter
    for (j in (i + 1):dim_x) {
      r_x = (x[i] - x[j])^2
      cov_ret[i, j] = alpha^2 * exp(-1 / (2 * len_scale^2) * r_x)
      cov_ret[j,i] = cov_ret[i, j]
    }
  }
  cov_ret[dim_x, dim_x] = alpha ^ 2 + jitter
  return(cov_ret)
}

## DGP

set.seed(320)

dim_x_1 <- 100
dim_x_2 <- 100
alpha <- 0.5
len_scale_x_1 <- 4
len_scale_x_2 <- 2

x_1 <- seq(0,20,length.out = dim_x_1)
x_2 <- seq(0,20,length.out = dim_x_2)
cov_mat_x_1 <- cov_exp_quad(x_1, 1.0, len_scale_x_1, 1e-12)
cov_mat_x_2 <- cov_exp_quad(x_2, alpha, len_scale_x_2, 1e-12)
L_x_1 <- t(chol(cov_mat_x_1))
L_x_2 <- t(chol(cov_mat_x_2))
y_tilde <- matrix(rnorm(dim_x_1 * dim_x_2),dim_x_1,dim_x_2)
gp_draw <- L_x_1 %*% y_tilde %*% t(L_x_2)

mu <- exp(gp_draw + matrix(0.5 * rnorm(dim_x_1 * dim_x_2), dim_x_1, dim_x_2))

y <- matrix(NA, nrow=100, ncol=100)
for (i in 1:100) {

 y[i,] <-rpois(100,mu[i,1:100])
}

## Generate data to pass to Stan model

stan_dat <- list(y = y,
                 N = prod(dim(y)),
                 dim_x_1 = dim_x_1,
                 dim_x_2 = dim_x_2,
                 x_1 = x_1,
                 x_2 = x_2)

fit <- stan('lgcp_2dim_ncp.stan', data = stan_dat, chains = 4, iter = 3000, control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95, max_treedepth = 15), cores = 4)

samps <- rstan::extract(fit)

print(fit, pars = c('alpha','len_scale_x_1','len_scale_x_2'))

messages.body_plain:
Hi,
this is something I am also struggling with. There is a lot of talk on non-centered parametrizations, but as far as I understand, this means making sure that _prior_ distribution is zero mean, unit covariance multinomial.
I think the question is: does it make sense to reparametrize according to the sensitivity of the log posterior to small changes in the parameters?

So for example:
if we have parameters:
alpha ~ normal(0,1)
beta ~ normal(0,1)

and data model
y ~ normal(2^alpha + beta, 1)

the prior is zero mean, unit covariance, but a small change in alpha will affect the posterior much more than a small change in beta. To my intuition this sounds like a typical "uneven curvature"

If this is the case, does it make sense to reparametrize to gamma = 2^alpha? This would give
log2(gamma) ~ normal(0,1)
beta ~ normal(0,1)

y ~ normal(gamma + beta, 1)

the paremetrization (gamma, beta) des not have zero mean, unit covariance, but the curvature of the log posterior should (in my intuition) be more even in all places and directions.

Thanks for any clarifications

Hi all,

Aki is giving a talk at the Bayesian Data Analysis meetup in NYC on 4/18 at 5:30 pm.

Title: Bayesian predictive methods for covariate selection in large p small n problems

Abstract:
I first present recent development in hierarchical shrinkage priors for presenting sparsity assumptions in covariate effects. I review an easy and intuitive way of setting up the prior for based on our prior beliefs about the number of effectively nonzero coefficients in the model. I also discuss the computational issues when using hierarchical shrinkage priors. I emphasize the separation between prior information on sparsity and decision theoretic approach for selecting a smaller set of covariates having good predictive performance. I briefly review comparison of Bayesian predictive methods for model selection and discuss in more detail projection predictive variable selection approach for regression.

Register here:

Daniel

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] matrix or array of integers?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] matrix or array of integers?
messages.body_plain:
You have to be careful with the ordering of columns vs. rows
in all of the conversion operators.  Underlyingly, our matrices
are column major (Eigen C++ library default) and our arrays are
row major (using standard C++ library vector).  So it's always
confusing going back and forth between them, in both the I/O
and the internal functions.

You can write a program with just generated quantities and
run it to do simple testing to make sure you have things in
the right order.

- Bob

> Like I said, my model is more complex than the example above. It was just meant as a minimal example to illustrate the question.
>
> In the real model, z is a matrix of roughly size 30,000*4. z_measurement are ordinal measurements, with around three outcomes per element of z. Y is also a matrix with ordinal outcomes. So it is like a bunch of IRT-models, where I identify latent traits along five different dimensions, and hence close to 500,000 evaluations of the categorical logit to calculate the likelihood. I use 2000 iterations total, 1000 adaptation, with several chains in parallel. I am using standard priors. Model converges nicely, with average tree-size around 6, and generally no divergent transitions. I'm not saying Stan is slow - it is doing lots of work.

Vectorizing ordinal logit will help.  Sean's nearly done with
the operands-and-partials generalization, so we'll be getting
to all of these multivariate parameter/outcome distributions
soon.

> You are right - I'm ignoring feedback from Y and X to z (akin to the "cut" function in Bugs), but it could speed things up a lot. I also doubt it would have a strong influence on the posterior densities of z, at least it hasn't with my data when I make changes to X. So I was wondering if anyone had tried this in a setting where I could pass general, posterior densitites as "data".

I don't think there's anything built into any of our interfaces
that would let you do that easily.  What people usually suggest
is some kind of normal approximation to a posterior to use
as a follow-on prior if there's not conjugacy.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
The index to the manual lists all the functions, so there's
no need to guess.  The language will also report all the legal
signatures for a function you try.

The next release (2.15, which is in the pipeline now), will let
you write:

  vector[2] L = [3, 5]';

where [3, 5] is a row vector and ' is the postfix transpose operator.

With 2.14, the closest you can get is:

  vector[2] L = to_vector({3, 5});

which uses the {3, 5} to construct an int[] and
then to_vector(int[]) to produce a vector.

If we eventually want a flattening operator like R's c(),
that'll be something completely different:

> c(c(1, 2, 3), 4)
[1] 1 2 3 4

> c(c(1, 2), c(3, 4))
[1] 1 2 3 4
>

In Stan, if you do { { 1, 2 }, { 3, 4 } }, you're going to
get a 2 x 2 array.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] scaling parameters & divergent transitions
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] scaling parameters & divergent transitions
messages.body_plain:
You have to look at what's happening on the unconstrained
scale.  That's where Stan's actually sampling.

I don't think it's so much sensitivity to parameters as you
want the unconstrained parameters to be relatively freely
moving between -2 and 2 and not allowed to get huge and
not constrained to stay small.  Then the initial mass matrix
guess will be right and everything will move well.

The best you can do is look at the pairs (or triples in
ShinyStan) plots to see what's happening to groups of
parameters.

By varying curvature in the posterior, we mean that the Hessian
(second derivative matrix) changes as the parameters change.
That's the hierarchical modeling case that the non-centered
parameterization avoids (see the manual chapter on reparameterization
and the funnel example for an extreme case).

Linas --- I don't know what the partially centered parameterization
is.  Did someone write that up somewhere?

- Bob

> On Apr 10, 2017, at 4:08 AM, Martin Cerny <cer...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi,
> this is something I am also struggling with. There is a lot of talk on non-centered parametrizations, but as far as I understand, this means making sure that _prior_ distribution is zero mean, unit covariance multinomial.
> I think the question is: does it make sense to reparametrize according to the sensitivity of the log posterior to small changes in the parameters?
>
> So for example:
> if we have parameters:
> alpha ~ normal(0,1)
> beta ~ normal(0,1)
>
> and data model
> y ~ normal(2^alpha + beta, 1)
>
> the prior is zero mean, unit covariance, but a small change in alpha will affect the posterior much more than a small change in beta. To my intuition this sounds like a typical "uneven curvature"
>
> If this is the case, does it make sense to reparametrize to gamma = 2^alpha? This would give
> log2(gamma) ~ normal(0,1)
> beta ~ normal(0,1)
>
> y ~ normal(gamma + beta, 1)
>
> the paremetrization (gamma, beta) des not have zero mean, unit covariance, but the curvature of the log posterior should (in my intuition) be more even in all places and directions.
>
> Thanks for any clarifications
> Martin
>
> On Sunday, 9 April 2017 02:14:33 UTC+2, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> It's all about the unconstrained scale.  The closer
> you can get to zero mean and unit covariance multinormal,
> the better.
>
> If there's too much correlation or varying curvature,
> reparameterization can help.  See the chapter in the manual
> and the Betancourt/Girolami paper on hierarchical models.
>
> Yes, performance will be sensitive to the tolerance of the ODEs.
> We're not even sure if this is model dependent.  There are
> absolute and relative tolerances.
>
> - Bob
>
> > On Apr 8, 2017, at 11:40 AM, Linas Mockus <linasm...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hi,
> >
> > Based on stan expert opinion scaling parameters is quite important to improve numerical stability. However so far I didn't find any guidelines - is it better to divide parameter by some constant or take log or some other tricks. I wish there was some discussion in the manual or github. For example, the approximated posterior in unscaled parameter space looks like:
> > theta4 ~ lognormal(-7.87,0.99)
> > theta7 ~ lognormal(12.55,0.91)
> > Does it make sense to work in the parameter space of scaled_theta4=exp(theta4) and scaled_theta7=log(theta7) or is it better to define scaled_theta4=theta4*0.0006 where 0.0006=mean(rlnorm(10000,-7.87,0.99) and scaled_theta7=theta7/400000 where 40000=mean(rlnorm(10000,12.55,0.91))?
> >
> > Experts tell us that divergent transitions may lead to bias (there is a lot in this list) but it is hard to mine this info and glue together to get a good guidance. I wonder if scaling parameters has anything to do with divergent transitions. It would be great to summarize this info similar to https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Prior-Choice-Recommendations.
> >
> > The model I am working with is a PBPK model defined as a system of ODEs. Solving ODEs has some tolerances associated with it. In a PBPK model material balances have to be conserved (in=out) however because of ODE solver the material balances range in -10-3 to 10-3. May this be a cause for divergent transitions?
> >
> > Thanks for any insight,
> > Linas

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] scaling parameters & divergent transitions
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] scaling parameters & divergent transitions
messages.body_plain:
There do exist continuous interpolations between centered and
non-centered distributions, but it turns out that the transition to
optimally centered and optimally non-centered happens so quickly
that in practice none of them are all that useful.

The general issue here is that because you can build a arbitrary
model in the Stan language it can have arbitrary pathologies and
there will be no general solution to sampling problems.  We have
worked to develop as many broad techniques as possible, but
that’s all we can do without interrogating the exact model.

At that most general level diverges occur when the posterior
on the unconstrained scaled features strong curvature.  This
is straightforward to identify by running many iterations and
looking at the sampled that diverged and those that didn’t to
hunt down the source of the problem, which can then inform
what in your model is ultimately being problematic and what
you might want to adjust.  If you are using many constrained
types then you’ll want to use the diagnostic file which outputs
the unconstrained parameters, although it may not be as easy
to use in some of the interfaces.

Any chance it makes sense to run these different tests with good initial guesses on the parameters? If you're happy with the posteriors from your previous estimate and have reason to believe they aren't really changing, then maybe just initialize your new chains with samples from the posterior of one of your previous estimates?

I dunno -- maybe that'd make the warmup easier for Stan and you could get away with less warmup samples. Not sure if it really applies, or what sorta tests you're trying to do. If your inference took days before, in a good case this would still take days (just less days) so I dunno if that means anything.

data {

  vector<lower=0>[J] lambda;

  vector[J] mu;

  cov_matrix[J] sig_mvn;// covariance matrix of multivariate normal distribution
}
model {

  for (j in 1:J)

  log(lambda)~multi_normal(mu,sig_mvn);

  target += -log(fabs(lambda));

  for (j in 1:J)

}

> Thank you for your reply. I think you are right about the reason for the error. I reinstall Rtools and ran the code again. This time the error meassage showed first was:

None of these are error messages.

> DIAGNOSTIC(S) FROM PARSER:
> Warning (non-fatal):
> Left-hand side of sampling statement (~) may contain a non-linear transform of a parameter or local variable.
> If it does, you need to include a target += statement with the log absolute determinant of the Jacobian of the transform.
> Left-hand-side of sampling statement:
>     log(lambda) ~ multi_normal(...)
>
> which I had already included in my Stan code, so it continued.

Yes, although this can (and should) be avoided by declaring

vector[J] log_lambda;

in the parameters block and

vector[J] lambda = exp(log_lambda);

in the transformed parameters block and

target += multi_normal(log_lambda | mu, sig_mvn);

in the model block.

Although it is better still to declare a vector of standard deviations and a Cholesky factor of a correlation matrix in the parameters block rather than a covariance matrix, git rid of the inverse Wishart prior in favor of some prior on the standard deviations and a LKJ prior on the correlation matrix. Also, it is often better to compose log_lambda in the transformed parameters block as

vector[J] log_lambda = mu + diag_pre_multiply(L, sds) * z;
vector<lower=0>[J] lambda = exp(log_lambda);

where z is declared in the parameters block as

vector[J] z;

and has a standard normal prior in the model block

target += normal_lpdf(z | 0, 1);

> [1] "The following numerical problems occured the indicated number of times on chain 4"
>                                                                                                      count

Make your outages.stan file end in a blank line

Read that link

Look at that pairs plot, especially the diagonal elements of sig_mvn

messages.subject: Question about implementing probability of equality
messages.subject_clean: Question about implementing probability of equality
messages.body_plain:
Hey all,

I have posted several times about a funky model of mine, but I'm looking into all the various ways of examining the same question using variations on the model itself.

In one part of the model, there's a probability, delta, that two parameters are actually the same thing. I don't mean "the parameter for this group is essentially the same value as the parameter for another group", but rather they are literally the same thing; one should assume theta_1 = theta_2. This matters for the model because if they are the same, then the two groups inform the estimation of the single parameter rather than the two groups informing separate parameters.

Conceptually, what I would /like/ to do, is something like this. Say D=0 means they are the same, and D=1 means they are not. Delta is the probability of D.
y ~ p(parameter[group])
D ~ bernoulli(Delta)
if (D == 0) { parameter[2] = parameter[1] }
if (D == 1)}{ parameter[2] ~ normal(0,1)}
I know one needs to marginalize this for it to work in stan, but I'm at a loss for how one could do it in this case.

Conceptually, this is a bit like a mixture prior, where if D=0, then parameter[2] ~ normal(parameter[1], .0000001) [no real difference between parameter[2] and parameter[1]) and if D=1, then parameter[2] ~ normal(0,1) [it is permitted various values]. This is easy enough to code, but normal(parameter[1],.0000001) is very slow to sample due to the crazy curvature introduced by the prior.
Ideally, it would be a mixture between "we know the value is equal to parameter[1]" and "we know the value is independent of parameter[1]".
The inference is /not/ about whether parameter[2] - parameter[1], but this is a simple example of a much more complex model assessing measurement invariance.

Any ideas come to mind?

>
> I dunno -- maybe that'd make the warmup easier for Stan and you could get away with less warmup samples. Not sure if it really applies, or what sorta tests you're trying to do. If your inference took days before, in a good case this would still take days (just less days) so I dunno if that means anything.

This is going to get easier in 2.16 when we can initialize mass matrices.

During warmup, we need to get to the typical set and then we need to
draw a large enough sample to allow us to estimate the posterior (co)variance
(aka inverse mass matrix).  The initial values only help us get to the typical
set.  In 2.16, we should be able to initialize mass matrices, so if you
can do both, then you'll be set and won't need any warmup at all.

- Bob

This example tries to find the year at which the rate of mining disasters switches from parameter to another. Similarly, you could switch models entirely, or switch between a two parameter/one parameter thing.

messages.body_plain:
The idea is that, say, two groups are measured using the same measurement technique. The goal is to see whether the some of the measurement model parameters are equal or sufficiently different between groups to justify saying that the measurement operates differently on the two groups.
Therefore, the parameter[2] could equal parameter[1] (groups' observations are driven by the same process) or parameter[2] may be independent of parameter[1] (groups' observations driven by different processes).

One way of expressing this is to put a mixture prior on the parameter[2]: parameter[2] ~ (1-Delta)N(parameter[1],.00001) + Delta*N(0,1), but sampling from N(anything,.00001) is difficult due to curvature.
It's not the end of the world if I have to do something similar to that (or less extreme: (1-Delta)N(parameter[1],.05)), but I was curious what other options there may be for expressing this in a way that can more easily explore.
Like I said, conceptually, it's parameter[2] = parameter[1] if D=0, or is an independent variable if D=1.

> It's not the end of the world if I have to do something similar to that (or less extreme: (1-Delta)N(parameter[1],.05)), but I was curious what other options there may be for expressing this in a way that can more easily explore.
> Like I said, conceptually, it's parameter[2] = parameter[1] if D=0, or is an independent variable if D=1.
>
> On Monday, April 10, 2017 at 1:48:29 PM UTC-5, Sebastian Weber wrote:
> I don't quite get the idea, but what I certainly miss here is: scale!
>
> No continuous random quantity is ever exactly equal to some value, the density of a point is zero. I think you need to rephrase your question...but I could fully misunderstand you intentions.
>
> Sebastian
>
> On Monday, April 10, 2017 at 8:23:40 PM UTC+2, Stephen Martin wrote:
> Hey all,
>
> I have posted several times about a funky model of mine, but I'm looking into all the various ways of examining the same question using variations on the model itself.
>
> In one part of the model, there's a probability, delta, that two parameters are actually the same thing. I don't mean "the parameter for this group is essentially the same value as the parameter for another group", but rather they are literally the same thing; one should assume theta_1 = theta_2. This matters for the model because if they are the same, then the two groups inform the estimation of the single parameter rather than the two groups informing separate parameters.
>
> Conceptually, what I would /like/ to do, is something like this. Say D=0 means they are the same, and D=1 means they are not. Delta is the probability of D.
> y ~ p(parameter[group])
> D ~ bernoulli(Delta)
> if (D == 0) { parameter[2] = parameter[1] }
> if (D == 1)}{ parameter[2] ~ normal(0,1)}
> I know one needs to marginalize this for it to work in stan, but I'm at a loss for how one could do it in this case.
>
> Conceptually, this is a bit like a mixture prior, where if D=0, then parameter[2] ~ normal(parameter[1], .0000001) [no real difference between parameter[2] and parameter[1]) and if D=1, then parameter[2] ~ normal(0,1) [it is permitted various values]. This is easy enough to code, but normal(parameter[1],.0000001) is very slow to sample due to the crazy curvature introduced by the prior.
> Ideally, it would be a mixture between "we know the value is equal to parameter[1]" and "we know the value is independent of parameter[1]".
> The inference is /not/ about whether parameter[2] - parameter[1], but this is a simple example of a much more complex model assessing measurement invariance.
>
> Any ideas come to mind?
>

> --

> To unsubscribe from this group and stop receiving emails from it, send an email to stan-users+...@googlegroups.com.
> To post to this group, send email to stan-...@googlegroups.com.

messages.body_snippet:
Use a hierchical model.  That's what they're there for!

If you insist on what you're doing, just marginalize out the
indicator.  But if you have a bunch of those that interact,
it'll be intractable.

messages.body_plain:
Ah. Well, my sense after playing around with this a bit is that what you're saying is similar to a non-centered reparameterizations.  In my case, I have enough data in the cross-section (>500) that I usually get worse results with a non-centered reparameterization. I think that's why I see worse results with the approach you're talking about.

Something I just tried helps illustrate why I think the problem is the non-linear relationship. I calculated the Mahalanobis distance of the empirical intercepts and log standard deviations. I then removed the top 5% or so of the results, simulated data, and ran the relevant Stan models. No divergences and about 400/1000 N_Eff on lp__ and all the results look sensible.

I'm still trying a few things. In particular, I had the idea last week to do a mixture distribution for the intercepts and log standard deviations. My first attempt didn't go so well (I had tried to do a mixture letting only the correlation change, but it's kind of tricky because the only way to constrain an ordered vector is to make it positive), but I'm still at the early stages of trying stuff.

On Fri, Apr 7, 2017 at 1:55 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

> I just mean rather than having
>
>   alpha ~ normal(0, 1e-3);
>
> define
>
>   alpha_raw ~ normal(0, 1);
>
>   alpha = 1e-3 * alpha_raw;
>
> Then the parameters over which Stan is actually sampling, alpha_raw,
> will be unit scale, but you'll still have your original value alpha.
>
> - Bob

>
>
> > On Apr 6, 2017, at 6:42 PM, John Hall <john.mic...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > I'm hoping to hang my hat on the non-linear relationship between intercepts and standard deviations.
> >
> > I had tried normalizing the variables in the past and it didn't make nearly as much a difference as when I did simulations where the relationship was more linear or uncorrelated. I also multiplied the number of iterations by 10 (to 10,000 total post-warm up across 4 chains) and that didn't make a noticeable impact.
> >
> > When normalizing, I had subtracted each series by the overall mean and divided by the overall standard deviation. So in this case, the cross-sectional variation in the intercepts and standard deviations increased by about a factor of 10, but not up to 1. The standard deviation of the intercepts becomes something like 0.1 empirically, but most of the time when I run Stan it still gets shoved down to 0.01 in some of the simpler variations and divergences (in a simple simulation, but preserving the non-linearity).
> >
> > It doesn't make sense to me to subtract the series mean and divide by the series standard deviation. If I fit a hierarchical model, all the means should be 0 and the standard deviations 1, which kind of defeats the purpose of doing a hierarchical regression. This actually makes the standard deviation of the cross sectional means even smaller (and more more divergences).
> >
> > On Wed, Apr 5, 2017 at 6:11 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> > Thanks for the report.
> >
> > You'll find Stan has a lot easier time adapting if the parameters

> > >
> > >

> > > interval coverage for simulated data --- that'll let you assess whether
> > > your model's coded properly.  Then it's a different matter to asses whether
> > > it matches some real data set.
> > >
> > > The actual value (of the standard deviation on the hierarchically varying intercept) was closer to 0.01 and I was getting like 0.001. The intervals were way different. This was also what was driving the divergences. Basically, this standard deviation was getting too low. I played around a little with the specification and was getting better results.
> > >
> > > Also, I started using some of the diagnostics from Michael Betancourt's case study on the subject. They are definitely valuable.
> > >
> > >
> > > This is a key step in debugging.  Isolate the problem in
> > > a reproducible example that is as simple as possible.  Often
> > > by the time you've done that, the debugging job is done.
> > >
> > > This is one of the main reasons we suggest building models
> > > up from simpler models wherever possible.  It's tedious to
> > > build up one feature at a time, but at least you know exactly
> > > where the problem comes from when it arises.
> > >
> > > Of course, but sometimes until you fit the actual data you don't know there are going to be problems. I began with simpler models. I just needed to work with different simple models...
> > >
> > > I actually was able to isolate things and confirm that it really isn't the correlation between the intercepts and slopes that is causing the problem. I had previously mentioned that the data also has varying standard deviations that I estimate. Focusing on just the varying intercepts and standard deviations caused divergences with the actual data but not some simpler adjustments.
> > >
> > > The problem is that the more the intercept is below zero, the higher the standard deviation tends to be. However, the standard deviation also gets larger when the intercept is above zero, just not by as much. So, it's not a linear relationship between the two. I did a few plots trying to make it clear, but it's most obvious just looking at the square of the intercepts above and below a certain bound. For instance:
> > >
> > > >
> > > cor(alpha_new[(alpha_new ^ 2)>0.000025] ^ 2, log(sigma_new[(alpha_new ^ 2)>0.000025]))
> > >
> > > [1] 0.5878579
> > > >
> > > cor(alpha_new[(alpha_new ^ 2)<0.000025] ^ 2, log(sigma_new[(alpha_new ^ 2)<0.000025]))
> > >
> > > [1] -0.09757556
> > >
> > > This also makes it clear why when I had tried to simulate the parameters from a multivariate normal distribution I didn't have any problems. The problem isn't there when the distribution is multivariate normal.
> > >

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Gamma reparametrization into mode / sd - Question on jacobian transformation
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Gamma reparametrization into mode / sd - Question on jacobian transformation
messages.body_plain:
Thanks Bob

On Tuesday, April 11, 2017 at 1:20:32 AM UTC+10, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> You should be able to test that it recovers simulated
> data.  You'll have to invert the function you computed
> the Jacobian of to do that, I think.
>
> - Bob
>
> > On Apr 9, 2017, at 2:13 AM, stefano <mangiol...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Thanks Bob,
> >
> > sorry for the images.
> >
> > the new Jacobian that I came up with is from (see also attachment, same image)
> >
> > <Capture.PNG>
> >
> > for which the absolute determinant is sqrt(x)/y^2 + 1/(2 sqrt(x) y)
> >
> > <Capture2.PNG>
> >
> > For which log increment is
> >
> > for(p in 1:P) for(g in 1:G)
> >     target += log(2*alpha[p,g] + beta[p,g]) - (0.5*log(alpha[p,g])) - (2*log(beta[p,g])) - log(2);
> >
> > I hope it makes sanse.
> >
> > Thanks for your support!
> >
> > 2017-04-08 9:14 GMT+10:00 Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com>:
> > The formulas didn't come through.
> >
> > You want to compute the Jacobian for
> >
> >  f : (alpha, beta) -> (alpha, sqrt(alpha) / beta)
> >
> > Then you can put priors on alpha and on sqrt(alpha) / beta.
> > You probably wouldn't also want a prior on beta, but if
> > you include one, it just gets multiplied into the density (added
> > to the log density).
> >
> > - Bob
> >
> >
> > > On Apr 4, 2017, at 10:40 PM, stefano <mangiol...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > Thanks Bob,
> > >
> > > 1)
> > >
> > > just to make sure that is correct, I share a possible solution.
> > >
> > > Considering that my priors will be
> > >
> > > alpha ~ gamma( .., ..)
> > > sqrt(alpha)/beta ~ normal( ang_coeff *  (alpha[n]-1)/beta[n], sigma )
> > >
> > > a possible solution will be adjusting for Jacobian with two variables
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > for(n in 1:N)
> > > target += log(alpha[n] + 1) - log2 - 3*log(beta[n]) - 0.5 * log(alpha[n])
> > >
> > > 2)
> > >
> > > it does not make sense to add
> > >
> > > beta ~ gamma( .., .. )
> > >
> > > right? Or it could be done? In this case alpha and beta would have overlapping priors.
> > >
> > > Thanks a lot!
> > >
> > >
> > > 2017-04-04 2:54 GMT+10:00 Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com>:
> > > You need the Jacobian of the f:R^2 -> R^2 function
> > >
> > >   f(alpha, beta) = sqrt(alpha / beta^2),  (alpha - 1) / beta
> > >
> > > if you're going to declare alpha and beta as parameters and
> > > put a prior on sqrt(alpha / beta^2) and (alpha - 1) / beta.
> > > I'd also recommend sqrt(alpha) / beta as it does less arithmetic
> > > and should also be more stable for small beta.
> > >
> > > Alternatively, you can declare a parameter
> > >
> > >   vector[N] sqrt_alpha_over_beta;
> > >
> > > and define
> > >
> > >   sqrt_alpha_over_beta ~ ...
> > >
> > > and then derive the inverse of f to get alpha and beta back.
> > > Then you won't need a Jacobian as you're putting the distribution
> > > right on the parameter.
> > >
> > > - Bob
> > >
> > >
> > > > On Mar 31, 2017, at 12:28 AM, Luke <mangiol...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > >
> > > > Hello, I'm loving Stan!
> > > >
> > > > I have a question on jacobians within Stan.
> > > >
> > > > A pattern is emerging on the sd sqrt(alpha/beta^2) and mode (alpha-1)/beta of a gamma distributed parameter.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Now I can reparametrize the gamma distribution for mode and sd but then I have to link mode and sd in, for example:
> > > >
> > > > sd[n] ~ normal( ang_coeff * mode, sigma[n] );  equal to

messages.body_plain:
Yes, I agree that being general precludes very detailed recipes. I found case studies very helpful. And perhaps adding couple of more studies where divergent transitions drive re-parametrization would be awesome. Since I am planning to contribute my 6+ month stan project maybe this could be such a study. One confounding factor is that my model is a bunch of ODEs and the accuracy of ODE solution may affect the divergencies.

Per Bob's advice I have scaled all my parameters to unit normal (single variate since parameters seems to be independent based on pairs plot).
stheta~N(0,1). The parameters passed to ODE solver are transformed parameters in the form: theta=exp(a+b*stheta). To represent individual parameters I used non-centered parametrization, i.e. theta_ind=theta*exp(u*sigma_ind) where u~N(0,1). I have used exponential form since physiological parameters are positive and presumably log normal. Then after plotting pairs plot I saw the dreaded shape of a funnel and it seems bunch of diverged (in red) were at the neck of the funnel while some others looked random. I am simply stuck with any ideas for further reparametrization since I am already using non-centered. For some pairs (theta,sigma_ind) divergencies were on the side. The model is attached.

Several months ago I experimented with various ways of bridging between the two parameterizations, hoping to get the best of both worlds, but it didn't work.
A

> On Apr 10, 2017, at 12:49 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> There do exist continuous interpolations between centered and
> non-centered distributions, but it turns out that the transition to
> optimally centered and optimally non-centered happens so quickly
> that in practice none of them are all that useful.
>
> The general issue here is that because you can build a arbitrary
> model in the Stan language it can have arbitrary pathologies and
> there will be no general solution to sampling problems.  We have
> worked to develop as many broad techniques as possible, but
> that’s all we can do without interrogating the exact model.
>
> At that most general level diverges occur when the posterior
> on the unconstrained scaled features strong curvature.  This
> is straightforward to identify by running many iterations and
> looking at the sampled that diverged and those that didn’t to
> hunt down the source of the problem, which can then inform
> what in your model is ultimately being problematic and what
> you might want to adjust.  If you are using many constrained
> types then you’ll want to use the diagnostic file which outputs
> the unconstrained parameters, although it may not be as easy
> to use in some of the interfaces.

dnorm(0, mean = 0, sd = 0.25, log = TRUE) # 0.467

Ben

I finally finished the case study I've been working on:

Typical Sets and the Curse of Dimensionality
---------------------------------------------

http://mc-stan.org/documentation/case-studies/curse-dims.html

This case study illustrates the so-called “curse of dimensionality,” starting from scratch and using simple examples based on simulation. For example, generating points uniformly at random in a unit hypercube, it is easy to see how the average distance between random points increases with dimensionality. Similarly, such points tend to increasingly fall outside the hypersphere inscribed within the unit hypercube, showing that in higher dimensions, almost all of the volume is in the corners of the hypercube.

Similarly, generating standard normal variates (zero mean, unit standard deviation) leads to draws that concentrate in a thin shell of increasing distance from the mean as dimensionality increases. The squared distance of a standard normal draw from the mode follows a standard chi-square distribution with degrees of freedom equal to the dimensionality. This allows the the precise bounds of the thin shell to be calculated using tail statistics, showing just how unlikely it is to get near the mode with a random draw from a standard multivariate normal.

These properties of the standard normal distribution provides a segue into discussing the important information-theoretic concept of the typical set for a probability distribution, which is roughly defined as the central log density band into which almost all random draws from that distribution will fall. The rather surprising result is that for a normal distribution in high dimensions, the typical set does not include the volume around the mode. The density is highest around the mode, but the volume is low, and the probability mass is determined as the product of the density and the volume (or more precisely, the integral of the density over the volume).

The standard normal log density is just negative squared Euclidean distance, which provides a straightforward demonstration of why the maximum likelihood estimate for a normal regression is identical to the least squares solution.
---------------------------------------------

- Bob

P.S.  I decided in the end not to rehash the discussion from Andrew's
blog which follows from this understanding of typical sets:

http://andrewgelman.com/2017/03/15/ensemble-methods-doomed-fail-high-dimensions/

I want to concentrate on things that will go into the Stan book,
though Michael will probably wind up writing about typical sets, not me!

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Explicitly Correlated Parameters
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Explicitly Correlated Parameters
messages.body_plain:
It seems like the problem is more evident the less data there is. I simulated 10, 5, 2.5, 2, 1.5, 1, 0.5 times the amount of data in the original data set (of 10 years of monthly data) and the results looked great at 5 and 10 times and then steadily get worse the less data is available.

In the past, I have used a formula from Gelman and Hill (21.14) to determine the amount of pooling in models. Near 0 and there is little pooling and near 1 and there is a lot of pooling. Sure enough, the pooling factor for the varying standard deviations was near 0 (little to no pooling) across all the simulations, but for the varying intercepts the more data was available the closer it was to 0 (and estimated well) and the less data available the closer it was to 1.

So my sense is that I shouldn't worry too much that it isn't estimated all that well...

On Mon, Apr 10, 2017 at 6:23 PM, John Hall <john.mic...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hmmm, I noticed an error in the code I thought illustrated the error well. I had accidentally removed the hierarchical prior from the intercepts so that it would just include a separate intercept for each one. Adding back the hierarchical prior results in divergences...even with the outliers removed...
>
> On Mon, Apr 10, 2017 at 5:57 PM, John Hall <john.mic...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Ah. Well, my sense after playing around with this a bit is that what you're saying is similar to a non-centered reparameterizations.  In my case, I have enough data in the cross-section (>500) that I usually get worse results with a non-centered reparameterization. I think that's why I see worse results with the approach you're talking about.
> >
> > Something I just tried helps illustrate why I think the problem is the non-linear relationship. I calculated the Mahalanobis distance of the empirical intercepts and log standard deviations. I then removed the top 5% or so of the results, simulated data, and ran the relevant Stan models. No divergences and about 400/1000 N_Eff on lp__ and all the results look sensible.
> >
> > I'm still trying a few things. In particular, I had the idea last week to do a mixture distribution for the intercepts and log standard deviations. My first attempt didn't go so well (I had tried to do a mixture letting only the correlation change, but it's kind of tricky because the only way to constrain an ordered vector is to make it positive), but I'm still at the early stages of trying stuff.
> >
> > On Fri, Apr 7, 2017 at 1:55 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> > > I just mean rather than having
> > >
> > >   alpha ~ normal(0, 1e-3);
> > >
> > > define
> > >
> > >   alpha_raw ~ normal(0, 1);
> > >
> > >   alpha = 1e-3 * alpha_raw;
> > >
> > > Then the parameters over which Stan is actually sampling, alpha_raw,

> > >
> > > - Bob
> > >
> > >
> > > > On Apr 6, 2017, at 6:42 PM, John Hall <john.mic...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > >
> > > > I'm hoping to hang my hat on the non-linear relationship between intercepts and standard deviations.
> > > >
> > > > I had tried normalizing the variables in the past and it didn't make nearly as much a difference as when I did simulations where the relationship was more linear or uncorrelated. I also multiplied the number of iterations by 10 (to 10,000 total post-warm up across 4 chains) and that didn't make a noticeable impact.
> > > >
> > > > When normalizing, I had subtracted each series by the overall mean and divided by the overall standard deviation. So in this case, the cross-sectional variation in the intercepts and standard deviations increased by about a factor of 10, but not up to 1. The standard deviation of the intercepts becomes something like 0.1 empirically, but most of the time when I run Stan it still gets shoved down to 0.01 in some of the simpler variations and divergences (in a simple simulation, but preserving the non-linearity).
> > > >
> > > > It doesn't make sense to me to subtract the series mean and divide by the series standard deviation. If I fit a hierarchical model, all the means should be 0 and the standard deviations 1, which kind of defeats the purpose of doing a hierarchical regression. This actually makes the standard deviation of the cross sectional means even smaller (and more more divergences).
> > > >
> > > > On Wed, Apr 5, 2017 at 6:11 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> > > > Thanks for the report.
> > > >
> > > > You'll find Stan has a lot easier time adapting if the parameters
> > > > are on the scale of 1 rather than 1e-3.  If you give Stan long
> > > > enough to warmup, it should adapt to the right scales, but it might
> > > > take a while.
> > > >
> > > > - Bob
> > > >
> > > > > On Apr 5, 2017, at 5:10 PM, John Hall <john.mic...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > On Tue, Apr 4, 2017 at 1:47 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> > > > > How are you assessing bias?  Are you talking about the posterior
> > > > > mean as an estimate of the parameter?  I'd recommend looking at posterior
> > > > > interval coverage for simulated data --- that'll let you assess whether
> > > > > your model's coded properly.  Then it's a different matter to asses whether
> > > > > it matches some real data set.
> > > > >
> > > > > The actual value (of the standard deviation on the hierarchically varying intercept) was closer to 0.01 and I was getting like 0.001. The intervals were way different. This was also what was driving the divergences. Basically, this standard deviation was getting too low. I played around a little with the specification and was getting better results.
> > > > >
> > > > > Also, I started using some of the diagnostics from Michael Betancourt's case study on the subject. They are definitely valuable.
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > This is a key step in debugging.  Isolate the problem in
> > > > > a reproducible example that is as simple as possible.  Often
> > > > > by the time you've done that, the debugging job is done.
> > > > >
> > > > > This is one of the main reasons we suggest building models
> > > > > up from simpler models wherever possible.  It's tedious to
> > > > > build up one feature at a time, but at least you know exactly
> > > > > where the problem comes from when it arises.
> > > > >
> > > > > Of course, but sometimes until you fit the actual data you don't know there are going to be problems. I began with simpler models. I just needed to work with different simple models...
> > > > >
> > > > > I actually was able to isolate things and confirm that it really isn't the correlation between the intercepts and slopes that is causing the problem. I had previously mentioned that the data also has varying standard deviations that I estimate. Focusing on just the varying intercepts and standard deviations caused divergences with the actual data but not some simpler adjustments.
> > > > >
> > > > > The problem is that the more the intercept is below zero, the higher the standard deviation tends to be. However, the standard deviation also gets larger when the intercept is above zero, just not by as much. So, it's not a linear relationship between the two. I did a few plots trying to make it clear, but it's most obvious just looking at the square of the intercepts above and below a certain bound. For instance:
> > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > cor(alpha_new[(alpha_new ^ 2)>0.000025] ^ 2, log(sigma_new[(alpha_new ^ 2)>0.000025]))
> > > > >
> > > > > [1] 0.5878579
> > > > > >
> > > > > cor(alpha_new[(alpha_new ^ 2)<0.000025] ^ 2, log(sigma_new[(alpha_new ^ 2)<0.000025]))
> > > > >
> > > > > [1] -0.09757556
> > > > >
> > > > > This also makes it clear why when I had tried to simulate the parameters from a multivariate normal distribution I didn't have any problems. The problem isn't there when the distribution is multivariate normal.
> > > > >
> > > > > Anyway, I tried to incorporate this into the simple model without much luck.
> > > > >

messages.body_plain:
I had a look at your model. Is this what you're trying to do with x_r : https://github.com/stan-dev/math/issues/58 ?

I think as of now there's not a clean built-in way to interpolate data like that in an ODE in Stan.

I think the issue is you need a smooth interpolation -- a simple 1D linear interpolation isn't differentiable at the data points. I think a lot of us with ODEs have run into this.

There's a dude in that post who shows a solution. I dunno how well it works. At one point I had a pretty simple function to interpolate and was able to approximate it using a cosine/sine expansion with a few terms (FFT).

Not sure on the vectorization. I think an ODE solve is usually a slow enough thing that there isn't a reason to try to vectorize it.

Ben

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Evaluating +inf and -inf to prevent overflow and underflow in Generated Quantities?
messages.body_plain:
inv_logit itself isn't very stable, as it's just this:

  inv_logit(x) = 1 / (1 + exp(-x))

No way to stop that exp from overflowing or rounding under
to zero.  Around x = -700 and we round to zero, and we should
round to 1 even sooner on the postive x side, probably around 25 or
30 or so.

What we may need in the RNG is something that tests for whether
the argument is 0 or 1 and just returns a string of those results.

- bob

> I had a look at your model. Is this what you're trying to do with x_r : https://github.com/stan-dev/math/issues/58 <https://www.google.com/url?q=https%3A%2F%2Fgithub.com%2Fstan-dev%2Fmath%2Fissues%2F58&sa=D&sntz=1&usg=AFQjCNGBqgEc5yG0HTzNQFcGs_kuRYki2Q> ?
>

>
> I think the issue is you need a smooth interpolation -- a simple 1D linear interpolation isn't differentiable at the data points. I think a lot of us with ODEs have run into this.
>
> There's a dude in that post who shows a solution. I dunno how well it works. At one point I had a pretty simple function to interpolate and was able to approximate it using a cosine/sine expansion with a few terms (FFT).

Maybe https://github.com/stan-dev/math/issues/58 is going to help me.

>
> Not sure on the vectorization. I think an ODE solve is usually a slow enough thing that there isn't a reason to try to vectorize it.

Well, it's just because there is a strange behavior, and I opened an issue here : https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/2272
>
> Ben

Virgile

Hi Liza.

Happy to hear how the Kronecker stuff works for you--hopefully the backend work that Rob Trangucci has been doing will mean some performance gains. How big is your dataset / how many grid cells do you have when you discretize?

Some other ideas for a Cox process, none of which I've quite implemented but seem like they should work okay based on some other projects in which I've tried similar things:

- Parameterize the intensity using a radial basis function network formulation, e.g. pick a set of "landmark" points and place kernels centered at these points. For mots kernel choices you should be able to work out the necessary integral in closed form, since the intensity is parametric. The reason I think this should work is that it's pretty similar to an standard version of the Hawkes process, which I have an implementation of in Stan (see: https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.06713) and will be cleaning up to share soon.

- Parameterize the intensity using some other set of simple basis functions (linear + quadratic?) - same idea as above in terms of working out the integral. Maybe someone out there already has a Stan implementation of this?

- Related to radial basis networks would be an inducing points approach. I know someone had inducing points in Stan but you'll have to search the list.

- Use Random Fourier Features. I've done this in other places and can share code, but not for Cox processes in Stan...

- Do something Bayesian based on my AISTATS '17 paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/1610.08623 ; I'm not exactly sure what it'd mean to do a Bayesian version of this yet. Maybe it'd work to simply put priors on the relevant hyperparameters and learn by sampling rather than crossvalidation? If other people have thoughts, let me know.

Seth

messages.body_plain:
Andrew,

I think if you read clinical studies for medical devices carefully enough the allowance for informative priors as long as they are scientifically based is there (we need to doublecheck). But prevailing recommendation is using non informative priors. Therefore my guess the conception is that FDA is not supporting strong priors. We can't deny that FDA has prominent Bayesists. The recent comment about using informative prior by FDA statistician was "how we defend the approach with industry" so there are some other aspects that are not so visible. In my case the strong prior is justified since 5% error in urine measurements is tight but still in the realm of reasonable. Since we had only few data points it was the only way to reconstruct the parameters and show that PBPK models fit clinical data well.

Perhaps it would be preferable to leave my name out.

Linas

messages.body_plain:
Yeah, linear interpolation is the thing you can't do very easily.

What you're saying in your comments is that you need to cast your time value (a real) to an integer somehow so you can index a lookup table somewhere.

I don't think there's a way in Stan to do this cast (correct me if I'm wrong?) because casting real parameters to integers messes up the derivatives you need for sampling. I think I misspoke about the linear interpolation differentiability thing (separate issue kinda).

That's why I ended up using a basis expansion for my function (cause then you never need to do this cast).

If you can build:

f_approx(t) = sum over i (a_i * basis_i(t))

Then there's no need to cast t from a real to an int.

You could do this with any sorta regression tool you want. Whatever is appropriate for the data. You may be able to build this regression into Stan, but dunno how much you want to try to do with one inference.

Not sure if this is a good way to proceed though. I didn't succeed with my inference, but I think it was more my problem. Maybe someone else knows a way to do this? I don't want to mislead you.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
You can interpolate without messing up derivatives if you're
careful, but to do it in Stan's a real hack because we don't
have a function to round/floor/ceiling a real value to an int.

If someone can characterize a general form of interpolation,
we could also build it in the way BUGS does.

- Bob

> On Apr 13, 2017, at 2:43 PM, Ben B <bbba...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Yeah, linear interpolation is the thing you can't do very easily.
>
> What you're saying in your comments is that you need to cast your time value (a real) to an integer somehow so you can index a lookup table somewhere.
>
> I don't think there's a way in Stan to do this cast (correct me if I'm wrong?) because casting real parameters to integers messes up the derivatives you need for sampling. I think I misspoke about the linear interpolation differentiability thing (separate issue kinda).
>
> That's why I ended up using a basis expansion for my function (cause then you never need to do this cast).
>
> If you can build:
>
> f_approx(t) = sum over i (a_i * basis_i(t))
>
> Then there's no need to cast t from a real to an int.
>
> You could do this with any sorta regression tool you want. Whatever is appropriate for the data. You may be able to build this regression into Stan, but dunno how much you want to try to do with one inference.
>
> Not sure if this is a good way to proceed though. I didn't succeed with my inference, but I think it was more my problem. Maybe someone else knows a way to do this? I don't want to mislead you.
>
> Ben

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Thanks for the great language and for everyone's contribution to this mailing list,

Hopefully this question is general enough to be of interest to more than my specific problem:

I'm trying to fit a Beta-Binomial model where the "true" N # of possible observations is considered an unknown mixture of data observations and missing counts, i.e.

where y is # of successes in n trials,

Y ~ BetaBinomial(N, alpha, beta)

N = Nobs + Nmiss

Nmiss ~ Poisson(lambda)

and etc. for the usual priors and additive link functions.

Marginalizing isn't terribly helpful in this situation, as the beta-binomial is constrained to require an 'int' input, and even if I were to marginalize the Poisson to a conjugate gamma posterior, I would lose in the 'Nobs + Nmiss' term.

Any ideas on how to work around this in Stan would be greatly appreciated!

Thanks,
Graeme

messages.subject: Regularised latent variable model converges on n=200 but fails on n=1000(same generative data model)
messages.subject_clean: Regularised latent variable model converges on n=200 but fails on n=1000(same generative data model)
messages.body_plain:
I'm trying to fit a latent variable model with 15 observed Gaussian variables all regressed onto 3 latent variables (observed vars are conditionally independent). The model differentiates between 'primary' and 'secondary' relationships between the latent and observed vars, with each observed variable having 5 primary relationships with one latent variable, and 5 secondary relationships with each of the other 2. The intent is to allow for the simultaneous estimation of all observed-latent relationships whilst maintaining model identifiability.  This is achieved by setting vague priors on the main relationships, N(0, 1), and regularising priors on all the secondary relationships, such as N(0, 0.1). My current model code is attached, primary relationships are also constrained positive for identifiability but secondary are not.

On simulated data with N=200 the model performs well, converging in a reasonable time. However, fitting it to an N=1000 data set produced by the same generative model convergence fails with different chains converging to different optimums. I've also tried fitting equivalent models where the variance of the regularising priors is itself a real valued parameter, in case the increase in sample size required a stronger shrinkage prior but the same convergence to separate optimums was observed in this new parameter, along with the others previously affected. It looks like nothing more than an increase in the sample size is pushing the model from identified to non-identified but I've not seen that type of behaviour before.

I've attached my model as I expect the issue may lie in my specification. If anyone has seen similar issues in scaling multivariate regularised models it would be great to hear of any workarounds. Any other model critique also very welcome!
