Andrew,

No problem, I don't think that my name substantiates the blog - I am not a prominent scientist. However, I completely agree with you - priors should be scientifically justified. Personally I am struggling with this - what prior should I use. When I have lots of data it becomes easy - slightly informative prior which makes sense works fine since data does the talking. There are some problematic situations - when you get several modes. Then I define the more informative prior on a parameter which leads to multiple modes - usually it is easy to figure out if parameters have physical meaning. When I have few data points (as in this case) I had to use reasonably tight prior based on historical experience in order to demonstrate that a good model is indeed good. I still plan to relax the prior and see how the fit changes.

Linas

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Beta-binomial w/poisson count of unknown total - working around int constraint?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Beta-binomial w/poisson count of unknown total - working around int constraint?
messages.body_plain:
There's no general way to marginalize out count variables in
Stan.

What does the rest of the model look like and is there
a reasonable upper and lower bound on Nmiss?  Sometimes
you can do continuous approximations (not by rounding, but
by considering Y to be continuous) and sometimes you can
marginalize out if the reasonable range for Nmiss is constrained
to the hundreds.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
It looks to me like you're putting a sampling statement into a variable, which doesn't make much sense.

I think what you would have wanted (based on https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/4d02/f73c1acf1af08090639f166ccde8f691e2bc.pdf) was something like
weights[k] = x^alpha * (1 - x)^beta / exp(lbeta(alpha, beta));
which might be equivalent to
weights[k] = inc_beta(alpha, beta, x);
but I would defer to someone else to confirm.

Anyway, I think the first one makes it pretty obvious why it cancels out when you divide by the sum.

You could also speed things up by doing the calculation of x in transformed data. You might also be able to vectorize the weights calculation.

messages.subject: bayesplot v1.2.0 released
messages.subject_clean: bayesplot v1.2.0 released
messages.body_plain:
Dear Stan+R users,

Version 1.2.0 of the bayesplot R package is now available on CRAN <https://cran.r-project.org/package=bayesplot>. It has a few fixes and also a lot of new features.
The release notes <https://github.com/stan-dev/bayesplot/releases/tag/v1.2.0> are copied below and the package can be installed in the standard way from CRAN using

install.packages("bayesplot")

 - Stan Development Team

-----

bayesplot 1.2.0 Release Notes

(GitHub issue/PR numbers in parentheses)

Fixes

* Avoid error in some cases when divergences is specified in call to
mcmc_trace but there are not actually any divergent transitions.
* The merge_chains argument to mcmc_nuts_energy now defaults to FALSE.

New features in existing functions

* For mcmc_* functions, transformations are recycled if the transformations argument is specified as a single function rather than a named list. Thanks to @tklebel. (#64)
* For ppc_violin_grouped there is now the option of showing y as a violin, points, or both. Thanks to @silberzwiebel. (#74)
* color_scheme_get now has an optional argument `i` for selecting only a subset of the colors.
* New color schemes: darkgray, orange, viridis, viridisA, viridisB, viridisC. The viridis schemes are better than the other schemes for trace plots (the
colors are very distinct from each other).

New functions

* mcmc_pairs, which is essentially a ggplot2+grid implementation of rstan's pairs.stanfit method. (#67)
* mcmc_hex, which is similar to mcmc_scatter but using geom_hex instead of geom_point. This can be used to avoid overplotting. (#67)
* overlay_function convenience function. Example usage: add a Gaussian (or any distribution) density curve to a plot made with mcmc_hist.
* mcmc_recover_scatter and mcmc_recover_hist, which are similar to mcmc_recover_intervals and compare estimates to "true" values used to simulate data. (#81, #83)
* New PPC category Discrete with functions:
    - ppc_rootogram for use with models for count data. Thanks to @paul-buerkner. (#28)
    - ppc_bars, ppc_bars_grouped for use with models for ordinal, categorical and multinomial data. Thanks to @silberzwiebel. (#73)
* New PPC category LOO (thanks to suggestions from @avehtari) with functions:
    - ppc_loo_pit for assessing the calibration of marginal predictions. (#72)
    - ppc_loo_intervals, ppc_loo_ribbon for plotting intervals of the LOO predictive distribution. (#72)

I am not sure if this is exactly what you need, but in the current development version of the bridgesampling package you can pass a fitted rstan object (i.e., which contains posteriors samples) directly to the bridge sampler to obtain the marginal likelihood. It is no Adiabatic MC, but the bridge sampler appears solid in getting the job done.

You currently have to use the stan_interface branch though: https://github.com/quentingronau/bridgesampling/tree/stan_interface
Install via devtools::install_github("quentingronau/bridgesampling@stan_interface")

For two examples see:
https://htmlpreview.github.io/?https://github.com/quentingronau/bridgesampling/blob/stan_interface/inst/doc/bridgesampling_example_stan.html
https://htmlpreview.github.io/?https://github.com/quentingronau/bridgesampling/blob/stan_interface/inst/doc/bridgesampling_stan_ttest.html

(The examples calculate the Bayes Factors but should get you going)

Best,
Henrik

messages.body_plain:
Thanks a lot Andrew. That is very encouraging feedback.

Quentin (who is the main author of the bridge sampler code and the vignettes) is a PhD student of E.J. Wagenmakers in Amsterdam. And we (i.e., Quentin, E.,J., and I) are definitely planning to keep you guys in the loop about the progress of the package. Right now we are still a little in the testing stage (but there do not appear to be any more major bugs).

As I already mentioned in a previous mail on the list, the main issue for us right now for the stan interface are related to the current rstan version. Our wishlist currently is:
- A method that recompiles the C++ code of a model from the fitted stanfit object. Currently we cannot call and rstan::log_prob() or rstan::unconstrain_pars() if the model was fitted in a different R session. Given that the stanfit object contains everything needed for compiling (minus the original data object), that seems in principle solvable.
- Ability to pass more than one set of samples per call to rstan::unconstrain_pars().
But we are obviously happy to wait until rstan3 as we found workarounds for both problems (in the first case the user needs to compile the model again just without samples and pass both).

Best,
Henrik

 CL[1, 15] ~ normal(0, 10);

Since y is data here and isn't being sampled over, wouldn't it make sense to change this example?

In that model,

log(y) ~ normal(mu, sigma)

and

y ~ lognormal(y | mu, sigma)

*Are*, from a sampling perspective, equivalent. The log probabilities are a bit off, but whatever. I was looking at this transformed parameter stuff a couple days ago and that was bugging me.

I think it'd just make more sense to show a manually constrained sigma parameter. Here's a gist comparing the two lognormal examples: https://gist.github.com/bbbales2/2f68c4a9111284c0df8ad2f56505b495 . Here's a gist showing a manually constrained sigma variable: https://gist.github.com/bbbales2/34602cacc6cddeae68c68228670882f3 .

Also, and I don't know if this is what Andre was asking, but if this were a parameter and we wanted to enforce a lower bound constraint:

real<lower = 0.0> sigma;

Then if we wrote that in the model, Stan would already apply that transformation, and so manually adding an adjustment would be like a 2nd adjustment (dunno if that's what he's asking). In this case, the <lower=0.0> specification is in the data block so it's only used to verify the input data and there's no transform, but again, in this example it doesn't really matter :D.

As a side note, it might be worth referencing chapter 20 (especially section 20.3, Change of Variables) as well as 33.1 in this section. It's got a good discussion about the transformations where you need the Jacobian and the ones where you don't. (Also, @Andre, check out Section 20.3)

Using the lognormal function is less numerically stable than using the normal function on the logarithm of the outcome.

> Also, and I don't know if this is what Andre was asking, but if this were a parameter and we wanted to enforce a lower bound constraint:
>
> real<lower = 0.0> sigma;

> Then if we wrote that in the model, Stan would already apply that transformation, and so manually adding an adjustment would be like a 2nd adjustment (dunno if that's what he's asking). In this case, the <lower=0.0> specification is in the data block so it's only used to verify the input data and there's no transform, but again, in this example it doesn't really matter :D.

For any constraints declared in the parameters block, Stan already does the Jacobian adjustment, in which case doing a second Jacobian adjustment would be wrong. For transformations in data or transformed data, no Jacobian adjustment is needed. If you use sampling statements, then Stan will warn you more than 100% of the time when a Jacobian adjustment is needed by the user. If you use target += statements, then Stan will not always warn you when a Jacobian adjustment is needed by the user.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Apologies for the self-advertising but as (I think) it is relevant:

We just put up a pre-print 'Continuously tempered Hamiltonian Monte Carlo <https://arxiv.org/abs/1704.03338>' on arXiv which presents a method for calculating normalising constants within HMC (or NUTS) frameworks such as Stan or PyMC3. It is related to Adiabatic Monte Carlo, but uses a different Hamiltonian formulation which makes it simpler to implement (it just requires integrating a standard Hamiltonian dynamic on a slightly extended state space), with the trade off of less coherent movement through the inverse temperature dimension than Adiabatic Monte Carlo.

Technically it can be applied already using Stan as it just requires defining an augmented target log density and then running NUTS (or static HMC) in that augmented space. For example Stan code for the experiments of a previous workshop version of the paper is available in Appendix G here <http://approximateinference.org/accepted/GrahamStorkey2016.pdf>.

A key factor of the performance in more complex models is however how 'close' the base density sampled from at zero inverse temperatures is to the target density. In the paper we suggest using a variational method such as ADVI to fit a parametric approximation to the target density (e.g. Gaussian) and then use this as the base density. Although the ADVI implementation in Stan can be used to fit such an approximate density, from my explorations in the Pystan source / documentation it did not seem possible at the moment to extract the mean / covariance parameters of the fitted ADVI Gaussian approximation directly, only to draw samples from the approximation (if there is a way to do this in Pystan or one of the other interfaces it would be great to find out how). Although the samples can be used to estimate the mean / covariance indirectly this is a bit clunky and slow. As an alternative the base density can be fitted externally and the its parameters fed in as 'data' to an extended Stan model (this was the approach used in the aforementioned Stan experiments in the workshop paper).

If using Python is an option (and if its not too heretical to mention alternative packages on this mailing list!), the current ADVI implementation in PyMC3 does allow directly accessing the parameters of the fitted ADVI density and together with the NUTS implementation in PyMC3, can be used to run the method in the paper and estimate normalising constants. A Jupyter notebook giving a PyMC3 implementation performing marginal likelihood estimation for the Bayesian hierarchical regression problem discussed in section 7.3 of the paper is available here <https://github.com/matt-graham/continuously-tempered-hmc/blob/master/notebooks/bayesian-hierarchical-regression-model.ipynb> (the PyMC3 model there is an adaption of the example Stan model here <https://github.com/stan-dev/example-models/blob/master/ARM/Ch.12/radon_group_chr.stan>).

Regards,
Matt

I've just started learning Stan (2.14.2) as part of my first foray into Bayesian statistics. I'm implementing a zero-inflated Poisson model. I've attached the data, model, and R driver file.

The problem is as follows. Whenever I include a squared term as a predictor in either the Bernoulli or Poisson component, I get several hundred divergent transitions. This only occurs for squared terms, regardless of which term I use. The problem persists regardless of scaling predictors in advance. Parameter estimates make sense. Setting a bunch of control options does not get rid of the divergent transitions. I've checked the documentation, and this recommends reparameterization, which I do not understand at this point. I adapted the model code from Bayesian Data Analysis in Ecology using Linear Models in R, BUGS, and Stan (chapter 14 section 2).

Can someone tell me what I'm doing wrong?

Thank you,
Michiel Pillet

This should be my final word on the subject. I think I finally have a decent understanding of why I was getting the results.

I did the above a little more thoroughly, plotting a wider range. Basically, I simulated data as above, such that T/N for the data from around 0.05 to 10. I then calculated the lambda formula I mentioned above, it looks something like
lambda = 1 - var(apply(e, 2, mean)) / mean(apply(e, 1, var))
where e is the de-meaned parameters (the varying intercepts and standard deviations. I had saved both the numerator and denominator to get some greater sense of everything.

In both cases, plotting lambda as a function of T/N looks like a 1/x graph. However, for small T/N, the varying standard deviation lambda is relatively small, whereas the varying intercept lambda is close to 1. By the time T/N gets to 2 or so, the lambda get relatively flat at low levels (the standard deviation lambda is still lower though).

It was also interesting to plot the numerator and the denominator of lambda against each other. For the varying standard deviation, it looked pretty linear, but the points eventually bunch up at some long-term values. However, the values for the varying intercept look a little different. For larger T/N, it looks linear, like the varying standard deviations. However, for smaller T/N, the numerator goes to zero faster than the denominator. So the bottom looks a bit like a square root plot, but the top is more linear.

So the way I read this is that when T/N is small, the intercepts all cluster around the pooled mean, but as T/N increases, then it increasingly becomes possible to differentiate between them.

The issue became a little more obvious to me when I wrote out what a multivariate distribution of all the data would look like. In particular, for the covariance, there would be a block diagonal matrix representing the covariance of the varying intercepts plus a diagonal matrix with a different value for each N representing the different variances. Compared to a simpler model with only varying intercepts, the second part would just be a constant diagonal matrix. This would allow the varying intercepts to pick up all the different variance between N. However, when the variance is able to vary (and does so much more than the intercept in my case), then the intercept is just left to pick up the covariance within the Ns. When T/N is small, it is much harder to pick up this relationship when the standard deviation of the alphas is relatively smaller.

Thanks Daniel,

The memory issue is occurring before any sampling (or optimization) happens, so I had assumed it must be related to autodiff. (To confirm this, I threw a bunch of print() statements into the code, and while it makes it through the transformed data block with no trouble, it doesn't get to anything in the transformed parameters or model blocks before crashing. But let me know if you think it could be something else. As you suggested, I'm also piping output to a file in rstan by default.)

In terms of calculating gradients, if necessary, I could code the derivatives of the full log-probability density wrt to the parameters, but I expect the memory issue is mainly down to one function in the transformed parameters block:

> R = calculate_rlevels(lambda, lambda_select, M, ht_select, ht_gmap, Ht,
> > Z, Z_type, Zdvec_sq, Zdmat_segments);

where the function signature for calculate_rlevels() in the functions block is:

> matrix calculate_rlevels(vector lambda, int[,] lambda_select,
> > matrix M,
> > int[,,] ht_select, int[,,,] ht_gmap, int[,] Ht,
> > matrix Z, int[] Z_type, vector Zdvec, int[,] Zdmat_segments)

There are a whole string of user-defined functions sitting behind this, the details of which I assume aren't especially relevant, but you can roughly think of each element of R as a kernel regression prediction of M|Z, based on a somewhat awkward subset of the other observations, and where the lambda parameters control the bandwidths of a K_lambda-dimensional gaussian kernel. The underlying code involves a lot more looping than I'd ideally like, but more efficient versions using matrix operations are unfortunately too memory intensive.

messages.body_plain:
One potential problem becomes more evident if you write
the mixture model directly,

if (y[i] == 0)
  target += log_sum_exp(log(theta[i]), log(1 - theta[i]) + poisson_lpdf(y[i] | lambda[i]);
else
  target += log(1 - theta[i]) + poisson_lpdf(y[i] | lambda[i]);

log(inv_logit(…)) and log(1 - inv_logit(…)) can be numerically
unstable for large arguments, which would not be uncommon
given how diffuse your priors are.

Fortunately there are special functions that compute these values
in a much more numerically stable way,

vector[N] alpha = a_0 + x_theta * a;

if (y[i] == 0)
  target += log_sum_exp(log_inv_logit(alpha[i]), log1m_inv_logit(alpha[i]) + poisson_lpdf(y[i] | lambda[i]);
else
  target += log1m_inv_logit(alpha[i]) + poisson_lpdf(y[i] | lambda[i]);

You can go another step further by using the log-link variant of the Poisson,

vector[N] alpha = a_0 + x_theta * a;
vector[N] log_lambda = b_0 + x_lambda * b + offset_interval;

if (y[i] == 0)
  target += log_sum_exp(log_inv_logit(…), log1m_inv_logit(…) + poisson_log_lpdf(y[i] | log_lambda[i]);
else
  target += log1m_inv_logit(…) + poisson_log_lpdf(y[i] | log_lambda[i]);

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Jacobian adjustment not caught by autodiff, how does Stan do it?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Jacobian adjustment not caught by autodiff, how does Stan do it?
messages.body_plain:
For explicit Jacobian adjustments, it's the log of the absolute
value of the determinant of the Jacobian matrix.

You need the adjustment whenever you have a parameter theta
and you have a function f and want to define your distribution
on f(theta) and then pull it back so it does the right thing
on theta.  Whereas if you have a variable theta and define the
density on theta, then f(theta) will be distributed correctly
without a Jacobian adjustment.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] multivariate normal distribution
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] multivariate normal distribution
messages.body_plain:
You say x1 and x2 are independent...

If x1 and x2 are independent in the statistical sense, your
posteriors on the predictors should remain independent.

If x1 and x2 are independent in the sense of being arguments,
then you might want to inspect the posterior for their coefficients
when you have independent priors.

But, if you only have one coefficient for each predictor (no
hierarchical structure), then the only thing you can do is give
them some fixed correlation in the prior---you can't fit the
dependency.

- Bob

When should I choose multivariate normal distributions over univariate normal distributions for coefficients on x1 and x2? That is, when should I believe the coefficients on x1 and x2 are correlated and model that structure?
> What problems will I have if I modeled the correlated coefficients on x1 and x2 as 2 univariate normally distributed parameters?

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Bypassing autodiff?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Bypassing autodiff?
messages.body_plain:
RStan allocates the memory to hold the draws ahead of time.
That's about 8 bytes per scalar parameter per iteration per chain.
That would presumably blow out before you started evaluating
the Stan model with data.

Autodiff memory will be around 40 bytes per subexpression evaluated
in the expression graph, and it'll remain roughly constant.

Autodiff memory won't kick in until the first iteration.  Data
gets read in and then transformed data calculated.

As Daniel says, you can definitely code functions in C++ with
derivatives and add them to Stan.

There's an extension way to do it built into RStan.  Or you can
just add new functions to the Stan math lib and to Stan in the other
interfaces.  We're working on a consistent way to do extensions
across interfaces.

- Bob

To respond to your points.

Am Montag, 17. April 2017 20:29:36 UTC+2 schrieb Bob Carpenter:
> [...]

>
> > - A method that recompiles the C++ code of a model from the fitted stanfit object. Currently we cannot call and rstan::log_prob() or rstan::unconstrain_pars() if the model was fitted in a different R session. Given that the stanfit object contains everything needed for compiling (minus the original data object), that seems in principle solvable.
>
> I've been lobbying for exactly the opposite approach.  If you have
> your model code somewhere (ideally in a standalone file), you don't
> need to reconsistitute a fit object.
>
> But I'm not a heavy or native R user, so take this with a grain of
> salt.  I think they're going to keep the
> god-object approach that's so common in R (e.g., return object for glm()):
>
> https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/God_object

I can see that for stanfit objects, which can be of considerable size, it might make sense to restrict them to the necessary bare bones (such as just the posterior samples and not also part of the model). But I also believe that for us it does not really matter in the end. We just need a reliable method to call log_prob() whether the samples were obtained in the current R session or a previous one.

>
> > - Ability to pass more than one set of samples per call to rstan::unconstrain_pars().
> > But we are obviously happy to wait until rstan3 as we found workarounds for both problems (in the first case the user needs to compile the model again just without samples and pass both).
>
> This is just a simple mapper function (something that applies a function to
> a sequence)?  You provide a sequence of parameter values and get a sequence of
> unconstrained values?
>

True, just a simple wrapper and only a question of interface. Currently this is just not optimal as there are too many steps: We first need to extract the samples, then transform each posterior sample individually into a list which can then be passed to the unconstrain_par() function, and then combine the resutls again.. It would be optimal if this function simply accepts the extracted samples without intermediary steps. But this is obviously just cosmetics.

Thanks again,
Henrik

> - Bob

messages.subject: Empirical Bayes
messages.subject_clean: Empirical Bayes
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am working on PK modeling and came up on software called BestDose and PMetrics which are not using parametric model for each individual PK parameters (as opposed to Torsten and other stan based PK packages). After some research I found that software is based on nonparametric maximum likelihood method (NLME) to determine distribution of individual PK parameters.The method can be viewed as empirical Bayes method to estimate the conditional probability of individual PK parameters given the data. I also found that empirical Bayes "may be viewed as an approximation to a fully Bayesian treatment of a hierarchical model wherein the parameters at the highest level of the hierarchy are set to their most likely values, instead of being integrated out". By perusing stan user group postings I found that empirical Bayes may be emulated in stan by using weakly informative priors. It looks like NLME should be more effective than using weakly informative prior. I am trying to build a coherent picture about the applicability of fully Bayesian hierarchical and empirical Bayes approaches to PKPD modeling - what are benefits, disadvantages, what classes of problems are solved better/faster with one versus another, possible biases etc. Can somebody help? Are the any publications which compare two approaches?

Thanks in advance,
Linas

messages.body_plain:
For reliable inference, are you simulating data according
to the model?  What have you done to debug the model to make
sure you're computing the right density?  Those look like complex
mean and scale caclulations involving only the single parameter
r (and lots of data).

For efficiency, you want to only compute expressions
once then reuse them, like exp(r * tcrit), and
exp(r * (t - tcrit)) * maxY.  It makes a big difference.

And you can vectorize mudenom and sddenom (and you can probably
make those locals---presumably you don't care about saving them).

And you can vectorize this:

 for (i in 1:M) {
    for (j in 1:N) {
      y[i, j] ~ normal(mupred[i], sdpred[i]);
    }
  }

as

  for (i in 1:M)
    y[i] ~ normal(mupred[i], sdpred[i]);

That'll make an even bigger difference.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] multivariate normal distribution
messages.body_plain:
Create a scatterplot of the posteriors.  In RStan, there's
a pairs() function which you can configure with the parameters
you want to look at.  Or view them in ShinyStan.

Because you don't have replications of the coefficients, it's
hard to get any mileage about having correlation on their prior
unless you know what it is.  You can have the coefficients for
x1 and x2 vary by maker if you want to build a hierarchical model.
That's where you'd use an unknown correlation prior.

There's nothing intrinsically problematic about correlation in
the posterior---we get it all the time in GLMs.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Empirical Bayes
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Empirical Bayes
messages.body_plain:
There's no way to do "empirical Bayes" in Stan (quotes for Andrew's
benefit---it's no more empirical than full Bayes).  You need to marginalize
out the low level parameters in order to maximize the high-level parameters
(or hack with cross-validation as is popular in machine learning).

We are working on adding max marginal likelihood (MML), which will let you
optimize the higher-level parameters.  NONMEM uses MML if you want
a comparison in the PK/PD world.

You're better off using full Bayes.  Empirical Bayes underestimates any
uncertainty having to do with high-level parameters by fixing them to
a single value.  Thus it tends to produce uncalibrated results that
underestimate uncertainty in predictions.  I just wrote a post on
Andrew's blog about why full Bayes is always calibrated (in expectation).

  http://andrewgelman.com/2017/04/12/bayesian-posteriors-calibrated/

and Andrew's blogged on it previously:

  http://andrewgelman.com/2012/12/06/yes-checking-calibration-of-probability-forecasts-is-part-of-bayesian-statistics/

- Bob

I also found that empirical Bayes "may be viewed as an approximation to a fully Bayesian treatment of a hierarchical model wherein the parameters at the highest level of the hierarchy are set to their most likely values, instead of being integrated out". However, there are still some pieces I'm not totally clear on, and I wanted to check I'm not on completely the wrong track before proceeding further.

As a recap, I want to bypass the full autodiff expression graph for a user-defined function, calculate_r(lambda, ...) that takes a parameter vector lambda (typically k=~5 rows) as its main argument (plus a bunch of data arguments "..." that I'll set aside for now), and returns another vector r with length NT=50-100k.* From Dan's previous email, and looking through the paper, I assume this means I need to:
Generate (a) a vector containing the 50-100k return values and (b) an NT x k matrix containing the 250-500k gradients d r[i] / d lambda [k]
Get both of these into an appropriate vari-derived storage class
Below is a bit more detail on how I'm thinking about how to do this, with specific questions underlined.

Storage class
It's going to be much quicker to calculate the gradients eagerly at the same time as calculating the r vector, so I think I should be using use something like the precomputed_gradients_vari class described in section 12.1.1. of the autodiff paper:

 struct precomputed_gradients_vari : public vari {
   const size_t size_;
   vari** varis_;
   double* gradients_;

   precomputed_gradients_vari(double val, size_t size,
                              vari** varis, double* gradients)
     : vari(val), size_(size),
       varis_(varis), gradients_(gradients) { }

   void chain() {
     for (size_t i = 0; i < size_; ++i)
       varis_[i]->adj_ += adj_ * gradients_[i];
   }
 };

This seems basically right for each row of r, but the bit I'm not sure about is what I need to do set this up to hold a vector of vals and matrix of gradients d r[i] / d lambda [k] - and in particular, how to adjust the chain method appropriately? (Or can this be dealt with in the function itself rather than changing the class?)

Implementation
In terms of implementing the function itself, I've taken the stan-generated cpp code for the calculate_r function as a base, and made the following adjustments (see attached code skeleton for details):
Removed the templating (as I know the types of the all the arguments and the return value, though maybe this wasn't necessary);
In addition to the original return vector r, calculated a matrix of derivatives of each r[i] wrt to each lamdba[k];
Used the log_determinant() code described in section 12.1.2 of the autodiff paper as a base to return the values, operands and gradients in a new vari implementation (currently based on precomputed_gradients_vari, although this won't be quite right yet)
(a) Sticking the return values into a val vector seems straightforward.
(b) However, while I'm sure this should be obvious, I'm not totally clear on what needs to populate that operands array. Is it just the elements of lambda, or am I on completely the wrong track here?
(c) I'm assuming once the appropriate chain method is in place in the storage class definition, filling the gradients array appropriately shouldn't be too difficult
In addition to the main function stan also generates a struct calculate_reflevel_functor__ { ... }. Is this still needed? (If so, I assume the templating - or lack thereof - should match the main function?)

Apologies if some (all?) of this is super obvious; I've never worked directly in C++ before, so am trying to figure things out as I go!

Thanks so much again for the help,

Glenn.

* In a previous email, I focused on another function, calculate_rlevels() that returned a matrix, R, but that function (usually) just loops a couple of times over calculate_r(), and it seems easier to deal with the latter.

messages.subject: Sum of Independent Gamma Random Variables within Multistate Model
messages.subject_clean: Sum of Independent Gamma Random Variables within Multistate Model
messages.body_plain:
Hello Stan Users,

I'm trying to do something which seems like it should be relatively simple, but is turning out to be nigh impossible (at least with my skillset). First some context: We (USGS Columbia River Research Lab) are working on implementing a multi-state mark recapture model in Stan to estimate survival and transition probabilities (between different migration routes) for individually marked fish migrating through a rather complicated river system. As part of a our multistate model we are interested in amount of time it takes a fish to transit the system depending on the route it takes. So for example consider the following ASCII schematic:

                      2           3
           A_____|______|__
       1  /                              \     4
R----|--                                 ----|
           \_____|______|___/
          B

A group of fish are released all at the same time at point R on the left-hand side of the schematic. They migrate towards the right. If they are detected at a station (denoted by  "|") their time of passage is detected. After station 1, fish encounter an intersection where they can take either path A or path B. These paths merge back together shortly after each path's respective station 3. We are interested in the distribution of travel times between each station. For example we want to know the mean travel time from R -> 1, from  1 -> 2A or 1->2B, 2A->3A, etc. If we had perfect detection at each station this wouldn't be a problem, but of course we don't. FIsh can pass a station or multiple stations without being detected. But for simplicity lets imagine that no fish die, all fish migrate downstream, and detection at station 4 (the last station) is perfect. So now let's consider three fish, Annie, Billy, and Pat. Annie is detected at station 1, 2A, 3A, and 4 and has the following travel times: R->1 = 1, 1->2A =  2 (cumulative 3), 2A -> 3A = 2 (cumulative 5), and 3A -> 4 = 1 (cumulative 6) days respectively. Billy  is detected at station 1, 2B, 3B, and 4 with travel times of 0.75, 4 (4.75), 4 (8.75), 2 (10.75). Pat on the other hand is detected only at station 1 and station 4 with a travel time of R -> 1 = 1.25 and 1 -> 4 of 7.75 (cumulative 9). So the question is what is the probability model for these travel times?

If these were nice independent Guassian fish, this wouldn't be a problem at all. For Annie we have R->1 ~ N(mu_1, sigma_1), 1->2A ~ N(mu_2A, sigma_2A), 2A->3A ~ N(mu_3A, sigma_3A), 3A->4 ~ N(mu_4A, sigma_4A). For Billy we have R->1 ~ N(mu_1, sigma_1), 1->2B ~ N(mu_2B, sigma_2B), 2B->3B ~ N(mu_3B, sigma_3B), 3B->4 ~ N(mu_4B, sigma_4B). Pat is just a little bit more complicated with R->1 ~ N(mu_1, sigma_1) and 1->4 ~ pA * N(mu_2A + mu_3A + mu_4A, sigma_2A + sigma_3A + sigma_4A) + (1-pA) * N(mu_2B + mu_3B + mu_4B, sigma_2B + sigma_3B + sigma_4B), where pA is the probability of going through route A. But this isn't a problem. It's just a mixture distribution and Stan does great with mixture distributions. I can figure out how to implement and wrap it up together using the forward algorithm within a comprehensive multistate model.

With me so far? Here's the problem: these aren't nice independent Gaussian fish. The travel times we observe are of course all non-negative, but they are also right skewed. So lognormal or gamma are the obvious choices here. Well no big deal right? In order to marginalize everything and get the likelihood for the mixture distribution that describes Pat's cumulative travel time we just need the pdf of the sum of lognormals or gammas. That's where I run into trouble. There is no closed-form pdf for the sum of lognormals. I also don't think I can do imputation because I don't see a way to do that within the mixture distribution framework and keep track of the state when imputing more than one travel time.

So that led me to attempt to implement a model for the sum of independent gammas (different alpha and beta, it's trivial if beta is the same) for which there is a closed form pdf. Paper attached.

Ok so after all that and before I get into my specific programming question let me lay out my goals for this post. I am primarily interested only in determining mean travel time for each station-to-station segment within a multistate model where I know travel-times are non-negative and right-skewed and where sometimes all I observe are cumulative travel times over multiple segments. I am not married to sum of independent gammas as the solution to this problem, but I latched onto it because I'm fairly certain I need some closed form pdf for the sum of travel times when all I observe is a cumulative travel time.

So onto the distribution of the sum of independent gamma random variables. The problem is that the pdf involves an infinite series. I went ahead an coded up some functions following the Moschopolous paper. The functions take a parameter "m", which is the number of terms of the series to use in approximating the log-likelihood.

I was able to verify that I've coded up the math correctly by specifying some arbitrarily selected values of shape and scale within the generated quantities step and comparing the log-likelihood to the log of empirical density function from a simulation in R. Here's what I noticed, the computation time for a single log-likelihood value for the infinite series as I've coded up increases at a rate of 2^m. For example I investigated the case of the sum of three gamma random variables [beta is rate parameter per Stan's parameterization] X1 ~ Gamma(2, 0.25), X2 ~ Gamma(2.5, 0.5), X3 ~ Gamma(3, 0.75), Y = X1 + X2 + X3.

In R I approximated the log of the empirical density for an arbitrary value as follows:

N = 10000000
alpha = c(2, 2.5, 3)
beta  = c(1/0.25, 1/0.5, 1/0.75)
x = matrix(rep(NA, 3*N), ncol = 3)

x[,1] = rgamma(N, shape = alpha[1], scale = beta[1])
x[,2] = rgamma(N, shape = alpha[2], scale = beta[2])
x[,3] = rgamma(N, shape = alpha[3], scale = beta[3])

Y = rowSums(x)
df = approxfun(density(Y))
plot(density(Y))

log(df(15))

Which for one run gives the following log likelihood:
[1] -2.751022

I compared this value to what I get from the Moschopolous equations in Stan using the generated quantities block with different values of m:

stan_dat = list(N = N,
                m = 25)

s = stan("sum_of_gammas_Moschopoulos.stan",
         data = stan_dat,
         chain = 1,
         iter = 1, algorithm = "Fixed_param")

############### y = 15 ##################
#log(df(15)) = -2.751022 #N = 10000000

#m = 10
#log likelihood: -2.76204
#0 seconds

#m = 15
#log likelihood: -2.75094
#0.06 seconds

#m = 20
#log likelihood: -2.75084
#1.929 seconds

#m = 25
#log likelihood: -2.75084
#62.881 seconds

 So the two things to notice are that 1) at least for this value, the series converged fairly quickly to what I believe is the true value (-2.75084), 2) computation time for a iteration of a single value is approximately 2^(-19 + m) seconds.

Things are less encouraging for value near the right hand tail of the empirical density:
############### y = 40 ##################
#log(df(40)) = -6.652416

#m = 10
#log likelihood: -8.60141
#0 seconds

#m = 15
#log likelihood: -7.24432
#0.077 seconds

#m = 20
#log likelihood: -6.76444
#2.031 seconds

#m = 25
#log likelihood: -6.65741
#64.137 seconds

So it seems like we need m =  25 to get close to what is probably the true value. But that's 60 seconds for a single iteration of a single log-likelihood value. That's a non-starter.

Undaunted, I attempted to fit simulated data (R code below, Stan code attached) with a fairly low value value of m. But I got nowhere. Stan is telling me that "Gradient evaluated at the initial value is not finite." And I'm not surprised given how poor the approximation seems to be with low values of m.

So I guess my question is whether there is a way to fit the Moschopolous pdf in Stan. Or is there another way to get at the parameters of independent gammas (or lognormals) when sometimes we only observe the sum (without using imputation)? Like I said at the start this seems like it should be simple, but it's most definitely not.

R code to simulate data to fit the model as outlined in the attached Stan code:

N = 1000
p = c(0.75, 0.75, 1)
alpha = c(2, 2.5, 3)
beta  = c(1/0.25, 1/0.5, 1/0.75)
y = matrix(rep(NA, 3*N), ncol = 3)
x = matrix(rep(NA, 3*N), ncol = 3)

x[,1] = rgamma(N, shape = alpha[1], rate = beta[1])
x[,2] = rgamma(N, shape = alpha[2], rate = beta[2])
x[,3] = rgamma(N, shape = alpha[3], rate = beta[3])

y[,1] = x[,1] * rbinom(N, 1, p[1])
y[,2] = (x[,2] + x[,1]) * rbinom(N, 1, p[2])
y[,3] = (x[,3] + x[,2] + x[,1]) * rbinom(N, 1, p[3])

stan_dat = list(N = N,
                y = y,
                m = 15)

s = stan("sum_of_gammas_Moschopoulos.stan",
         data = stan_dat,
         chain = 4,
         iter = 1000)

Good stuff! Looks like you've done your homework.

I went through the file you posted and modified it: https://gist.github.com/bbbales2/e351f1b3815f3cc875a36b39d5ef69ea

(I can get rid of that gist after this thread is over if you don't want that floating around)

There's a class in Stan, stored_gradient_vari, that does what precomputed_gradients_vari does, so you don't have to worry about that.

1. I'm not 100% sure, but I think you need to keep the templating to keep the linker happy. Not sure. The issue I had was that Stan wanted a copy of my function with the parameters instantiated as vars as well as a version with doubles. I think you need to define the function with all the templating, and then provide the two template specializations the linker wants. This is just for linking with an actual Stan model though. You can prototype this as just a Stan Math thing without having to deal with the templating at first.

2. I changed around how you were doing this (https://gist.github.com/bbbales2/e351f1b3815f3cc875a36b39d5ef69ea). The big thing is you want the input and output of your new autograd-friendly function to be the same shapes as if the autograd wasn't there. The derivatives hide inside the vars. You don't want to flatten that structure.

3. (b) Operands is just a list of pointers to other varis, I think you did it right

Hahaha, you've picked a good place to start learning C++ (this isn't trivial)!

I'd recommend that you build a little cpp test file separately to get this stuff working. Don't try to get it all linking up with Stan in one go. Just pretend you're adding another operator to the Stan Math library. Get that working first (by comparing with finite difference derivs) and then move on from there.

Here are links to the code I wrote (if it helps):
This is my function that does a similar thing as yours does (computes the derivs manually) -- input lower triangle of 6x6 matrix of parameters (21 vals), output vector of values: https://github.com/bbbales2/modal_cpp/blob/master/stan_mech.hpp#L79
Here is the autodiff-free version (so you can see the differences -- same input same output, just no derivs): https://github.com/bbbales2/modal_cpp/blob/master/stan_mech.hpp#L138
Here is a C++ function that is entirely autodiff'd by Stan for what it's worth: https://github.com/bbbales2/modal_cpp/blob/master/stan_mech.hpp#L35
Here's an example of me just using the Stan Math to directly test my function. This might not be very easy to read... (probly better to look at Stan math examples than my garbage here): https://github.com/bbbales2/modal_cpp/blob/master/stan_test_r.cpp
This make sense at all?

Ben

messages.subject: Bimodal posterior
messages.subject_clean: Bimodal posterior
messages.body_plain:
Thought I'd share something I ran across. To my dismay, a model I was fitting proved to have a bimodal posterior. See the attached pairs plot. On the other hand, even though I had to set adapt_delta=0.95, I'm astonished that Stan was able to sample from this posterior at all.

BTW, this was a case where it was really important to pay attention to those "divergent transition" warnings. At the default value for adapt_delta you only get one of the modes.

If you're wondering, this was time-series data and a single-source-of-error state-space model with local level and local trend. The data have a clear seasonality with period 7, which is not included in the model.

> On Apr 18, 2017, at 3:21 AM, Henrik Singmann <sing...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> H Bob,
>
> To respond to your points.
>
> Am Montag, 17. April 2017 20:29:36 UTC+2 schrieb Bob Carpenter:
> [...]
> > - A method that recompiles the C++ code of a model from the fitted stanfit object. Currently we cannot call and rstan::log_prob() or rstan::unconstrain_pars() if the model was fitted in a different R session. Given that the stanfit object contains everything needed for compiling (minus the original data object), that seems in principle solvable.
>
> I've been lobbying for exactly the opposite approach.  If you have
> your model code somewhere (ideally in a standalone file), you don't
> need to reconsistitute a fit object.
>
> But I'm not a heavy or native R user, so take this with a grain of
> salt.  I think they're going to keep the
> god-object approach that's so common in R (e.g., return object for glm()):
>
> https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/God_object
>
> I can see that for stanfit objects, which can be of considerable size, it might make sense to restrict them to the necessary bare bones (such as just the posterior samples and not also part of the model). But I also believe that for us it does not really matter in the end. We just need a reliable method to call log_prob() whether the samples were obtained in the current R session or a previous one.

I think that's fine if you're on the same hardware platform.
When you change hardware, R versions, C++ libs, etc., you run
into incompatibilities.

The bit you need is the compiled model, which is specifically what
you're having trouble reconstituting.  No way to get the log densities,
gradients, or transforms out without it (and with data loaded).

>
>
>
> > - Ability to pass more than one set of samples per call to rstan::unconstrain_pars().
> > But we are obviously happy to wait until rstan3 as we found workarounds for both problems (in the first case the user needs to compile the model again just without samples and pass both).
>
> This is just a simple mapper function (something that applies a function to
> a sequence)?  You provide a sequence of parameter values and get a sequence of
> unconstrained values?
>
>
> True, just a simple wrapper and only a question of interface. Currently this is just not optimal as there are too many steps: We first need to extract the samples, then transform each posterior sample individually into a list which can then be passed to the unconstrain_par() function, and then combine the resutls again.. It would be optimal if this function simply accepts the extracted samples without intermediary steps. But this is obviously just cosmetics.

My own philosophy here is to provide minimal tools that can then be
combined in useful ways (you can tell I "borrowed" my philosophy from unix).
Again, that seems like not the R way of doing things.

But why not just write the function yourself to do these things?

The problem with dumping things in packages is that then we have to anticipate
all the uses, doc them, test them, and then answer questions about them on
our lists.  If we provide only simple primitives, they're much easier to
document, test, and understand for users.  I think the R philosophy is that
users are better at poking around in the doc of big packages than writing glue
functions (exactly the opposite of my own experience with R, but then I'm not
a native R coder).

- Bob

> On Apr 18, 2017, at 3:35 PM, Max Farrell <maxwell...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi Bob,
>
> I tried my hand at vectorizing the model once more, but again have run up against divergent transitions, and some Rhats of NaN for some of my generated quantities.
>
> I couldn't find a specific entry in the most recent manual about vectorizing nested hierarchical levels, so I did what I think would be the most obvious syntax.

I don't think there's anything special about which level you're
at.  The vectorization always works the same way.

> So that you can better see how p is being constructed, attached are my original and vectorized models. The original nonvectorized model I ended up moving the intermediate grouping level "parasite" from transformed parameters into the model block, then had to use a normal_rng to get my generated quantities for the parasite effects - (This feels wrong to me as I want  to use the estimated parasite effects, not generate random ones for my ppcs, but it was the only way I could get the model to run without divergent transitions).

You absolutely need to use normal_rng for the posterior predictive
checks---it's the only way to draw from the proper posterior predictive
distribution.

>
> I have also attached my ideal, vectorized, model that is fully vectorized and using the non-centered parameterization throughout. With this model, I get about 600 divergent transitions when running for 10k iterations, and some Rhats of NaN for my generated quantities.
>
> I've reverted to using my original model for now, but still wonder if / why my attempt at vectorization is causing these errors.

Vectorization in and of itself won't cause divergences.  It will generate
the same density.  So presumably the two programs are not calculating the
same densities.  So I'd try to isolate where they differ by printing out
intermediate results or breaking things out into functions to evaluate on
their own.

- Bob

> > [...]
> > > - A method that recompiles the C++ code of a model from the fitted stanfit object. Currently we cannot call and rstan::log_prob() or rstan::unconstrain_pars() if the model was fitted in a different R session. Given that the stanfit object contains everything needed for compiling (minus the original data object), that seems in principle solvable.
> >
> > I've been lobbying for exactly the opposite approach.  If you have
> > your model code somewhere (ideally in a standalone file), you don't
> > need to reconsistitute a fit object.
> >
> > But I'm not a heavy or native R user, so take this with a grain of
> > salt.  I think they're going to keep the
> > god-object approach that's so common in R (e.g., return object for glm()):
> >
> > https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/God_object
> >
> > I can see that for stanfit objects, which can be of considerable size, it might make sense to restrict them to the necessary bare bones (such as just the posterior samples and not also part of the model). But I also believe that for us it does not really matter in the end. We just need a reliable method to call log_prob() whether the samples were obtained in the current R session or a previous one.
>
> I think that's fine if you're on the same hardware platform.
> When you change hardware, R versions, C++ libs, etc., you run
> into incompatibilities.
>
> The bit you need is the compiled model, which is specifically what
> you're having trouble reconstituting.  No way to get the log densities,
> gradients, or transforms out without it (and with data loaded).
>

Yes, of course. Sorry for being unclear here. What I meant is that I would be very happy with a log_prob function that always needs to receive model code and data in addition to the desired parameter set and not only a god object that might or might not fail. A function that requires the user to specify more information, but works more reliably, is what we need. I hope that makes clearer that I agree with you here.

messages.body_plain:
If you're using Rstan, check out the "init" and "init_r" parameters in the Stan function call (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/rstan/rstan.pdf)

If Stan isn't successfully guessing a good initial value, then it'd just be worth changing the initialization. I believe Stan just randomly picks initial parameters between -2 and 2 on the unconstrained parameter space. You could make this bigger. I'm not sure what (-2, 2) means exactly for your alpha, but check out chapter 33 in the manual and you could figure it out. What your tests seem to mean is that -2 to 2 on the uncontrained space doesn't contain alphas that do anything other than blow up (so Stan can't start sampling).

Worst case, if you know a value of alpha that *will* work, you can start your chains there (using "init").

Ben

It depends how you put your libs together.

If your function takes N arguments and you want to include it in Stan,
it needs to admit all 3^N combinations of integer/double/autodiff var.
You can do this with a single templated function, multiple templated
functions (either overloads or specializations), or with pure overloading.
Which is easiest will depend on the size of N and the nature of the function.

No kidding on the non-trivial part.  It tooks us years to
work up to this, which is why I tried to write it all out
in the autodiff paper.  Wish we'd had that before we started (but
then I always write papers aimed at my younger self).

> I'd recommend that you build a little cpp test file separately to get this stuff working. Don't try to get it all linking up with Stan in one go. Just pretend you're adding another operator to the Stan Math library. Get that working first (by comparing with finite difference derivs) and then move on from there.

Absolutely the only sensible way to proceed.  People always think writing
tests will slow them down, but the key thing to do is to design top down,
but code bottom up, testing each infrastructure layer very thoroughly so
that when you go a layer up, you can trust your foundation.  Anything else
is too unpredictable and prone to lead to impossibly tangled debugging
situations.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I saw a bunch of these models for the Columbia river at
the ADMB meeting and ISEC last year.

More below.  These involved questions are daunting.

If I may summarize, I'm thinking you want to have

  X ~ foo(alpha);

  Y ~ bar(beta);

and you only observe Z = (X + Y) and want to estimate alpha and
beta?   I don't know how to do this in general, other than to have
a latent variable for X for each observation

data {
  real Z[N];

parameters {
  real X[N];
}
model {
  X ~ foo(alpha);
  (Z - X) ~ bar(beta);
}

I don't know how to do this in general.  Obviously, you'd need to respect
other constraints, but that can be tricky with our language---it won't let
you put varying constraints on parameter vectors, so you need to do the
transform and Jacobian by hand.  Suppose you need X and Y to
both be positive and Z is positive.  Then you'd have

parameters {
  real X_raw[N];
  ...
transformed parameters {
  real X[N] = inv_logit(X) .* Z;  // X[n] now in (0, Z[n])
  ...

model {
  // log Jacobian of X_raw -> X transform
  target += Z .* log_inv_logit(X) + log1m_inv_logit(X);

- Bob

> On Apr 19, 2017, at 1:11 PM, Dalton Hance <dalton...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hello Stan Users,
>
> I'm trying to do something which seems like it should be relatively simple, but is turning out to be nigh impossible (at least with my skillset). First some context: We (USGS Columbia River Research Lab) are working on implementing a multi-state mark recapture model in Stan to estimate survival and transition probabilities (between different migration routes) for individually marked fish migrating through a rather complicated river system. As part of a our multistate model we are interested in amount of time it takes a fish to transit the system depending on the route it takes. So for example consider the following ASCII schematic:
>
>                       2           3
>            A_____|______|__
>        1  /                              \     4
> R----|--                                 ----|
>            \_____|______|___/
>           B
>

> A group of fish are released all at the same time at point R on the left-hand side of the schematic. They migrate towards the right. If they are detected at a station (denoted by  "|") their time of passage is detected. After station 1, fish encounter an intersection where they can take either path A or path B. These paths merge back together shortly after each path's respective station 3. We are interested in the distribution of travel times between each station. For example we want to know the mean travel time from R -> 1, from  1 -> 2A or 1->2B, 2A->3A, etc. If we had perfect detection at each station this wouldn't be a problem, but of course we don't. FIsh can pass a station or multiple stations without being detected. But for simplicity lets imagine that no fish die, all fish migrate downstream, and detection at station 4 (the last station) is perfect. So now let's consider three fish, Annie, Billy, and Pat. Annie is detected at station 1, 2A, 3A, and 4 and has the following travel times: R->1 = 1, 1->2A =  2 (cumulative 3), 2A -> 3A = 2 (cumulative 5), and 3A -> 4 = 1 (cumulative 6) days respectively. Billy  is detected at station 1, 2B, 3B, and 4 with travel times of 0.75, 4 (4.75), 4 (8.75), 2 (10.75). Pat on the other hand is detected only at station 1 and station 4 with a travel time of R -> 1 = 1.25 and 1 -> 4 of 7.75 (cumulative 10). So the question is what is the probability model for these travel times?

>
> If these were nice independent Guassian fish, this wouldn't be a problem at all. For Annie we have R->1 ~ N(mu_1, sigma_1), 1->2A ~ N(mu_2A, sigma_2A), 2A->3A ~ N(mu_3A, sigma_3A), 3A->4 ~ N(mu_4A, sigma_4A). For Billy we have R->1 ~ N(mu_1, sigma_1), 1->2B ~ N(mu_2B, sigma_2B), 2B->3B ~ N(mu_3B, sigma_3B), 3B->4 ~ N(mu_4B, sigma_4B). Pat is just a little bit more complicated with R->1 ~ N(mu_1, sigma_1) and 1->4 ~ pA * N(mu_2A + mu_3A + mu_4A, sigma_2A + sigma_3A + sigma_4A) + (1-pA) * N(mu_2B + mu_3B + mu_4B, sigma_2B + sigma_3B + sigma_4B), where pA is the probability of going through route A. But this isn't a problem. It's just a mixture distribution and Stan does great with mixture distributions. I can figure out how to implement and wrap it up together using the forward algorithm within a comprehensive multistate model.
>
> With me so far?

Yes.

> Here's the problem: these aren't nice independent Gaussian fish. The travel times we observe are of course all non-negative, but they are also right skewed. So lognormal or gamma are the obvious choices here. Well no big deal right? In order to marginalize everything and get the likelihood for the mixture distribution that describes Pat's cumulative travel time we just need the pdf of the sum of lognormals or gammas. That's where I run into trouble. There is no closed-form pdf for the sum of lognormals. I also don't think I can do imputation because I don't see a way to do that within the mixture distribution framework and keep track of the state when imputing more than one travel time.
>
> So that led me to attempt to implement a model for the sum of independent gammas (different alpha and beta, it's trivial if beta is the same) for which there is a closed form pdf. Paper attached.
>
> Ok so after all that and before I get into my specific programming question let me lay out my goals for this post. I am primarily interested only in determining mean travel time for each station-to-station segment within a multistate model where I know travel-times are non-negative and right-skewed and where sometimes all I observe are cumulative travel times over multiple segments. I am not married to sum of independent gammas as the solution to this problem, but I latched onto it because I'm fairly certain I need some closed form pdf for the sum of travel times when all I observe is a cumulative travel time.

Usually you can choose a latent parameterization where you
introduce the intermediate steps.

>
> So onto the distribution of the sum of independent gamma random variables. The problem is that the pdf involves an infinite series. I went ahead an coded up some functions following the Moschopolous paper. The functions take a parameter "m", which is the number of terms of the series to use in approximating the log-likelihood.
>
> I was able to verify that I've coded up the math correctly by specifying some arbitrarily selected values of shape and scale within the generated quantities step and comparing the log-likelihood to the log of empirical density function from a simulation in R. Here's what I noticed, the computation time for a single log-likelihood value for the infinite series as I've coded up increases at a rate of 2^m. For example I investigated the case of the sum of three gamma random variables [beta is rate parameter per Stan's parameterization] X1 ~ Gamma(2, 0.25), X2 ~ Gamma(2.5, 0.5), X3 ~ Gamma(3, 0.75), Y = X1 + X2 + X3.
>
> In R I approximated the log of the empirical density for an arbitrary value as follows:
>
> N = 10000000
> alpha = c(2, 2.5, 3)
> beta  = c(1/0.25, 1/0.5, 1/0.75)
> x = matrix(rep(NA, 3*N), ncol = 3)
>
> x[,1] = rgamma(N, shape = alpha[1], scale = beta[1])
> x[,2] = rgamma(N, shape = alpha[2], scale = beta[2])
> x[,3] = rgamma(N, shape = alpha[3], scale = beta[3])
>
> Y = rowSums(x)
> df = approxfun(density(Y))
> plot(density(Y))
>
> log(df(15))
>
> Which for one run gives the following log likelihood:
> [1] -2.751022
>
> I compared this value to what I get from the Moschopolous equations in Stan using the generated quantities block with different values of m:
>
> stan_dat = list(N = N,
>                 m = 25)
>
> s = stan("sum_of_gammas_Moschopoulos.stan",
>          data = stan_dat,
>          chain = 1,
>          iter = 1, algorithm = "Fixed_param")
>
> ############### y = 15 ##################
> #log(df(15)) = -2.751022 #N = 10000000
>
> #m = 10
> #log likelihood: -2.76204
> #0 seconds
>
> #m = 15
> #log likelihood: -2.75094
> #0.06 seconds
>
> #m = 20
> #log likelihood: -2.75084
> #1.929 seconds
>
> #m = 25
> #log likelihood: -2.75084
> #62.881 seconds
>
>  So the two things to notice are that 1) at least for this value, the series converged fairly quickly to what I believe is the true value (-2.75084), 2) computation time for a iteration of a single value is approximately 2^(-19 + m) seconds.
>
> Things are less encouraging for value near the right hand tail of the empirical density:
> ############### y = 40 ##################
> #log(df(40)) = -6.652416
>
> #m = 10
> #log likelihood: -8.60141
> #0 seconds
>
> #m = 15
> #log likelihood: -7.24432
> #0.077 seconds
>
> #m = 20
> #log likelihood: -6.76444
> #2.031 seconds
>
> #m = 25
> #log likelihood: -6.65741
> #64.137 seconds
>
> So it seems like we need m =  25 to get close to what is probably the true value. But that's 60 seconds for a single iteration of a single log-likelihood value. That's a non-starter.
>
> Undaunted, I attempted to fit simulated data (R code below, Stan code attached) with a fairly low value value of m. But I got nowhere. Stan is telling me that "Gradient evaluated at the initial value is not finite." And I'm not surprised given how poor the approximation seems to be with low values of m.
>
> So I guess my question is whether there is a way to fit the Moschopolous pdf in Stan. Or is there another way to get at the parameters of independent gammas (or lognormals) when sometimes we only observe the sum (without using imputation)?

Not that I know of, but somebody else may know.  If it's
just purely a sum, though, it won't be identified.

> Like I said at the start this seems like it should be simple, but it's most definitely not.
>
> R code to simulate data to fit the model as outlined in the attached Stan code:
>
>
> N = 1000
> p = c(0.75, 0.75, 1)
> alpha = c(2, 2.5, 3)
> beta  = c(1/0.25, 1/0.5, 1/0.75)

>
> y[,1] = x[,1] * rbinom(N, 1, p[1])
> y[,2] = (x[,2] + x[,1]) * rbinom(N, 1, p[2])
> y[,3] = (x[,3] + x[,2] + x[,1]) * rbinom(N, 1, p[3])

>                 y = y,

>
> s = stan("sum_of_gammas_Moschopoulos.stan",

messages.body_plain:
Thanks Bob,

Yes, we work on some pretty challenging models here. Our shop has gone almost 100% Bayesian because of it. But we're also hitting the limits of JAGS. We have a version of this model coded up in JAGS, but it takes about 4 weeks to run. So we're definitely interested in trying to fit more of these models in Stan. We've actually got our first two papers featuring Stan in the works right now.

After perusing the mailing list yesterday, I think I've come to realize that we're dealing with the convolution of multiple random variables. It sounds like we might have to wait for the fast Fourier transforms to be implemented to try to do the numerical integration. For now, I think my two choices are either to use the Normal distribution which would allow us to account for correlation but not right-skew or strict non-negativity or to use the Gamma distribution with a common rate parameter and assume independence of travel times. We're going to move forward with the Gamma distribution because it's better than what we've got in JAGS.

Just to clarify using your notation below: sometimes we observe only Z, but for some individuals we observe both X and Y. To speak to your suggestions, I don't think the latent variable approach will work within a general multi-state framework. There are two related reasons for this. First, we have to keep track of the number of unobserved travel times because I've discovered Stan does not like imputing a variable that will not be used later. Second, I don't see a way to work with multiple latent variables within a multistate model.

I got as far as figuring out how to do the latent variable approach within a simple three-occasion, three state model (based off the BPA example code on the Stan github page). That code is attached. In the model, I assume that travel time from occasion to occasion is simply based on what the state the individual was in during the last occasion.

The key addition to the basic multistate model is:

  miss_count = 1;

  for (i in 1:N) {
    if (y[i,2] != 3){
      obs_cuml_trav_time[i,2] ~ lognormal(mu[y[i,1]], sigma[y[i,1]]);
      if (y[i,3] !=3){
        real diff;
        diff = obs_cuml_trav_time[i,3] - obs_cuml_trav_time[i,2];
        diff ~ lognormal(mu[y[i,2]], sigma[y[i,2]]);
      }
    } else { //y[i,2] == 3
      if (y[i,3] !=3){
        real diff;
        tt_1_missing[miss_count] ~ lognormal(mu[y[i,1]], sigma[y[i,1]]);
        diff = obs_cuml_trav_time[i,3] - tt_1_missing[miss_count];
        miss_count = miss_count + 1;
        if (y[i,1] == 1)
          target += log_sum_exp(log(1 - psiAB[1]) + lognormal_lpdf(diff | mu[1], sigma[1]), //probability fish was in state 1 during time 2
                                log(psiAB[1]) + lognormal_lpdf(diff | mu[2], sigma[2]));//probability fish was in state 1 during time 2
        if (y[i,1] ==2)
          target += log_sum_exp(log(psiBA[1]) + lognormal_lpdf(diff | mu[1], sigma[1]), //probability fish was in state 1 during time 2
                                log(1 - psiBA[1]) + lognormal_lpdf(diff | mu[2], sigma[2]));//probability fish was in state 1 during time 2
      }
    }
  }

But this becomes intractable when you get beyond three occasions because we'd need a discrete latent variable to keep track of which state the individual was actually in to avoid impossible sums.

> > Hello Stan Users,

> > I'm trying to do something which seems like it should be relatively simple, but is turning out to be nigh impossible (at least with my skillset). First some context: We (USGS Columbia River Research Lab) are working on implementing a multi-state mark recapture model in Stan to estimate survival and transition probabilities (between different migration routes) for individually marked fish migrating through a rather complicated river system. As part of a our multistate model we are interested in amount of time it takes a fish to transit the system depending on the route it takes. So for example consider the following ASCII schematic:
> >
> >                       2           3
> >            A_____|______|__
> >        1  /                              \     4
> > R----|--                                 ----|
> >            \_____|______|___/
> >           B
> >
> > A group of fish are released all at the same time at point R on the left-hand side of the schematic. They migrate towards the right. If they are detected at a station (denoted by  "|") their time of passage is detected. After station 1, fish encounter an intersection where they can take either path A or path B. These paths merge back together shortly after each path's respective station 3. We are interested in the distribution of travel times between each station. For example we want to know the mean travel time from R -> 1, from  1 -> 2A or 1->2B, 2A->3A, etc. If we had perfect detection at each station this wouldn't be a problem, but of course we don't. FIsh can pass a station or multiple stations without being detected. But for simplicity lets imagine that no fish die, all fish migrate downstream, and detection at station 4 (the last station) is perfect. So now let's consider three fish, Annie, Billy, and Pat. Annie is detected at station 1, 2A, 3A, and 4 and has the following travel times: R->1 = 1, 1->2A =  2 (cumulative 3), 2A -> 3A = 2 (cumulative 5), and 3A -> 4 = 1 (cumulative 6) days respectively. Billy  is detected at station 1, 2B, 3B, and 4 with travel times of 0.75, 4 (4.75), 4 (8.75), 2 (10.75). Pat on the other hand is detected only at station 1 and station 4 with a travel time of R -> 1 = 1.25 and 1 -> 4 of 7.75 (cumulative 10). So the question is what is the probability model for these travel times?
> >
> > If these were nice independent Guassian fish, this wouldn't be a problem at all. For Annie we have R->1 ~ N(mu_1, sigma_1), 1->2A ~ N(mu_2A, sigma_2A), 2A->3A ~ N(mu_3A, sigma_3A), 3A->4 ~ N(mu_4A, sigma_4A). For Billy we have R->1 ~ N(mu_1, sigma_1), 1->2B ~ N(mu_2B, sigma_2B), 2B->3B ~ N(mu_3B, sigma_3B), 3B->4 ~ N(mu_4B, sigma_4B). Pat is just a little bit more complicated with R->1 ~ N(mu_1, sigma_1) and 1->4 ~ pA * N(mu_2A + mu_3A + mu_4A, sigma_2A + sigma_3A + sigma_4A) + (1-pA) * N(mu_2B + mu_3B + mu_4B, sigma_2B + sigma_3B + sigma_4B), where pA is the probability of going through route A. But this isn't a problem. It's just a mixture distribution and Stan does great with mixture distributions. I can figure out how to implement and wrap it up together using the forward algorithm within a comprehensive multistate model.
> >
> > With me so far?
>
> Yes.
>
> > Here's the problem: these aren't nice independent Gaussian fish. The travel times we observe are of course all non-negative, but they are also right skewed. So lognormal or gamma are the obvious choices here. Well no big deal right? In order to marginalize everything and get the likelihood for the mixture distribution that describes Pat's cumulative travel time we just need the pdf of the sum of lognormals or gammas. That's where I run into trouble. There is no closed-form pdf for the sum of lognormals. I also don't think I can do imputation because I don't see a way to do that within the mixture distribution framework and keep track of the state when imputing more than one travel time.
> >
> > So that led me to attempt to implement a model for the sum of independent gammas (different alpha and beta, it's trivial if beta is the same) for which there is a closed form pdf. Paper attached.

I am primarily interested only in determining mean travel time for each station-to-station segment within a multistate model where I know travel-times are non-negative and right-skewed and where sometimes all I observe are cumulative travel times over multiple segments. I am not married to sum of independent gammas as the solution to this problem, but I latched onto it because I'm fairly certain I need some closed form pdf for the sum of travel times when all I observe is a cumulative travel time.
>

I went ahead an coded up some functions following the Moschopolous paper. The functions take a parameter "m", which is the number of terms of the series to use in approximating the log-likelihood.

Here's what I noticed, the computation time for a single log-likelihood value for the infinite series as I've coded up increases at a rate of 2^m. For example I investigated the case of the sum of three gamma random variables [beta is rate parameter per Stan's parameterization] X1 ~ Gamma(2, 0.25), X2 ~ Gamma(2.5, 0.5), X3 ~ Gamma(3, 0.75), Y = X1 + X2 + X3.

> >
> > #m = 15

> >

> > #1.929 seconds
> >
> > #m = 25
> > #log likelihood: -2.75084
> > #62.881 seconds
> >
> >  So the two things to notice are that 1) at least for this value, the series converged fairly quickly to what I believe is the true value (-2.75084), 2) computation time for a iteration of a single value is approximately 2^(-19 + m) seconds.
> >
> > Things are less encouraging for value near the right hand tail of the empirical density:
> > ############### y = 40 ##################

Thanks Bob,

One (hopefully) last question re the templating:

I ended up needing to code two separate specializations for the function depending on whether the first argument (and therefore return type) was var or double.

However, the way I ended defining the double specialisation was somewhat unsatisfactory: I just copied wholesale the var specialisation and then manually removed all the pieces that weren't related to the gradient calculations. This isn't great from a maintainability perspective, as the code is 80% identical, with only 4 short code chunks that aren't needed in the double version (a set of declarations; extraction of the var elements into a double for further calculations; calculation of the gradient matrix; and population and return of the stored_gradient_vari).

I'd ideally like (and thought I should be able) to have a single templated version of the code, just with conditional execution of the gradient/var-related bits. However, my naive attempt to do this using type traits didn't work. In particular, e.g.:
I defined a bool ret_type_double = is_same<fun_return_scalar_t__, double>::value, to switch the gradient-related code off
But the compiler would complain if I tried to use something like if (!ret_type_double) lambda_double(k) = lambda_var(k).val() to extract the var values as doubles (because .val() doesn't work on doubles, even though the condition could only be met if lambda_var were a var).
If anyone could suggest a (better) way to achieve this sort of type-dependent execution, while minimising the amount of duplicated code floating around, future me will likely be very grateful when it inevitably comes time to tweak something.

Also, as an aside, I notice that the struct calculate_r_functor__ {...} code that stan generated from my original user-defined function calculate_r() is no longer generated if I just declare the function in the .stan file and define it in calculate_r.hpp. Everything seems to be working fine without it, so I assume that it isn't needed any more, but is there any reason to include it in the .hpp file?

Thanks again,

Glenn.

Very late to this conversation, but just in case it's useful to anyone else, you could #include a custom c++ function that executes the cast - something like:

template <typename T0__>

int

real_to_int_cast(const T0__& x, std::ostream* pstream__) {

    return int (x);

};

This is pretty easy in rstan, using the instructions here: https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/rstan/vignettes/external.html. I assume it should also be easy in cmdstan, though I can't actually get it to compile property myself. Not sure about pystan.

messages.body_plain:
I just got an email asking for more detail re: deploying a Shiny app that contains an RStan model to shinyapps.io <http://shinyapps.io>, so I figured I'd respond here such that all can see.

In short, there are two steps:
Create a secondary package containing your RStan model, and push the code to GitHub
Install this secondary package via `devtools::install_github` into your project (i.e. your Shiny application)
Once you complete Step 2, you proceed as normal with the deployment to shinyapps.io <http://shinyapps.io>. Here is the more detailed breakdown of how to complete Step 1:
 `library(rstantools);  rstan_package_skeleton(name = "MySecondaryPackageName", stan_files = "/path/to/model.stan", path = "path/to/secondary/package")` (in R console)
` cd path/to/secondary/package` (on the command line)
`chmod u+x cleanup; chmod u+x cleanup.win` (on the command line)
manually write `useDynLib(MySecondaryPackageName, .registration = TRUE)` in the `NAMESPACE` file, as well as the methods you'd like to export, i.e. be able to use externally as  `MySecondaryPackageName::myMethod`, and the packages (dependencies) you need to import.
`install.packages("devtools"); library(devtools); load_all()` (in R console)
press `Check` in the RStudio console
ensure that `Module.o` and `MySecondaryPackageName.so` are not found in `src/`; these files will be built when we install this package from our GitHub via `devtools::install_github("me/MySecondaryPackageName")`. if they're already in `src/`, this step will fail.
I forget what Step 5 is supposed to do. I believe the desired outcome of Step 6 is simply "no horrible errors." I apologize for the ambiguity here: this is how I have it in my notes. I'll clarify these points the next time I undertake this process.

Here are two examples of packages containing RStan models which were then included in Shiny apps:
OrderedCategoricalGLM <https://github.com/cavaunpeu/OrderedCategoricalGLM>
RescueTimeEstimator <https://github.com/cavaunpeu/RescueTimeEstimator>
Finally, nota bene:

I'm yet unsuccessful at freshly installing RStan, <all other packages I'm using>, and MySecondaryPackageName from a packrat spec. Therein, the build of MySecondaryPackageName always fails at "no member named 'max_step_checker' in namespace 'boost::numeric::odeint'." <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!msg/stan-users/Q5aCotBsC8U/1H-eLPC_EAAJ;context-place=searchin/stan-users/max_step%7Csort:relevance> At this point, I believe this is a problem with the way in which packrat installs RStan itself.

Alternatively, when installing MySecondaryPackageName using the RStan I have installed globally on my machine, it works. This is all to say: before thinking about installing MySecondaryPackageName, ensure that you have RStan itself installed as intended (as described in their docs), and that packrat is possibly incapable of doing this within its normal usage.

Hope this helps.

messages.subject: The easy way to calculate euclidean distances in Stan (for 2D points)
messages.subject_clean: The easy way to calculate euclidean distances in Stan (for 2D points)
messages.body_plain:
This isn't a question, just an answer I found that I wanted to share.

I'm working on a model that heavily uses euclidean distances, which lend some awkwardness to the code. BUT, at some point in time (or maybe I missed it), the Stan team added a hypotenuse function (hypot(), page 423), that calculates the following function for two reals (x,y) --> sqrt( x^2 + y^2). So it only works for 2-D points, and it isn't vectorized, but still, a time-saver.

OK, commercial over... Just wanted to post this in case anyone has a similar coding issue.
