Thanks, Jonah!
Sorry for not replying immediately, I was caught up in the end-of-term rush and had fallen behind. Your post was very helpful. I have always undertaken comparisons in-text by using the coefficients to calculate an estimate for each level of a given condition (or range of values for continuous predictors), used the inverse transformation on the resulting posterior for each of those conditions and then subtract them to get an estimated difference in probability space (in the case of logistic regression). This was cumbersome, and from what I understand, posterior_linpred with transform=TRUE does the same thing in a single function call. Fantastic!

I have one more question for you, if I may. In addition to the analyses detailed above, I am also conducting analyses of the individual experiments, each with their own unique predictors. In one example, I have 96 participants in a within-subject design with 7 predictors. I have appended simulated data that matches the properties of my actual data very closely. The DV is still decision and the participant identifier is still participant_id, but the other variables are slightly different. condition and order are categorical (each with two levels) and they have been centred by defining these levels as -0.5 and 0.5; the remaining variables (choices, relprefc1, ici, bore, fat) are either continuous or ordinal and have been centred at their respective means. I analyze them using:

simdat2 = readRDS('sample_dat2.rds')
simmod2 = stan_glmer(decision ~ condition + order + choices + relprefc1 + ici + bore + fat + (condition|participant_id), data = simdat2, family = binomial, adapt_delta=.999, prior_covariance=decov(scale=.5))

I tweaked the prior on the RE covariance structure to be more constrained, because otherwise the random slope by condition takes on some pretty unreasonable values. In any event, using posterior_linpred as you suggested allows me to estimate the mean marginal probability for each level of condition – at the mean of all other variables – using the function call:

sim_conditions = posterior_linpred(simmod2, re.form=NA, transform=TRUE, newdata=expand.grid(condition=c(-.5,.5), order=0, choices=0, relprefc1=0, ici=0, bore=0, fat=0))
apply(sim_conditions, 2, function(x){return(quantile(x, probs=c(.025,.5,.975)))})

#                  1          2
#  2.5%  0.004359592 0.02508615
#  50%   0.032214613 0.10240261
#  97.5% 0.079338786 0.19666528

This is great! However, my question pertains to the fact that these estimates (M = .03 and .10) are quite different from the simple proportions obtained from the same data by calling (M = .08 and M = .22):

library(dplyr)
summarize(group_by(simdat2, condition), mean=mean(decision))

#  condition       mean
#      <dbl>      <dbl>
#1      -0.5 0.08333333
#2       0.5 0.21875000

I believe the reason for this is a consequence of modelling random effects so close to a boundary (i.e., 0). If I were to simulate the dataset as a whole, accounting for the random effects, as such:

y_rep <- posterior_predict(simmod2)
summary(apply(y_rep, 1, mean))

#   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.
# 0.05729 0.13020 0.15100 0.15120 0.17190 0.27080

The resulting distribution of means is spot on ([0.08 + 0.22] / 2 = 15). So, the question here is how to best interpret the output from posterior_linpred. Could this be viewed as the most credible median value for each condition – at the mean of every other variable – for an “average” participant? The implication would be that the difference between these estimates and the simple proportions would then be attributed to heterogeneity across subject. Or is there an even better way to compare the two conditions?

Cheers!
Jon

On Friday, March 3, 2017 at 3:50:01 PM UTC-3:30, Jonah Gabry wrote:

> Thanks Jon, that's helpful. Ok, so you have a logistic regression with a model formula of
>
> decision ~ condition * design + (condition |participant_id) + (condition | experiment_id)
>
> which corresponds to a linear predictor that is a function of:
>
> - a global intercept ((Intercept))
> - a global "main effect" of condition (condition)
> - a global "main effect" of design (designwithin)
> - a global interaction term (condition:designwithin)
> - shifts to the intercept and coefficient on condition specific to each participant_id (e.g. b[(Intercept) participant_id:1], b[condition participant_id:1])
> - shifts to the intercept and coefficient on condition specific to each experiment_id (e.g. b[(Intercept) experiment_id:1], b[condition experiment_id:1])
>
> and there will also be estimated covariance matrices for the multivariate normal prior on the participant-specific varying intercept/slope and for the experiment-specific varying intercept/slope.
>
> That corresponds to what you're intending to do, correct?
>
> Regarding the comparison of conditions across the two designs, I think preferable to focusing directly on the sign/magnitude of the interaction term would be to
>
> (1) use your posterior distribution to predict a bunch of outcomes from the posterior predictive distribution under the various possible scenarios you have  (you can use posterior_predict to get the 0/1 outcomes themselves or posterior_linpred with transform=TRUE to get the posterior probabilities of the outcomes)
>
> and then
>
> (2) make the comparison of interest on the scale of the outcome via summaries of those predictions (rather than on the scale of the interaction coefficient).
>
> I think that's generally much more intuitive than directly interpreting interaction coefficients (especially when the linear predictor is transformed by a non-linear inverse-link function) and also the implications for the outcome tend be what's of practical interest. What do you think?
>
> Best,
>
> Jonah
>
> P.S. It might also be interesting to do this both with the model that has the interaction term explicitly included and for the same model but without the interaction term so that you can compare that too.

> Hamed,
>
> You are confusing the target distribution with the expectation that you want

>
> If you want to define the target distribution as being zero for g <= 0 then
> you have to specify a truncated distribution which may require a normalizing
> constant.  There is discussion of this in the manual.  Note that outside of
> one dimension, truncated distributions are hard to derive analytically.
>
> On the other hand, it looks like you’re trying to compute the expectation
> of I[g > 0] with respect to an IID gaussian target distribution (i.e. the probability
> of g > 0).  In that case you want to compute the indicator in generated
> quantities,
>
>
> parameters {
>   vector[2] x;
> }
>
> model {
>   x ~ normal(0, 1);
> }
>
> generated quantities {
>   int I = 0;
>   {
>     real g = 3 - (sum(x)/sqrt(2));
>     if (g > 0) I = 1;
>   }
> }
>
> Then the average of I across your chain will be P[g > 0].

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Distribution of standard deviations
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Distribution of standard deviations
messages.body_plain:
> On Apr 26, 2017, at 12:18 PM, Gregory <gregor...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hello everyone
>
> My question may be more theoretical than technical, but I'm building a model to approximate a task where users aim to correctly place a series of objects on a continuous scale. Some objects are more difficult to place correctly than others however, and therefore the variances for some placements are higher than are others. I'd like to model these parameters hierarchically, because some objects are not rated by many users or only by a single user (the latter of which are therefore not identified). My first thought was to model these with a gamma distribution, but is it more reasonable to use a normal or something else?

This is a kind of multiple rater problem making it a lot like IRT.
You want a component of variance to come from the user and one component
of the variance to come from the item.

You may also want to model a bias (mean) from the user and from
the item (let's say you're placing colors on a spectrum and some
users may tend more toward the red side than others;  or let's say
you have some color that somehow looks more red than it is [context
maybe] and causes users to judge it as more red than it really is.

> If I can put this more concretely by analogy: among professional archers, each archer has a variance on the distance of his or her shots from the bulleye. Assuming unbiasedness in shots, low variance means that an archer typically hits close to the target; high variance, the archer typically hits far from the target. Imagine we know the variances for all archers. Would one want to model these as gamma distributed? Normally distributed? Otherwise?

We'd want to plot what all those variances looked like to get an
idea of which distribution to use.  It's not a theoretical question.
In practice, it may not matter much, especially if you have more than
a few dozen observations.

You also want to look at how the abilities of the users and the
difficulties of the items interact.  Are they additive or are there
interactions?

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Polar coordinates
messages.body_plain:
Polar coordinates are not isomorphic to R^{2} —
you’re missing the origin.  Topologically polar
coordinates describe an annulus and not a plane.
The difference is small and doesn’t really affect
expectations or probabilities, but it does prevent
one from mapping a distribution back and forth
exactly.

The way to see that is to compute the Jacobian
and remember that you have to sum over _all_
possible zeros of the transformation.  Because
sin and cos are multivalued this leads to an
infinite number of terms, one for each possible
choice of phase.  To collapse all of those terms
into a single term you have to ignore the hole
at zero which, as I note above, doesn’t make
a practical difference but it does affect things
theoretically.

In any case, there are well-behaved transformations
from R^{2} -> R^{2} that do map a unimodal
density to a multimodal density so you do have
to be careful with nonlinear transformations, even
ignoring the topological issues with polar coordinates.

messages.body_plain:
On Thursday, April 27, 2017 at 2:51:41 PM UTC-4, Christopher Fisher wrote:
> I'm working with the developer of the Julia interface for Stan on validating the manual initialization of parameter values. When I print out the parameters to the runlog (see below), only one of the parameters is equal to the values I set manually. This strikes me as odd. I expected the first set of parameters to be the initial values I set.  Is it possible that the printing is suppressed for the initial parameters?

The initial parameters you pass from Julia (or whatever interface) start going through the leapfrog process before the first execution of the print statements in the model block. In RStan, we basically had to save the initial values before NUTS starts in order to preserve them in the stanfit object at the end.

Ben

messages.subject: Understanding a very simple multi-logit model
messages.subject_clean: Understanding a very simple multi-logit model
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I’m trying to understand a very simple multi-logit regression, but my intuition is not matching up to the results I am getting….. perhaps I am missing something fundamental.

In the attached R file I generate data from a categorical distribution in which there are 6 equally probably outcomes.

I then fit the model using a simplified version of the multi_logit model from the stan user manual (see attached multi_logit.stan). Once fitted I then transform the beta parameter to a vector of probabilities using the softmax function.

When I fit the model with reasonably large N then the theta parameters recover the true value (1/6) well.

However, if I fit the model with very few data points (say N = 2) the 90% intervals are often quite narrow and exclude the 1/6 value. For example, the attached plot shows the intervals I generated with N = 2. My intuition is that these intervals should span 1/6 with a high degree of uncertainty (i.e. be very wide)…

My question is – why is this not the case?

Many thanks,

Oscar

messages.subject_clean: Model comparison using a multilevel structure via Stan
messages.body_plain:
Hello dear professor,

Let me know if I understood:
(1) From what I've studied, I concluded that multilevel models need to have verisimilitude marginalized by random effects, such as the figure I've shown, by Fox (2010).
(2) Despite the fact in (1), the likelihood in my Stan code is correct (although I do not consider integration over betas).
(3) Integration over betas can be considered approximately by later predictive densities.

So, from this code in the R, the WAIC and loo measurements would be being calculated from the posteriori predictive density and, therefore, considering the integration of betas, how do I want it?

library(rstan)
library(loo)

waic <- function(stanfit){
  log_lik <- extract (stanfit, "log_lik")$log_lik
  dim(log_lik) <- if (length(dim(log_lik))==1) c(length(log_lik),1) else
  c(dim(log_lik)[1], prod(dim(log_lik)[2:length(dim(log_lik))]))
  S <- nrow(log_lik)
  n <- ncol(log_lik)
  lpd <- log(colMeans(exp(log_lik)))
  p_waic <- colVars(log_lik)
  elpd_waic <- lpd - p_waic
  waic <- -2*elpd_waic
  loo_weights_raw <- 1/exp(log_lik-max(log_lik))
  loo_weights_normalized <- loo_weights_raw/
  matrix(colMeans(loo_weights_raw),nrow=S,ncol=n,byrow=TRUE)
  loo_weights_regularized <- pmin (loo_weights_normalized, sqrt(S))
  elpd_loo <- log(colMeans(exp(log_lik)*loo_weights_regularized)/
  colMeans(loo_weights_regularized))
  p_loo <- lpd - elpd_loo
  pointwise <- cbind(waic,lpd,p_waic,elpd_waic,p_loo,elpd_loo)
  total <- colSums(pointwise)
  se <- sqrt(n*colVars(pointwise))
  return(list(waic=total["waic"], elpd_waic=total["elpd_waic"],
  p_waic=total["p_waic"], elpd_loo=total["elpd_loo"], p_loo=total["p_loo"],
  pointwise=pointwise, total=total, se=se))
}
...
stanfit <- stan(...)
calc.WAIC <- waic(stanfit)
calc.LOO  <- loo(extract_log_lik(stanfit))

messages.subject_clean: Understanding a very simple multi-logit model
messages.body_plain:
Howdy Oscar!

Your question is perfectly reasonable, but I think you'll have a better time working directly with the theta simplex and a Dirichlet prior. I attached a modified model.

The Dirichlet distribution is the conjugate prior for the categorical, so there are analytical solutions for this model (the posterior is also a Dirichlet distribution -- here's a pretty terse version of that): https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~stephentu/writeups/dirichlet-conjugate-prior.pdf

The neat thing about the Dirichlet prior is that the parameters correspond pretty closely (they're real numbers > 0, so not exactly...) to how many times you've seen each object before, and because it's conjugate we can get the posterior by simply updating these parameters with how many more samples we see.

The prior (pcounts) specified in the model says we've seen each object once. Mess around with this prior and see how your posterior estimates change and see if this makes more sense to you.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: Understanding a very simple multi-logit model
messages.subject_clean: Understanding a very simple multi-logit model
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ben,

Thanks for taking a look for me! I very much appreciate it.

Your model makes a lot of sense! And much more intuitive. I guess that while this solution is great for the problem I've posted, it's not so easy when you want to expand the model to have multiple predictors?

I see now that I really hadn't thought through the implications of the normal prior on beta. When the scale parameter of the prior is 5 (as in the model) it's placing quite a strong prior on theta values being near zero, with a smaller peak near 1. So the over fitting makes sense to me now.

And when the scale parameter of the normal prior gets smaller the more the density shifts to equal probabilities across outcomes. So I can probably aim for something sensible and then fit the models with a few different priors.

I wonder what the least informative prior would be for 6 outcomes?

All the best,

Oscar

On Friday, 28 April 2017 15:48:02 UTC+1, Ben B wrote:
> Howdy Oscar!
>
> Your question is perfectly reasonable, but I think you'll have a better time working directly with the theta simplex and a Dirichlet prior. I attached a modified model.
>
> The Dirichlet distribution is the conjugate prior for the categorical, so there are analytical solutions for this model (the posterior is also a Dirichlet distribution -- here's a pretty terse version of that): https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~stephentu/writeups/dirichlet-conjugate-prior.pdf
>
> The neat thing about the Dirichlet prior is that the parameters correspond pretty closely (they're real numbers > 0, so not exactly...) to how many times you've seen each object before, and because it's conjugate we can get the posterior by simply updating these parameters with how many more samples we see.
>
> The prior (pcounts) specified in the model says we've seen each object once. Mess around with this prior and see how your posterior estimates change and see if this makes more sense to you.
>
> Ben
>

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Polar coordinates
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Polar coordinates
messages.body_plain:
There's a chapter in the manual on circular statistics
that answers some of Ben B's and Kevin's questions.

The unit_vector[N] type puts you on the unit hypersphere in
N dimensions.  It uses N parameters despite there only
being (N - 1) degrees of freedom (there is no isomorphism from
R^(N-1) to the hypersphere as Michael points out).  Rather
than this being improper, it controls the extra parameter with
a latent normal distribution to make sure the result is uniform
over the unit vectors.  So you get the continuity bit of the
morphism, but not monotonicity in the metric (a point can be
more distant in R^N from another point and still be closer
in the transform to S^(N-1) [the hypersphere].

- Bob

> On Apr 27, 2017, at 3:52 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Don’t use polar coordinates.
>
> The problem is actually worse because the Jacobian
> is an infinite sum that can’t be calculated exactly.
>
>
>> On Apr 27, 2017, at 3:11 PM, Kevin Van Horn <ke...@ksvanhorn.com> wrote:
>>
>> When using polar coordinates, it is possible to turn a unimodal posterior into a bimodal posterior -- for example, if you have theta going from -pi to +pi, and the posterior distribution for theta overlaps the cutpoint at +/- pi. Is there any good way of dealing with this problem in Stan, other than "don't use polar coordinates"?

messages.body_plain:
If you put constraints on a parameter, you sample from the tail.
But as we keep trying to tell you, if it's Gaussian, you can
just calculate this quantity directly with the CDF functions.

parameters {
  real<lower=a, upper = b> a;

model {
  a ~ normal(0, 1);

What you get is the proper truncation here to a.  If rather than 0 and 1
you have non-data arguments to the normal, then you need to write something
like:

  a ~ normal(mu, sigma) T[a, b];

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
"Least informative" could mean a few different things I think. From the BDA3 book, page 69, the Dirichlet prior with all the alphas equal to 1 samples uniformly from all K-simplexes, so that means you're not favoring any set of probabilities over another one (the x dependence goes away in the pdf if all alphas == 1, make plots of the pdf of a 3-value Dirichlet distribution with various parameters to convince yourself of this).

I don't think it's a crime to put hyperpriors on your Dirichlet distribution either if that's the thing you aren't sure about. Google around for "multinomial dirichlet hyperprior" and you'll see folks talking about various things they've tried.

For the multiple predictors, you're moving into GLM territory I think. That's chapter 16 in BDA3, or check out the Rstanarm examples (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/rstanarm/vignettes/pooling.html).

Ben

messages.subject_clean: Reproducing "Circular Inference" model in Stan - Divergent iterations issue
messages.body_plain:
I don't know about the divergent iterations thing, but if you have a low neff and a high Rhat, it'd be a good idea to go look at the posterior distributions/traceplots.

You might look at the posterior distributions of each chain to make sure everything is converging to the same solution. Multimodal distributions could give these the Rhat/neff metrics trouble I think.

You might also look at pairplots for your parameters too see if things are really tightly correlated. Maybe there are identifiability issues that are giving the sampler problems (that could be addressed with some priors).

Do you have simulated data for this problem? Might also scale around the size of the data and see if anything changes if so.

messages.body_plain:
> On Apr 28, 2017, at 12:02 PM, Oscar <oscart...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi Ben,
>
> Thanks for taking a look for me! I very much appreciate it.
>
> Your model makes a lot of sense! And much more intuitive. I guess that while this solution is great for the problem I've posted, it's not so easy when you want to expand the model to have multiple predictors?
>
> I see now that I really hadn't thought through the implications of the normal prior on beta. When the scale parameter of the prior is 5 (as in the model) it's placing quite a strong prior on theta values being near zero, with a smaller peak near 1. So the over fitting makes sense to me now.

It's not overfitting so much as model misspecification.  If you
draw the parameters from the priors, then simulate data, you're
guaranteed to get proper coverage.

> And when the scale parameter of the normal prior gets smaller the more the density shifts to equal probabilities across outcomes. So I can probably aim for something sensible and then fit the models with a few different priors.

You should use whatever prior knowledge you actually have.

> I wonder what the least informative prior would be for 6 outcomes?

Ben Bales pointed out that the Dirichlet with unit vector is uniform.
That uniformity means you can just drop it from Stan if
you use a simplex.  But that uniformity is with respect to a particular
parameterization.  A prior that's uniform on one parameterization won't
be uniform on another, so you have to be careful about what you mean here.

For example, an improper uniform prior on log odds is nothing like
a uniform prior on the probabilities of getting an outcome.

- Bob

messages.subject: Words of wisdom from Bob: "It's not overfitting so much as model misspecification."
messages.subject_clean: Words of wisdom from Bob: "It's not overfitting so much as model misspecification."
messages.body_plain:
I love this slogan of Bob's . . . maybe it could be embroidered and hung on the wall:

"It's not overfitting so much as model misspecification."

So true.  If your model is correct, "overfitting" is impossible.  In its usual form, "overfitting" comes from using too weak of a prior distribution.

A

> On Apr 28, 2017, at 2:38 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
>
>> On Apr 28, 2017, at 12:02 PM, Oscar <oscart...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>
>> Hi Ben,
>>
>> Thanks for taking a look for me! I very much appreciate it.
>>
>> Your model makes a lot of sense! And much more intuitive. I guess that while this solution is great for the problem I've posted, it's not so easy when you want to expand the model to have multiple predictors?
>>
>> I see now that I really hadn't thought through the implications of the normal prior on beta. When the scale parameter of the prior is 5 (as in the model) it's placing quite a strong prior on theta values being near zero, with a smaller peak near 1. So the over fitting makes sense to me now.
>
> It's not overfitting so much as model misspecification.  If you
> draw the parameters from the priors, then simulate data, you're
> guaranteed to get proper coverage.
>
>> And when the scale parameter of the normal prior gets smaller the more the density shifts to equal probabilities across outcomes. So I can probably aim for something sensible and then fit the models with a few different priors.
>
> You should use whatever prior knowledge you actually have.
>
>> I wonder what the least informative prior would be for 6 outcomes?
>
> Ben Bales pointed out that the Dirichlet with unit vector is uniform.
> That uniformity means you can just drop it from Stan if
> you use a simplex.  But that uniformity is with respect to a particular
> parameterization.  A prior that's uniform on one parameterization won't
> be uniform on another, so you have to be careful about what you mean here.
>
> For example, an improper uniform prior on log odds is nothing like
> a uniform prior on the probabilities of getting an outcome.
>
> - Bob
>

Lots of things can go wrong, but when they do it should be apparent in the results. In this case, it shows up as lack of convergence. Thank you very much for your comment, Dr. Carpenter.

Instead of using multivariate truncated distribution, Is there anyway we could solve it through univariate truncated distributions (component-wise)? If it is inside NUTS then we have chains of 1D and maybe we can go through each one sequentially...

I highly appreciate your consideration.
Hamed

On Friday, April 28, 2017 at 2:22:03 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> No.  And we don't have multivariate CDFs, either.

>

>
> > On Apr 28, 2017, at 2:11 PM, Hamed Nikbakht <hamednik...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Dear Dr. Carpenter,
> >
> > Thank  you for your reply.

> >
> > Just one quick question, Can i apply it for multivariate normal distribution as well? because, the manual is saying "Truncation in Stan is restricted to univariate distributions..."
> >
> > Thanks a lot.
> > Hamed
> >
> > On Friday, April 28, 2017 at 1:16:02 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > If you put constraints on a parameter, you sample from the tail.
> > But as we keep trying to tell you, if it's Gaussian, you can
> > just calculate this quantity directly with the CDF functions.
> >
> > parameters {
> >   real<lower=a, upper = b> a;
> >
> > model {
> >   a ~ normal(0, 1);
> >
> > What you get is the proper truncation here to a.  If rather than 0 and 1
> > you have non-data arguments to the normal, then you need to write something

> > >
> > > Dear Dr. Carpenter,
> > >
> > > Thank you very much for your comment.
> > > I rewrite my question and I hope my question is understandable.
> > >
> > > If I go for the calculating expectation of I[g < 0] with respect to the Gaussian target distribution,
> > > Is there anyway i could directly involve the indicator function or the limit state function (g) into the Gaussian target distribution (Into model block of Stan, NOT as a post-processing step in generated quantities block)?
> > > The reason for doing that is to explore better/faster the failure region.
> > >
> > > I am interested in using this information (g) into my model to have efficient sampling from that failure region.
> > >
> > > Thanks a lot,
> > > Hamed
> > >
> > >
> > > On Thursday, April 27, 2017 at 1:47:26 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > > What do you mean by "likelihood function"  The model block?
> > >
> > > That generated quantities block can be simplified to
> > >
> > >   int I = sum(x) > 3 * sqrt(2);
> > >
> > > - Bob
> > >
> > >
> > > > On Apr 26, 2017, at 8:05 PM, Hamed Nikbakht <hamednik...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > >
> > > > In another case, If I will go for the calculating expectation of I[g < 0] with respect to the gaussian target distribution, Can i shift the likelihood function and center it on my limit state function (g)?
> > > > The reason for doing that is to explore better the failure region. if yes, Is the following Stan code correct?
> > > > mu is calculated from g = 0 which is mu = [3/sqrt(2), 3/sqrt(2)]
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > data {
> > > > real mu[2]
> > > > }
> > > >
> > > > parameters {
> > > >   vector[2] x;
> > > > }
> > > >
> > > > model {

> > > > }
> > > >

> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Thank you very much for your consideration.
> > > >
> > > > Hamed

> > > > On Wednesday, April 26, 2017 at 9:53:35 AM UTC-4, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> > > > Hamed,
> > > >
> > > > You are confusing the target distribution with the expectation that you want
> > > > to take.
> > > >
> > > > If you want to define the target distribution as being zero for g <= 0 then

> > > > constant.  There is discussion of this in the manual.  Note that outside of
> > > > one dimension, truncated distributions are hard to derive analytically.

> > > > On the other hand, it looks like you’re trying to compute the expectation

messages.body_plain:
Hamed,

No, you are not understanding how all of this works.
Probability can be very subtle and we highly encourage
you to work through the basics before trying to tackle
trickier problems like this.

If you want to sample from a truncated distribution
efficiently then you’ll have to evaluate the integral

\int_{invalid neighborhood(hyper params) d(params) pi(params, hyperparams)

analytically.  We can do this for univariate densities,
thence the discussion in the manual.  But we cannot
in general do this for multivariate densities, even if
your target is a truncated multivariate Gaussian.

The best you can hope for is that the truncating
boundary is a plane so that you can rotate your
system such that the truncation lies alone one
axis only and your and the integral analytically.
For nonlinear truncations the problem will in
general be intractable.

you to work through the basics before trying to tackle
trickier problems like this.

Dear Michael,

Thank you for getting back to me.

It was just a brainstorm and i understand sometimes it will be ended up some dumb questions. I'm sorry in this regard.

I thought maybe it is doable to break it to component-wise univariate truncated dist. and solve this multivariate normal dist. for univariate truncated ones sequentially. (something like Gibbs sampling).

Highly appreciate it.
Regards,
Hamed

> Probability can be very subtle and we highly encourage

> If you want to sample from a truncated distribution
> efficiently then you’ll have to evaluate the integral
>
> \int_{invalid neighborhood(hyper params) d(params) pi(params, hyperparams)

> in general do this for multivariate densities, even if
> your target is a truncated multivariate Gaussian.
>
> The best you can hope for is that the truncating
> boundary is a plane so that you can rotate your
> system such that the truncation lies alone one
> axis only and your and the integral analytically.
> For nonlinear truncations the problem will in
> general be intractable.

messages.subject: Re: Model comparison using a multilevel structure via Stan
messages.subject_clean: Model comparison using a multilevel structure via Stan
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Stan is sampling from the joint posterior distribution including betas. Using the obtained draws you can approximate the integration over betas. I recommend to read some introduction to Monte Carlo (and Markov chain Monte Carlo) methods to understand how Monte Carlo integration works.

Instead of using truncated importance sampling and WAIC as in the code you posted, we recommend using PSIS-LOO. If you are 100% certain that you need WAIC, you can get that using loo package, too.

Aki

On Friday, April 28, 2017 at 4:48:38 PM UTC+3, Marcelo Silva wrote:
> Hello dear professor,
>
> Let me know if I understood:
> (1) From what I've studied, I concluded that multilevel models need to have verisimilitude marginalized by random effects, such as the figure I've shown, by Fox (2010).
> (2) Despite the fact in (1), the likelihood in my Stan code is correct (although I do not consider integration over betas).
> (3) Integration over betas can be considered approximately by later predictive densities.
>
> So, from this code in the R, the WAIC and loo measurements would be being calculated from the posteriori predictive density and, therefore, considering the integration of betas, how do I want it?
>
> library(rstan)
> library(loo)
>
> waic <- function(stanfit){
>   log_lik <- extract (stanfit, "log_lik")$log_lik
>   dim(log_lik) <- if (length(dim(log_lik))==1) c(length(log_lik),1) else
>   c(dim(log_lik)[1], prod(dim(log_lik)[2:length(dim(log_lik))]))
>   S <- nrow(log_lik)
>   n <- ncol(log_lik)
>   lpd <- log(colMeans(exp(log_lik)))
>   p_waic <- colVars(log_lik)
>   elpd_waic <- lpd - p_waic
>   waic <- -2*elpd_waic
>   loo_weights_raw <- 1/exp(log_lik-max(log_lik))
>   loo_weights_normalized <- loo_weights_raw/
>   matrix(colMeans(loo_weights_raw),nrow=S,ncol=n,byrow=TRUE)
>   loo_weights_regularized <- pmin (loo_weights_normalized, sqrt(S))
>   elpd_loo <- log(colMeans(exp(log_lik)*loo_weights_regularized)/
>   colMeans(loo_weights_regularized))
>   p_loo <- lpd - elpd_loo
>   pointwise <- cbind(waic,lpd,p_waic,elpd_waic,p_loo,elpd_loo)
>   total <- colSums(pointwise)
>   se <- sqrt(n*colVars(pointwise))
>   return(list(waic=total["waic"], elpd_waic=total["elpd_waic"],
>   p_waic=total["p_waic"], elpd_loo=total["elpd_loo"], p_loo=total["p_loo"],
>   pointwise=pointwise, total=total, se=se))
> }
> ...
> stanfit <- stan(...)
> calc.WAIC <- waic(stanfit)
> calc.LOO  <- loo(extract_log_lik(stanfit))

messages.body_plain:
So if Einstein summation notation is what you want, and

A_skp * B_pgk -> C_sg

is what you need (multiplying and summing across k and p [I transposed your output also])

Then rearrange the B indices (call it B'):

A_skp * B'_kpg -> C_sg

Flatten the kp indices together into one new index (j) and call things matrices (Am, Bm):

Am_sj * Bm_jg -> C_sg

And that's just regular matrix multiplication I think.

Here's a little python snippet to play with:

import numpy

A = numpy.random.rand(3, 4, 5)
B = numpy.random.rand(4, 5, 3)

print numpy.einsum('ijk, jkl', A, B)

Am = A.reshape(3, 4 * 5)
Bm = B.reshape(4 * 5, 3)

print Am.dot(Bm)

Ben
